questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A male child presented with arthralgia and abdominal pain. On examination, there was palpable purpura over the lower limbs. There is a past history of upper respiratory tract infection prior to the onset of presenting symptoms. Which of the following is the treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucocorticoids

IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura) is a small-vessel vasculitis seen in children, typically following an upper respiratory infection, presenting with palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and possible renal involvement.

• Classic tetrad:
• Palpable purpura (non-thrombocytopenic, mainly lower limbs)
• Arthralgia/arthritis
• Abdominal pain
• Renal involvement (hematuria/proteinuria)

Treatment: Usually self-limiting; supportive care is mainstay. Glucocorticoids are used in moderate to severe cases (significant abdominal pain, renal involvement)

Why others are incorrect:

• Azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine are not first-line and used only in severe/refractory cases

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a neck swelling and laboratory results showing elevated T4 levels with suppressed TSH. He has a prior history of treatment with radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation. Which of the following is a likely adverse effect of this therapy?
questions.explanation: Radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation therapy is used to treat conditions like Graves' disease or toxic nodules by destroying thyroid tissue. The most common long-term side effect of this destruction is a progressive decline in thyroid hormone production, eventually resulting in hypothyroidism. Most patients who undergo this therapy will eventually require lifelong levothyroxine replacement. Acute Thyroiditis (Option A) is a transient inflammatory reaction that can occur early after treatment but is not a permanent side effect. Hyperthyroidism (Option C) might occur briefly during a "flare" phase as damaged cells release stored hormones, but it is not the intended long-term outcome. Thyroid Storm (Option D) is a rare, life-threatening crisis usually seen in untreated patients, not as a direct consequence of ablation therapy. Therefore, the destruction of the thyroid gland essentially trades hyperthyroidism for easily managed hypothyroidism
questions.learning: Radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation therapy is used to treat conditions like Graves' disease or toxic nodules by destroying thyroid tissue. The most common long-term side effect of this destruction is a progressive decline in thyroid hormone production,…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What are the components of attitude?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cognition, behavior, affective

Attitude is a learned predisposition to respond consistently toward an object, person, or situation. It comprises three interrelated components, collectively known as the ABC model of attitude:

• Affective: Feelings or emotions toward an object (e.g., liking or disliking vaccination).
• Behavioral: The tendency or intention to act in a particular way (e.g., getting vaccinated).
• Cognitive: Knowledge, beliefs, or thoughts about the object (e.g., believing vaccines prevent disease).

Why not the other options?

• B. Affective, responsive, social: “Responsive” and “social” are not recognized components of attitude.
• C. Knowledge, income status, education: Income and education are determinants, not components of attitude.
• D. Social, confidence, knowledge: Social and confidence are not core components of the ABC model.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden, severe headache unlike any previous episodes, accompanied by elevated blood pressure and nuchal rigidity on examination. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's description of a "worst headache of their life" (thunderclap headache) combined with nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness) is the classic clinical presentation of a Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH). The accompanying NCCT brain image provides definitive evidence, showing hyperdense (bright white) areas in the basal cisterns, Sylvian fissures, and sulci, representing acute blood in the subarachnoid space. Cluster headache (Option A) causes excruciating unilateral orbital pain but would not cause nuchal rigidity or CT findings. Encephalitis (Option C) and Meningitis (Option D) can cause headache and nuchal rigidity (signs of meningism), but they would typically be accompanied by fever and would not show acute intracranial blood on a CT scan. SAH is most commonly caused by a ruptured berry aneurysm and is a neurosurgical emergency. Therefore, based on the pathognomonic "thunderclap" history and the bright blood visible on CT, SAH is the diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient's description of a "worst headache of their life" (thunderclap headache) combined with nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness) is the classic clinical presentation of a Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is an X-linked disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Color blindness

Color blindness is primarily inherited as an X-linked recessive trait. The genes for color vision are located on the X chromosome.

Males have a single X chromosome inherited from mothers. If the X chromosome inherited carries a mutation, males exhibit the disease. However, females become carriers of the color blindness gene and have a 50% chance of passing it on to their children.

Female carriers usually are protected because of the random inactivation of one X chromosome. But there is a possibility that the mutant X chromosome remains active if the normal alleles are inactivated in some of the cells so the heterozygous female can express the disorder partially.

The image shows the pattern of X-linked inheritance:

In color blindness, the mechanism to appreciate one or more primary colors is either defective (anomalous) or absent (anopia). It may be congenital or acquired. Congenital color blindness can be dyschromatopsia (defective color vision of any one of the RGB colors) or achromatopsia (complete color blindness of all three RGB colors). RGB colors are red, green, and blue.

Tests for color blindness include the Ishihara test, Hardy–Rand–Rittler test, and Farnsworth–Munsell 100-hue test.
questions.learning: Color blindness Color blindness is primarily inherited as an X-linked recessive trait. The genes for color vision are located on the X chromosome.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When the fetal scalp becomes visible at the vulva, the maneuver performed to control delivery of the head and prevent perineal tears is the Ritgen’s maneuver.
questions.explanation: The image depicts the Ritgen maneuver, a clinical technique used during the second stage of labor when the fetal scalp is visible at the vulva (crowning). The clinician applies pressure through the perineum onto the fetal chin with one hand while the other hand controls the crowning vertex. The primary objective is to facilitate the slow, controlled delivery of the fetal head in a state of extension, thereby minimizing the risk of severe perineal tears. By ensuring the head emerges during the interval between contractions, the maneuver protects the maternal pelvic floor. Loveset’s maneuver (Option B) is used for delivering the arms in a breech presentation. Pinard maneuver (Option C) is utilized to bring down a leg in a frank breech. The Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit maneuver (Option D) is employed for the delivery of the after-coming head in breech. Therefore, given the visual of head crowning and the specific protective hand placement shown, Ritgen maneuver is the correct identification for this obstetric procedure
questions.learning: The image depicts the Ritgen maneuver, a clinical technique used during the second stage of labor when the fetal scalp is visible at the vulva (crowning).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with altered sensation in the extremities and impaired coordination. On examination, the pupillary light reflex is absent, but the accommodation reflex is intact. Which condition is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of absent pupillary light reaction in the presence of a preserved accommodation reaction is known as light-near dissociation. This specific sign is classically called the Argyll Robertson pupil. It is the pathognomonic ocular hallmark of late-stage Neurosyphilis (Tabes Dorsalis), which also explains the patient's symptoms of altered sensation and coordination (sensory ataxia). The lesion is thought to involve the pretectal nucleus in the midbrain, sparing the more ventral fibers involved in the near reflex. Horner's syndrome (Option B) presents with miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis, but the light reflex remains intact. Papilledema (Option C) involves bilateral optic disc swelling due to increased intracranial pressure. Optic Neuritis (Option D) causes sudden vision loss and a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD), but both the light and near reflexes are typically impacted relative to the visual deficit. Diagnosis of neurosyphilis is confirmed by positive CSF-VDRL testing. Early treatment with intravenous penicillin is mandatory to halt neurological progression
questions.learning: The clinical combination of absent pupillary light reaction in the presence of a preserved accommodation reaction is known as light-near dissociation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 24-year-old male is brought to the ER after he was hit by a motorbike while he was crossing the road. He sustained injuries over his abdomen with visible bruising. His blood pressure is 88/60 and IV fluids are immediately instituted. A FAST was done and it was positive. Which of the following is the next step in the management of this patient? FAST: (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exploratory laparatomy

The clinical vignette describes a case of blunt abdominal injury. In hemodynamically unstable patients with FAST positive, the next step of management is exploratory laparotomy.

Blunt abdominal injury:

Primary assessment (i.e the primary survey) follows the ABCDE pattern: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability (neurologic status), and Exposure. It is crucial to realize that the absence of abdominal pain or tenderness does not rule out the presence of significant intra-abdominal injury.

The following signs strongly correlate with intraabdominal injury

* Seatbelt sign

* Rebound tenderness

* Hypotension

* Abdominal distension

* Abdominal guarding

* Concomitant femur fracture

The management is as detailed in the protocol given below:

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following vasculitis does not involve medium-sized arteries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis

Vasculitides are classified according to the predominant size of the blood vessels involved. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis, whereas Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) and Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) primarily involve medium-sized arteries, and Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) predominantly affects small vessels but may occasionally involve medium-sized arteries.

• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is an immune complex– mediated small-vessel vasculitis involving postcapillary venules, characterized histologically by neutrophilic infiltration with leukocytoclasia (nuclear debris) and palpable purpura.

Key vessel involvement:

• PAN → Medium-sized muscular arteries (spares pulmonary arteries)
• Buerger disease → Small- and medium-sized arteries and veins of the extremities
• GPA → Predominantly small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles), but medium arteries may also be involved
• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis → Small vessels only

| Vessel size | Entities

| ----------- | --------

| Large | Takayasu, GCA

| Medium | PAN, Kawasaki

| Small — ANCA-associated | GPA, MPA, EGPA

| Small — immune complex | Cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, IgA vasculitis (HSP), cryoglobulinaemic, anti-GBM, hypocomplementaemic urticarial

| Variable vessel | Behçet, Cogan

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient involved in a road traffic accident is assessed and found to have a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10. Based on this score, how would the severity of the head injury be classified?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the universal clinical tool used to categorize the severity of traumatic brain injuries (TBI). Head injuries are classified based on the following total GCS scores: 1. GCS 13–15: Mild TBI (Option D) or Minor TBI (Option C) 2. GCS 9–12: Moderate TBI (Option A) 3. GCS 3–8: Severe TBI (Option B) A score of 10 falls clearly within the intermediate range. Patients with a moderate TBI are typically conscious but often confused or lethargic and may have significant neurological deficits. They require urgent CT imaging and close monitoring, as they are at risk for secondary brain injury or deterioration into the "severe" category. Therefore, based on the standardized GCS-severity scale, a patient with a score of 10 is definitively classified as having a moderate traumatic brain injury

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the maneuver shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ritgen’s manoeuvre

The above image depicts Ritgen’s manoeuvre, a technique used during the second stage of labor to assist in the controlled delivery of the fetal head, reducing the risk of perineal tears and trauma.

Steps in Ritgen’s Maneuver:

* The right hand is draped with a sterile towel.

* The fingers of the right hand pressing posterior to the rectum exerts upward pressure to the chin and extends the head. The extension of the head prevents the head from slipping back in between the contractions.

* The left hand placed over the occiput exerts a downward counterpressure to prevent the rapid extension of the head

* The ritgen’s manoeuvre thus helps in the controlled delivery of the head of the fetus.

Other options:

Option B: Pinard’s manoeuvre is used to facilitate the delivery of legs in case of frank breech presentation.

Option C: Lovset’s manoeuvre is used to facilitate the delivery of arms in breech presentation.

Option D: In Zavanelli maneuver is an obstetric procedure used as a last-resort technique during shoulder dystocia when other manoeuvres fail to deliver the baby vaginally. The fetal head is rotated to the pre-restitution position and pushed back into the pelvis to perform an emergency cesarean section.
questions.learning: Ritgen’s manoeuvre — The above image depicts Ritgen’s manoeuvre, a technique used during the second stage of labor to assist in the controlled delivery of the fetal head, reducing the risk of perineal tears and trauma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the most effective indicator for assessing the overall disease burden?
questions.explanation: The Disability Adjusted Life Year (DALY) is a composite time-based measure that combines years of life lost due to premature mortality (YLL) and years lived with a disability (YLD). It is widely considered the most effective indicator for assessing the global burden of disease because it quantifies the "gap" between current health status and an ideal health situation where the entire population lives to an advanced age, free of disease and disability. Quality-adjusted life years (QALY, Option A) are primarily used in cost-utility analysis to measure the quality and quantity of life gained from an intervention. Health adjusted life expectancy (HALE, Option B) estimates the number of years a person can expect to live in "full health". Disability-free life expectancy (DFLE, Option D) measures the remaining years of life spent without any functional limitations. DALY stands out because it captures both fatal and non-fatal health outcomes in a single metric, allowing for a comprehensive comparison across different diseases and populations
questions.learning: The Disability Adjusted Life Year (DALY) is a composite time-based measure that combines years of life lost due to premature mortality (YLL) and years lived with a disability (YLD).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is ECG change associated with the use of anti-tubercular drug bedaquiline?
questions.explanation: Bedaquiline is a critical newer drug used in the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Its most significant and life-threatening adverse effect is QT interval prolongation on the ECG. This prolongation increases the risk of Torsades de Pointes, a potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmia. PR interval prolongation (Option B) relates to AV block. QRS widening (Option C) occurs with bundle branch blocks or hyperkalemia. ST-segment elevation (Option D) is the hallmark of acute myocardial infarction. Because of this risk, patients on bedaquiline must undergo regular ECG monitoring, especially if they are also taking other QT-prolonging drugs like moxifloxacin or clofazimine. Clinicians must be prepared to stop the medication if the QTc exceeds . This pharmacological safety requirement is a major focus in MDR-TB clinics to ensure that the benefits of treatment outweigh the cardiac risks
questions.learning: Bedaquiline is a critical newer drug used in the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Its most significant and life-threatening adverse effect is QT interval prolongation on the ECG.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A child involved in a train accident presents with stable vital signs but has a large laceration on the leg. Under disaster triage principles, which triage category does this patient fall into?
questions.explanation: In disaster triage systems, the Yellow category represents "Delayed" care. This is assigned to patients who have significant injuries but are hemodynamically stable. In this case, the child has stable vitals (no immediate life threat) but a "big laceration" that requires surgical repair and medical attention, making them a priority after the most critical cases are handled. The Red category (Option A) is for "Immediate" life-threatening emergencies like airway obstruction. Green (Option C) is for the "walking wounded" with minor cuts or sprains. The Black category (Option D) is for the deceased or those with injuries incompatible with survival. Since the child is stable but has a serious wound needing hospital care, Yellow is the appropriate classification for prioritizing treatment in a mass casualty event
questions.learning: In disaster triage systems, the Yellow category represents "Delayed" care. This is assigned to patients who have significant injuries but are hemodynamically stable.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Erythropoietin is produced by:

1. Kidney
2. Liver
3. Spleen
4. Lungs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1,2

Erythropoietin is produced mainly by kidney and liver.

In adults, approximately 85% of erythropoietin is produced by the kidneys, while 15% is synthesized by the liver. Both of these organs possess the mRNA necessary for erythropoietin production. Although erythropoietin can be found in the spleen and salivary glands, these tissues lack the mRNA required for its synthesis, indicating that they do not produce the hormone.

Erythropoietin is secreted by interstitial cells in the peri-tubular capillary bed of the kidneys and by perivenous hepatocytes in the liver. It is also generated in the brain, where it provides a safeguarding effect against excitotoxic harm caused by hypoxia; and in the uterus and oviducts, where it is stimulated by estrogen and seems to facilitate estrogen-driven angiogenesis.
questions.learning: 1,2 Erythropoietin is produced mainly by kidney and liver. In adults, approximately 85% of erythropoietin is produced by the kidneys, while 15% is synthesized by the liver.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A specific class of medications targets the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-alpha) to modulate lipid metabolism. Identify the drug that is known for its ability to activate PPAR-alpha?
questions.explanation: Gemfibrozil belongs to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering drugs. The mechanism of action for all fibrates is the activation of the nuclear receptor PPAR-alpha. Upon activation, PPAR-alpha increases the transcription of several genes involved in lipid metabolism, most notably increasing the expression of Lipoprotein Lipase (LPL). This leads to a profound decrease in serum triglyceride levels and a modest increase in HDL ("good") cholesterol. Ezetimibe (Option B) works by inhibiting cholesterol absorption in the small intestine. Colestipol (Option C) is a bile acid sequestrant that prevents the reabsorption of bile acids. Simvastatin (Option D) is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) that blocks endogenous cholesterol synthesis. Fibrates like gemfibrozil are the first-line treatment for severe hypertriglyceridemia, which is a major risk factor for acute pancreatitis. Clinicians must monitor for muscle toxicity, especially when fibrates are used in combination with statins. This specific molecular target is a fundamental concept in cardiovascular pharmacology
questions.learning: Gemfibrozil belongs to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering drugs. The mechanism of action for all fibrates is the activation of the nuclear receptor PPAR-alpha.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old man presents with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain, constipation for one day, persistent hiccups, and occasional episodes of vomiting. An abdominal X-ray has been performed. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The abdominal X-ray shows a classic "coffee bean" sign or "omega loop," which is pathognomonic for sigmoid volvulus. This occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on its mesentery, causing a high-grade mechanical obstruction. Clinical features like absolute constipation and persistent hiccups (due to diaphragmatic irritation from massive distension) further support this diagnosis. Caecal volvulus (Option B) typically presents with a "comma" or kidney-shaped loop in the right or central abdomen. Intussusception (Option C) is more common in children and usually presents with a "target sign" on ultrasound rather than massive dilation on X-ray. Dynamic obstruction (Option D) refers to functional or paralytic ileus where the bowel is not mechanically twisted. Initial treatment for a stable sigmoid volvulus is sigmoidoscopic detorsion
questions.learning: The abdominal X-ray shows a classic "coffee bean" sign or "omega loop," which is pathognomonic for sigmoid volvulus. This occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on its mesentery, causing a high-grade mechanical obstruction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A diabetic patient came with the complaint of pedal edema due to congestive heart failure and was prescribed a medication that is preferred in the setting of cardiac and renal failure. What is the drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SGLT-2 inhibitor

In this case, a diabetic patient with cardiac and renal failure is started on a suitable medication. The drug is likely an sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor.

SGLT-2 inhibitors include canafliflozen, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin. They act by inhibiting the SGLT-2 transporter which is present on the proximal segment of the renal tubule. It is responsible for the reabsorption of 80-90% of filtered glucose. It inhibits glucose reabsorption resulting in glycosuria and a change in the renal threshold.

SGLT2 inhibitors can lower blood pressure and cause a slight decrease in body weight. Drugs like empagliflozin and canagliflozin are found to reduce major cardiovascular events. SGLT2 inhibitors also exhibit a known nephro-protective effect.

The common side effects include urinary tract infections and genital mycotic infections due to the high glucose content of the urine. There is a risk of the development of diabetic ketoacidosis. It increases the risk of fractures and lower limb amputations due to the creation of an imbalance with the minerals and circulating parathormone and vitamin D.

Other options :

Option A:  Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor. It reduces the intestinal absorption of glucose by inhibiting the intestinal brush border enzyme, alpha-glucosidase. These drugs also increase GLP-1 levels in circulation. They reduce post-prandial glucose levels.

Option C: Linagliptin is a dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor. It is used in type 2 diabetes as monotherapy or in combination therapy when metformin is not tolerated or contraindicated. It binds extensively to plasma proteins and is cleared primarily by the hepatobiliary system. Hence, no dosage adjustment is needed in renal failure. Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors enhance the release of insulin postprandially, decrease glucagon, and thereby lower mealtime as well as fasting glucose. They are weight-neutral.

Option D: Liraglutide is also a GLP-1 receptor agonist and is given only in the subcutaneous injectable form. It was recently approved for the treatment of obesity.
questions.learning: SGLT-2 inhibitor — In this case, a diabetic patient with cardiac and renal failure is started on a suitable medication. The drug is likely an sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with a severe, sudden-onset, throbbing headache and double vision for the past 30 minutes. She has a history of migraine and reports frequent headaches. She has not had her period for several months. On examination, her blood pressure is 95/61 mm Hg, and visual field testing reveals decreased visual acuity and loss of peripheral vision in both eyes. MRI of brain is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pituitary apoplexy

Key clues:

• 42-year-old woman
• Sudden severe throbbing headache
• Loss of peripheral vision in both eyes → bitemporal hemianopia
• MRI shows a sellar/suprasellar mass
• Hypotensive (95/61 mmHg)

👉 Acute hemorrhage/infarction into a pituitary adenoma. Diagnosis: Pituitary apoplexy

Pituitary apoplexy = Acute hemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary tumor.

• It is a neurosurgical and endocrine emergency requiring urgent steroids and decompression.

Classic presentation:

• Sudden severe headache
• Visual field defects (optic chiasm compression → bitemporal hemianopia)
• Hypotension (acute ACTH deficiency → adrenal crisis)
• The MRI image shows a sellar mass consistent with this.

Transient ischemic attack:

• DOES NOT cause chiasmal compression pattern.
• Does not show sellar mass on MRI.

Sheehan syndrome:

• Postpartum pituitary infarction.
• No obstetric history here.

Migraine with aura: Can cause visual symptoms but: No chiasmal defect, No hypotension, No sellar mass

TAKEAWAY:

Sudden worst headache + bitemporal hemianopia + hypotension = Think pituitary apoplexy

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presented with recurrent URTI, poor growth, high-arched palate, and impaired hearing. Tympanogram is given as follows. What would be the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

The given clinical scenario along with type B tympanometry curve is suggestive of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion would be the most appropriate management.

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, rhinolalia clausa, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Adenoid facies, characterized by an elongated face, open mouth, teeth crowding, high arched hard palate, and pinched-in nose, may also be present.

Serous otitis media also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, tumors of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections).

Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild ear aches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

• Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex
• Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus
• Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss and audiometry reveals hearing loss in the range of 20–40 dB. The fluid accumulation in glue ear causes decreased mobility (compliance) of the tympanic membrane leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve or type B curve on a tympanogram.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

• Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.
• Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion — The given clinical scenario along with type B tympanometry curve is suggestive of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old farmer working in rodent-infested rice fields presents with fever, conjunctival suffusion, and signs of liver failure. Which stage of the disease does this presentation correspond to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Weil's disease

Weil’s disease, the severe immune phase of leptospirosis, characterized by high fever, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, acute kidney injury, hemorrhagic manifestations, and hepatic dysfunction. It occurs after exposure to water or soil contaminated with the urine of infected animals, especially rats, making farmers, sewage workers, and veterinarians high-risk groups.

Why not the other options?

• A. Leptospirosis: Refers to the overall infection caused by Leptospira interrogans; the severe icteric form is specifically called Weil’s disease.
• C. Convalescent stage: Recovery phase with resolution of symptoms; not associated with acute liver failure.
• D. Weil–Felix: An agglutination test used for the diagnosis of rickettsial infections, unrelated to leptospirosis.
questions.learning: Weil's disease Weil’s disease, the severe immune phase of leptospirosis, characterized by high fever, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, acute kidney injury, hemorrhagic manifestations, and hepatic dysfunction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following forms the lateral boundary of the anatomical snuff box?
options: Extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus
Extensor pollicis longus and abductor pollicis brevis
Extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Abductor pollicis longus and abductor pollicis brevis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus

The lateral boundary of the anatomical snuff box is formed by extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus.

Boundaries of the anatomical snuffbox:

• Lateral wall:

• Abductor pollicis longus (APL)
• Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)

• Medial wall:

• Extensor pollicis longus (EPL)

• Roof:

• Cephalic vein
• Superficial branch of the radial nerve

• Floor:

• Radial styloid, scaphoid, trapezium, and 1st metacarpal

Only content: Radial artery
questions.learning: Extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus The lateral boundary of the anatomical snuff box is formed by extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient with an acute ischemic stroke is planned for thrombolytic therapy using alteplase. The patient weighs 80 kg. What is the appropriate immediate (stat) dose of alteplase for this patient?
questions.explanation: The standard protocol for intravenous thrombolysis in acute ischemic stroke using Alteplase (rt-PA) is a total dose of of body weight, with a maximum dose of . For a patient weighing 80 kg, the total dose would be . The protocol dictates that 10% of this total dose must be administered as an immediate (stat) intravenous bolus over 1 minute. Therefore, the bolus dose is . Among the provided options, 8 (Option A) is the closest standard dose increment. The remaining 90% (64.8 mg) is then infused over the next 60 minutes. Options B (10), C (12), and D (15) exceed the required 10% bolus dose for this patient. Accurate dosing is critical to achieve effective clot dissolution while minimizing the severe risk of intracerebral hemorrhage. Thrombolysis must be initiated as early as possible, typically within a 4.5-hour "golden hour" window from the onset of stroke symptoms, provided that a non-contrast CT head has ruled out intracranial hemorrhage

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not involved in the repair of DNA following double-stranded breaks?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MSH2

MSH2 is involved in mismatch repair and is not involved in the repair of double-stranded DNA breaks as the repair involves the correction of a single mismatch base pair e.g. C to A, instead of T to A.

DNA mismatch repair proteins function as spell checkers during DNA replication by correcting the incorrect pairing. In HNPCC, the proofreading function of the mismatch repair systems (majorly MLH1 and MSH2) is lost, leading to the accumulation of errors throughout the genome. The genomes of these patients show microsatellite instability, which is characterized by changes in the length of short repeats.

Double-strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA pose a significant concern.  Genetic recombination events can give rise to chromosomal translocation, chromosomal breakage, and ultimately cellular demise. Double-strand breaks (DSBs) have the potential to undergo repair through two distinct mechanisms: homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining. Homologous recombination is observed in yeasts, whereas in mammals, non-homologous end joining predominates.

Non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) is a mechanism by which a group of proteins mediates the recognition, processing, and direct ligation of the ends of two DNA fragments where a double-strand break in DNA has occurred. This is in contrast to homologous repair (HR), another mechanism, where an undamaged homologous DNA template is required to replace an adjacent damaged one.

The type of repair depends on the phase of cell cycles:

Phase of the cell cycle
Repair mechanism

G0 /G1 Phase
Nonhomologous End Joining Repair

S, G2, M Phase
Homologous Repair

Other options:

Option A: The protein known as ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) serves as a crucial kinase that triggers a wide range of cellular stress responses through its signalling activity. The activation of ATM is induced by DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and oxidative stress, resulting in the phosphorylation of a wide range of target proteins. Recent advancements in molecular biology have brought to light the participation of the ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) protein in a range of cellular mechanisms triggered by DNA damage. These mechanisms encompass the repair of double-strand breaks (DSBs), the halting of cell cycle progression through checkpoint activation, the initiation of programmed cell death (apoptosis), and the cessation of transcriptional activity. The compromised precision of repair resulting from the combinational failure of stress responses leads to heightened sensitivity to ionizing radiation (IR) in ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) cells.

Option B: CtIP which is a DNA repair protein involved in Homologous Repair whose function is dependent on phosphorylation at serine 327 as well as the recruitment of BRCA 1.

Option D: The Ku heterodimer, consisting of Ku70 and Ku80 subunits, plays a pivotal role in the nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) pathway, which is responsible for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). Ku protein mediates the binding of the damaged DNA fragment and orchestrates the recruitment of additional proteins to enable the subsequent processing and ligation of the broken DNA end.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A full-term baby born with birth weight of 2000 g comes for well-baby visit at two months of age. Which of the following nutritional supplements would you advise?
options: Vitamin D orally 200 IU/day up to 3 months of age
Vitamin D orally 200 IU/day up to 1 year of age
Iron orally 2 mg/kg/day up to 3 months of age
Iron orally 2 mg/kg/day up to 1 year of age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Iron orally 2 mg/kg/day up to 1 year of age

Low birth weight (LBW) infants (<2500 g) are at increased risk of iron deficiency due to lower iron stores at birth. Term LBW infants should receive oral iron supplementation (2 mg/kg/day) starting at 2 months of age and continued up to 1 year of age to prevent iron deficiency anemia.

Why not the other options?

• A. Vitamin D orally 200 IU/day up to 3 months of age & B. Vitamin D orally 200 IU/day up to 1 year of age: Vitamin D supplementation is recommended at 400 IU/day, not 200 IU/day.
• C. Iron orally 2 mg/kg/day up to 3 months of age: Iron should be continued up to 1 year, not stopped at 3 months.
questions.learning: Iron orally 2 mg/kg/day up to 1 year of age Low birth weight (LBW) infants (<2500 g) are at increased risk of iron deficiency due to lower iron stores at birth.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman with a history of dilation and curettage (D&C) presents with amenorrhea. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) shows a characteristic honeycomb appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Asherman syndrome involves the formation of intrauterine adhesions (synechiae), most commonly following excessive curettage during a dilation and curettage (D&C) procedure for pregnancy-related events. These adhesions obliterate the uterine cavity, leading to amenorrhea (secondary) and infertility despite normal ovulation. The diagnostic hallmark on Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) is the visualization of multiple irregular filling defects, described as a "honeycomb appearance" or "shredded appearance" . Kallman syndrome (Option B) involves anosmia and low gonadotropins. Sheehan syndrome (Option C) is pituitary necrosis following postpartum hemorrhage, causing a global lack of pituitary hormones. Stein-Leventhal syndrome (Option D) is the classic name for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS), which presents with irregular cycles rather than total amenorrhea following a procedure. Treatment for Asherman’s requires hysteroscopic adhesiolysis followed by hormonal therapy to regenerate the endometrium. Therefore, the procedural history and HSG finding confirm the diagnosis
questions.learning: Asherman syndrome involves the formation of intrauterine adhesions (synechiae), most commonly following excessive curettage during a dilation and curettage (D&C) procedure for pregnancy-related events.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following methods is not effective against preventing the spread of COVID 19?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1% glutaraldehyde

1% glutaraldehyde is not effective against preventing the spread of COVID 19.

Effective everyday practices that prevent the spread include actions like keeping a social distance (at least 6 feet) from others, washing your hands with soap and water for 20 seconds or using a hand sanitizer with at least 70% alcohol, and wearing a face mask when you have to go out in public.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presented to a surgical emergency with complaints of severe epigastric pain for 1 day. On examination, HR was 120/min and BP was 100/60 mm Hg. On palpation, there is tenderness, guarding and rigidity. What is the probable cause of the condition shown in the X-ray below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hollow viscus perforation

The clinical scenario of hypotension and tachycardia with abdominal tenderness, guarding and rigidity with free air under the diaphragm in X-ray is indicative of hollow viscus perforation.

Acute abdomen is a common surgical emergency. Common causes include appendicitis, hollow viscus perforation, cholecystitis, and pancreatitis. An erect abdominal X-ray is commonly done as the first investigation. Free air under the diaphragm can result from hollow viscus perforation including Gastric, duodenal, small bowel and large bowel perforations.

Causes of hollow viscus perforation are blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, infections(TB, typhoid, Crohn's), corrosive agents etc.

Clinical features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Features of septic shock can be seen at later stages.

Investigations include estimation of the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel suggestive of paralytic ileus. However, CECT is the most sensitive investigation to detect minimal/ suspected pneumoperitoneum.

Management of a hollow viscous perforation mainly includes resuscitation, analgesics, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency exploratory laparotomy.

Other options: None of the other options have free air under the diaphragm.

Option A: Acute cholecystitis presents with pain in the right upper quadrant with fever and nausea. They may have tenderness and guarding. Rigidity is uncommon. Additionally, free air under the diaphragm may be seen in cases of gall bladder perforation only.

Option B: Sigmoid volvulus shows a large, dilated loop of the colon, often with a few air-fluid levels. Specific signs include the coffee bean sign and the absence of rectal gas. On the x-ray abdomen, the apex of the sigmoid volvulus extends towards the right upper quadrant and the haustrations are usually lost.

Option D: In small bowel obstruction, the obstructed bowel loops are centrally located and lie transversely. In cases of jejunal obstruction, valvulae conniventes, which are mucosal folds that span the entire diameter of the bowel, create a ladder effect. Additionally, a distended cecum may exhibit a gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.
questions.learning: Hollow viscus perforation — The clinical scenario of hypotension and tachycardia with abdominal tenderness, guarding and rigidity with free air under the diaphragm in X-ray is indicative of hollow viscus perforation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old unvaccinated child presents with fever, rash, and Bitot spots. What is the most appropriate line of management in this case?
questions.explanation: The presence of a maculopapular rash and fever in an unvaccinated child suggests an active measles infection, while Bitot spots (keratinized patches on the conjunctiva) indicate severe concurrent Vitamin A deficiency. In cases of measles, Vitamin A supplementation is the critical intervention required to reduce morbidity and prevent blindness. The Measles vaccine (Option A and B) is not useful once the child is already symptomatic, as the infection itself will provide lifelong natural immunity. While general supportive care (Option D) is necessary for managing symptoms like fever, it does not address the specific and urgent need for Vitamin A in a child with ocular signs of deficiency. Therefore, the priority management focuses exclusively on high-dose Vitamin A to stabilize the corneal surface and support recovery from the viral insult
questions.learning: The presence of a maculopapular rash and fever in an unvaccinated child suggests an active measles infection, while Bitot spots (keratinized patches on the conjunctiva) indicate severe concurrent Vitamin A deficiency.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which contrast agent is safe in a patient with renal failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. USG contrast agents

USG contrast agents, such as SONOVUE (sulfur hexafluoride microbubbles), are the only contrast agents safe for use in patients with renal failure, as they are excreted via the lungs and do not rely on renal clearance.

Composition: Microbubbles (gas-filled)

Excretion:

• Eliminated via lungs (exhaled air)
• NOT dependent on kidneys

So: No renal burden → safe in renal failure

| Contrast Type | Modality | Risk in Renal Failure

| ------------- | -------- | ---------------------

| USG contrast | Ultrasound | ✅ SAFE

| MRI contrast (Gadolinium) | MRI | NSF risk

| Iodinated contrast | CT | ❌ Contrast nephropathy
questions.learning: USG contrast agents USG contrast agents, such as SONOVUE (sulfur hexafluoride microbubbles), are the only contrast agents safe for use in patients with renal failure, as they are excreted via the lungs and do not rely on renal clearance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Marked structure is connected to which part of basal nuclei?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Corpus striatum

The correct answer is Corpus striatum.

The marked structure is the substantia nigra, which is connected to the corpus striatum (caudate + putamen) via the nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway, essential for motor control.

Degeneration of this pathway leads to Parkinson disease.

Thalamus and subthalamic nucleus are relay/modulatory nuclei, while globus pallidum is an output nucleus, not the primary nigral connection.
questions.learning: Corpus striatum — The correct answer is Corpus striatum. The marked structure is the substantia nigra, which is connected to the corpus striatum (caudate + putamen) via the nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway, essential for motor control.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old female complains of foul-smelling vaginal discharge. A giemsa stained smear of the discharge is shown below. Which of the following is not seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Curdy white discharge

The image shows Trichomonas vaginalis and infection causes a frothy, greenish-yellow discharge. Curdy white discharge is seen in vaginal candidiasis.

Trichomonas is a protozoan that’s slightly larger than a leucocyte with four anterior flagella and a single posterior flagellum. It exhibits jerky or twitching motility.

Infection of the female genital tract causes the following symptoms:

* Foul-smelling, frothy, greenish-yellow discharge per vaginum

* Itching around the vulva

* Dysuria and frequent micturition

The vagina looks red and inflamed. The inflamed cervix looks like a strawberry with punctate hemorrhagic spots.

The condition is treated with a single 2 gm dose of metronidazole or tinidazole. The female’s partner must also be treated simultaneously.
questions.learning: Curdy white discharge — The image shows Trichomonas vaginalis and infection causes a frothy, greenish-yellow discharge. Curdy white discharge is seen in vaginal candidiasis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Mention the purpose of the instrument shown below in the image:
options: To differentiate between chronic inversion and fibroid polyp
It is used to diagnose cervical stenosis
It is used in Fallopian tube recanalization
It is used to measure the uterine cavity and the cervical length
questions.explanation: The instrument shown in the image is a uterine sound. This is a graduated, flexible or rigid metal probe with a bulbous tip. Its primary clinical purpose is to measure the depth of the uterine cavity and the length of the cervical canal (Option D). This measurement is essential before procedures like IUD insertion, dilatation and curettage, or hysterosalpingography to ensure safety and proper device placement. Uterine sounding can also help determine the position (anteversion/retroversion) of the uterus. While it can be used to differentiate between a fibroid polyp and chronic inversion (Option A) by checking the depth of the fornix, its most common and fundamental use is measuring cavity length. It is not a primary tool for diagnosing stenosis (Option B) or recanalizing fallopian tubes (Option C). Therefore, measuring uterine depth is the definitive functional identification for this tool
questions.learning: The instrument shown in the image is a uterine sound. This is a graduated, flexible or rigid metal probe with a bulbous tip.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the function of utricle and saccule?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Linear acceleration

The function of utricle and saccule is linear acceleration.

Utricle and saccule which contain sensory epithelium called macula that are stimulated by linear acceleration and deceleration or gravitational pull during the head tilts.

The ampullated end of each semicircular canal contains a thickened ridge of neuroepithelium called crista ampullaris that respond to angular acceleration and deceleration.

Hearing is mediated by the organ of Corti on the basilar membrane of the inner ear.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: Consider the following regarding salicylate poisoning: I. Arterial pH of 7.25, anion gap of 18 mmol/L II. Arterial pH of 7.25, anion gap of 10 mmol/L III. pCO₂ of 20 mmHg IV. pCO₂ of 48 mmHg Which disturbance is likely to be encountered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I and III

Salicylate (aspirin) poisoning produces a mixed acid-base disorder. Initially, salicylates stimulate the medullary respiratory center, causing primary respiratory alkalosis. As toxicity progresses, accumulation of salicylic acid, lactic acid, and ketoacids leads to high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA).

Therefore, severe salicylate poisoning is characterized by:

• Low arterial pH
• High anion gap metabolic acidosis
• Low pCO₂ due to compensatory hyperventilation (and respiratory center stimulation)
questions.learning: I and III Salicylate (aspirin) poisoning produces a mixed acid-base disorder. Initially, salicylates stimulate the medullary respiratory center, causing primary respiratory alkalosis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A cohort study was done with a sample size of 500, and 20 of them developed the disease over two years. Total person-time observed was 950 years. Calculate the incidence rate.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2.1 per 100 person-years

Incidence rate is calculated as the number of new cases divided by total person-time at risk.

Here, incidence rate = 20 ÷ 950 = 0.021 per person-year, which when expressed per 100 person-years equals 2.1 per 100 person-years.

Incidence rate uses person-time, not total population or duration alone, distinguishing it from cumulative incidence.
questions.learning: 2.1 per 100 person-years Incidence rate is calculated as the number of new cases divided by total person-time at risk. Here, incidence rate = 20 ÷ 950 = 0.021 per person-year, which when expressed per 100 person-years equals 2.1 per 100 person-years.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A post-menopausal woman presented with pain in her lower abdomen for the past 4 months. She was informed to have fibroids for a long time. The radiological investigation is shown below. What is the type of degeneration that occurred in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Calcific degeneration

The X-ray shows calcified fibroids and is due to the calcific degeneration of fibroids.

Calcific or calcareous degeneration most often involves subserous fibroid with small pedicle or myomas in post menopausal women.

In calcareous degeneration, phosphates and carbonates of lime are deposited in the periphery along the course of the vessels. The best examples of calcareous myomas are those in old patients with long-standing myomas. They are like ‘womb-stones’ in graveyards.

Another radiograph showing large calcified myoma:

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A male presented with the following findings which he noticed when he woke up in the morning. There was no history of associated fever or rash. What is the drug of choice for this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prednisone

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Bell's palsy and steroids are the drug of choice for Bell's palsy

Bell's palsy is a lower motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve and involves the ipsilateral side of the upper and lower halves of the face. Bell's palsy is idiopathic, peripheral facial paralysis, or paresis of acute onset. The onset of Bell's palsy is fairly abrupt.

If the patient attempts to close the eye, the eyeball would turn up and out - this is known as the Bell's phenomenon. Decreased tearing, hyperacusis, taste disturbances, otalgia, weakness of the facial muscles, poor eyelid closure, etc can be seen. When the patient smiles, the face becomes distorted and lateralizes to the side opposite the palsy. Flattening of the forehead and nasolabial fold on the side affected by palsy.

Treatment of Bell's palsy involves prednisone 60-80 mg daily during the first 5 days and then tapered over the next 5 days. The use of artificial tears and covering the eye at night prevents corneal drying.

Approximately 85 to 95% of patients recover fully. The presence of incomplete paralysis in the first week is the most favourable prognostic sign. Recurrences are seen in some cases. Bell's palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion. All other possible causes of facial paralysis should be ruled out by investigation.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 21-year-old man presents with episodic chest pain. On examination, he has a bisferiens pulse and a heaving apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of a bisferiens pulse (a double-peaked arterial pulse) and a heaving (forceful) apex beat in a young man with chest pain is classic for Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM), specifically the obstructive type. HCM is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by asymmetric septal hypertrophy. Dilated Cardiomyopathy (Option A) would present with a displaced and weak apical impulse rather than a heaving one. Mitral Stenosis (Option C) is characterized by a "tapping" apex beat and an opening snap, with no bisferiens pulse. Pure Aortic Stenosis (Option D) typically produces a "slow-rising" (pulsus parvus et tardus) pulse rather than a bisferiens one, though a bisferiens pulse can be seen in combined aortic stenosis and regurgitation. HCM is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes due to ventricular arrhythmias, often triggered by exertion. Diagnosis is confirmed by echocardiography showing a thickened ventricular wall
questions.learning: The combination of a bisferiens pulse (a double-peaked arterial pulse) and a heaving (forceful) apex beat in a young man with chest pain is classic for Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM), specifically the obstructive type.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to shortness of breath, poor appetite, and abdominal distension for the past 3 months. His symptoms have progressively worsened, and he is now unable to perform his daily activities. The patient has a history of ischemic heart disease and underwent coronary artery bypass grafting 5 years ago. Physical examination shows jugular venous distension, abdominal distension, hepatomegaly, and bilateral lower extremity edema. A representative liver biopsy image is shown in the exhibit. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s liver findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Passive hepatic congestion

Chronic right-sided heart failure causes passive hepatic congestion due to elevated central venous pressure transmitted to the hepatic veins and sinusoids.

Increased venous pressure leads to dilation of hepatic sinusoids, particularly around the central vein (zone 3).

Reduced hepatic blood outflow causes centrilobular hypoxia and hepatocyte necrosis, with red blood cell congestion in the sinusoids.

Histologic and gross features: Centrilobular congestion and hemorrhage with relatively preserved periportal hepatocytes produce the characteristic “nutmeg liver” appearance seen in congestive hepatopathy.
questions.learning: Passive hepatic congestion Chronic right-sided heart failure causes passive hepatic congestion due to elevated central venous pressure transmitted to the hepatic veins and sinusoids.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 19-year-old man presents with persistent night pain localized to the distal femur. An X-ray of the femur is provided. What is the most likely radiologic diagnosis suggested by this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Codman's triangle

Codman’s triangle is a type of aggressive periosteal reaction produced when a rapidly growing bone lesion lifts the periosteum away from the cortex, forming a triangular area of new subperiosteal bone. It is classically associated with osteosarcoma, especially in adolescents involving the metaphysis of long bones (most commonly around the knee).

Why not the other options?

• A. Sun-ray appearance: Another periosteal reaction seen in osteosarcoma, characterized by spiculated bone radiating perpendicular to the cortex.
• C. Onion peel appearance: Lamellated periosteal reaction classically seen in Ewing sarcoma.
• D. Osteochondroma: A benign exostosis showing cortical and medullary continuity with the parent bone, not an aggressive periosteal reaction.
questions.learning: Codman's triangle Codman’s triangle is a type of aggressive periosteal reaction produced when a rapidly growing bone lesion lifts the periosteum away from the cortex, forming a triangular area of new subperiosteal bone.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Early onset pre-eclampsia is defined before:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 34 weeks

Early onset pre-eclampsia is defined before 34 weeks.

Pre-eclampsia is characterized by hypertension and end-organ dysfunction that typically develops after 20 weeks of gestation in a previously normotensive individual.

Features of pre-eclampsia:

1. Hypertension:
Blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg on 2 occasions at least 4 hours apart, or ≥160/110 mmHg in a single measurement.
2. Proteinuria:
≥300 mg of protein in a 24-hour urine collection.
Protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3.
Dipstick reading of ≥1+ (though less specific).
3. End-Organ Dysfunction (may occur even without proteinuria):
Renal: Elevated serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubling of baseline.
Hepatic: Elevated liver transaminases (AST/ALT).
Hematologic: Thrombocytopenia (<100,000/µL).
Neurologic: Severe headache, visual disturbances (e.g., scotoma, blurred vision).
Pulmonary: Pulmonary edema.

Early-onset pre-eclampsia:

• Occurs before 34 weeks of gestation.
• Associated with more severe complications, including fetal growth restriction and placental insufficiency.
• Requires careful monitoring and often early delivery if maternal or fetal conditions worsen.

Late-onset pre-eclampsia:

• Occurs at or after 34 weeks of gestation.
• Typically milder, with fewer complications.

Management

1. Mild pre-eclampsia: Close monitoring, antihypertensives (e.g., labetalol, nifedipine), and maternal-fetal surveillance.
2. Severe pre-eclampsia: Hospitalization, magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, and delivery planning (often the definitive treatment).
3. Timing of Delivery:
Recommended at ≥37 weeks for mild pre-eclampsia.
Earlier delivery for severe cases.
questions.learning: 34 weeks Early onset pre-eclampsia is defined before 34 weeks. Pre-eclampsia is characterized by hypertension and end-organ dysfunction that typically develops after 20 weeks of gestation in a previously normotensive individual.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
Match the following in the Japanese encephalitis virus life cycle.

(1) Accidental host
(a) Ardeid birds

(2) Amplifier
(b) Culex

(3) Reservoir
(c) Human

(4) Vector
(d) Pigs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b

The correct match is 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b

1. Accidental host
c. Human

2. Amplifier
d. Pigs

3. Reservoir
a. Ardeid birds

4. Vector
b. Culex

Japanese encephalitis virus is a virus from the family Flaviviridae. It is the leading cause of vaccine-preventable encephalitis in Asia and the western Pacific.

Transmission of Japanese encephalitis virus: Natural infection has been demonstrated in Ardeid birds (herons and egrets). Bird-to-bird transmission takes place through the vectors Culex tritaeniorhynchus and Culex vishnui (common in India). Ardeid birds act as reservoir hosts, while pigs and cattle act as amplifier hosts. Humans are accidental dead-end hosts.

The image below shows the life cycle of Japanese encephalitis virus.

Most people infected with JE do not have symptoms or have only mild symptoms. Less than 1% of people infected with Japanese encephalitis (JE) virus develop clinical illness. The incubation period is typically 5-15 days in persons who develop symptoms. Initial symptoms often include fever, headache, and vomiting. Mental status changes, neurologic symptoms, weakness, and movement disorders might develop over the next few days. Seizures are common, especially among children.

No specific treatments have been found to benefit patients with JE, but hospitalization for supportive care and close observation is generally required. Treatment is symptomatic. Rest, fluids, and the use of pain relievers and medication to reduce fever may relieve some symptoms.

Prevention: In India, inactivated vero cell culture-derived SA-14-14-2 is used. Japanese encephalitis vaccine has been introduced in selected endemic districts. 2 doses of 0.5 ml are given in the left upper arm subcutaneously.

Vaccine
Due age
Maximum age

Japanese encephalitis - 1

9-12 months
15 years

Japanese encephalitis - 2
16-24 months
15 years

If the first dose is delayed beyond 12 months, a minimum of 3 months gap should be there between the two JE doses.
questions.learning: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b The correct match is 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b 1. Culex Japanese encephalitis virus is a virus from the family Flaviviridae.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to you with pain and redness in the right eye following an injury during welding. On examination, the image as seen below is observed. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Removal by 26G needle

A history of injury to the eye while welding along with the the given image is suggestive of a superficial foreign body in the eye. Removal of the foreign body using a 26G needle is the next step in the management of this patient.

Foreign bodies, which are usually small particles of dust, iron, steel, etc., may impinge upon the conjunctiva or cornea and cause sudden discomfort and reflex blinking. The foreign body sticks to the palpebral conjunctiva and is liable to be dragged across the cornea, causing excoriation. Particles of steel and iron fly straight onto the cornea and penetrate the epithelium or substantia propria.

Fluorescein or oblique illumination of the anesthetized eye with a slit lamp can be used to determine the position of a foreign body. If not removed, they expose the cornea to organisms in the conjunctival sac causing ulceration and extrusion of the foreign body in the slough. The ulcer thus formed may heal, but if virulent organisms are present, a spreading ulcer, with or without hypopyon, may develop.

Foreign bodies are managed by removal as soon as possible.

* If the foreign body is found lying loose in either fornix, it can be removed with a clean swab after everting the eyelids.

* Double-eversion of the upper eyelid with a Desmarres retractor can be done if required.

* If embedded in the bulbar conjunctiva or cornea, it can be removed by a foreign body spud or fine forceps under topical anesthesia.

* A disposable hypodermic (26 or 27 gauge) needle can be used.

Following removal in all cases, an antibiotic ointment should be applied and the eye kept bandaged for a day. Foreign bodies in the eye are extremely common in industrial workers, especially in those working with grinding tools, lathe work, or hammering on a chisel, and thus eye must be protected by educative notices, lectures, and the provision of comfortable goggles.

Cases of ferruginous intraocular foreign bodies (IOFB) may give rise to anterior capsular cataracts and reddish-brown staining of the iris leading to heterochromia iridis. MRI is contraindicated here and instead, CT with axial and coronal cuts is used to localize a metallic IOFB. Magnetic removal is done for the removal of ferrous foreign bodies.
questions.learning: Removal by 26G needle — A history of injury to the eye while welding along with the the given image is suggestive of a superficial foreign body in the eye.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is the most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. S phase

S phase is the most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle.

The replication of the DNA genome occurs only at a specified time period during the cell cycle. This period is referred to as the synthetic or S phase. The S phase is separated from the mitotic, or M phase, by nonsynthetic periods referred to as gap 1 (G1) and gap 2 (G2) phases, occurring before and after the S phase, respectively. The cell prepares for DNA synthesis in G1, and for mitosis in G2.

The most radiosensitive phase of the cell cycle is the G2-M phase. Cells in the G2 or M phase do not have time to repair DNA damage that occurs before they start to divide. This affects mitosis, leading to catastrophe.

Cells become gradually less sensitive to radiation in the G1 phase to the early S phase and are least sensitive in the late S phase.
questions.learning: S phase S phase is the most radioresistant phase of the cell cycle. The replication of the DNA genome occurs only at a specified time period during the cell cycle.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 22 year old came with thigh pain. X ray was done as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chronic osteomyelitis

The given clinical scenario of a patient with thigh pain and an X-ray of the lower limb revealing involucrum and cloaca in the femur, strongly suggests a diagnosis of chronic osteomyelitis.

Chronic osteomyelitis may occur by direct inoculation of the infective organism during trauma (like road traffic accidents). The infection continues to thrive within the bone leading to alternating quiescent and flare-up stages of chronic osteomyelitis.

Sequestrum is a piece of dead bone. It is formed when a fragment of bone gets separated from the healthy bone due to necrosis. It varies in size from a spicule to a large fragment and acts as a nidus for infection. It leads to abscess and persistent pus discharge in the bone. Sinus tracts are formed when the abscess from the infected bone drains out through the skin.

The involucrum is the dense new sclerotic bone surrounding the sequestrum. It is formed from deep layers of stripped periosteum. Cloacae are the perforations in the involucrum. Pus and tiny spicules of bone may be discharged through them.

The radiograph below shows sequestrum, involucrum and cloacae:
questions.learning: Chronic osteomyelitis — The given clinical scenario of a patient with thigh pain and an X-ray of the lower limb revealing involucrum and cloaca in the femur, strongly suggests a diagnosis of chronic osteomyelitis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: An 18-year-old boy is brought to you by his concerned grandmother with a history of having experienced several episodes of jerking of the body the day before his final exam. There was no history post-ictal confusion or tongue bite and his investigations were normal. Which of the following conditions should be considered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malingering

In the given scenario, absence of muscle spasm, tongue thrusting, or post-ictal confusion, and normal investigations just before the final exam (personal gain), points towards malingering.

Deliberate production of symptoms for external benefits—such as avoiding work, gaining financial compensation, evading criminal responsibility, or escaping military duty—indicates malingering.

In contrast, factitious disorder (Munchausen syndrome) involves intentionally producing physical symptoms to gain medical attention rather than any external or practical reward.
questions.learning: Malingering — In the given scenario, absence of muscle spasm, tongue thrusting, or post-ictal confusion, and normal investigations just before the final exam (personal gain), points towards malingering.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The respiratory motor neuron associated with origin of respiratory cycle is located in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior medulla oblongata

The dorsal respiratory group (DRG), located in the posterior (dorsal) medulla oblongata within the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), is classically regarded as the inspiratory centre responsible for initiating the normal respiratory cycle. It generates the inspiratory drive during quiet breathing and receives afferent input from peripheral chemoreceptors and pulmonary stretch receptors via the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 54-year-old postmenopausal woman presents to the OPD with increasing vaginal pressure for the past 3 months. She reports no vaginal bleeding or abnormal discharge. Her BMI is 18 kg/m², and vital signs are normal. On speculum examination, the anterior vaginal wall bulges with the Valsalva maneuver. On bimanual examination, the uterus is small and mobile. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pudendal nerve injury

This patient has anterior vaginal wall prolapse (cystocele) --> suggested by bulging of the anterior vaginal wall during the Valsalva maneuver and a sensation of vaginal pressure.

Pelvic organ prolapse occurs due to weakness of the pelvic floor muscles and connective tissue support.

One important mechanism is injury to the Pudendal nerve, which innervates the levator ani muscles and external sphincters.

Damage to this nerve leads to:

• Loss of pelvic floor muscle tone ; Weak support of pelvic organs

• Descent of the bladder into the vagina (cystocele)

Common causes of pudendal nerve injury:

• Vaginal childbirth (most common)

• Chronic increased intra-abdominal pressure

• Aging and postmenopausal estrogen deficiency

• Pelvic floor trauma

Why other options are incorrect:

• Chronic endometriosis → causes pelvic pain and infertility, not prolapse.

• Prior uterine artery ligation → affects uterine blood supply but not pelvic support.

• Uterine leiomyomas → cause menorrhagia and enlarged uterus, not anterior vaginal wall prolapse.
questions.learning: Pudendal nerve injury — This patient has anterior vaginal wall prolapse (cystocele) --> suggested by bulging of the anterior vaginal wall during the Valsalva maneuver and a sensation of vaginal pressure.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A chronic smoker presents with hoarseness of voice. Laryngoscopy findings are shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reinke's oedema

Recognize Reinke’s edema (polypoid corditis) as a benign chronic swelling of the superficial lamina propria (Reinke’s space) of the vocal cords, most commonly seen in chronic smokers, patients with voice abuse, and laryngopharyngeal reflux. It typically presents with progressive, deep hoarseness of voice and bilateral, translucent, balloon-like swelling of the vocal folds on laryngoscopy.

Why not the other options?

• B. Vocal polyp: Usually solitary and unilateral, arising from phonotrauma; does not cause the diffuse bilateral edema seen here.
• C. Vocal cyst: Appears as a well-circumscribed submucosal lesion, usually unilateral, without generalized cord swelling.
• D. Respiratory papillomatosis: Caused by HPV 6 and 11, presenting as multiple warty, papillomatous lesions rather than smooth edematous vocal folds.

High-yield Pearl:

• Smoker + Deep hoarse voice + Bilateral boggy vocal cord swelling = Reinke’s edema.
• Treatment: Smoking cessation, voice therapy, treatment of reflux, and microlaryngoscopic excision if symptoms persist or airway compromise occurs.
questions.learning: Reinke's oedema Recognize Reinke’s edema (polypoid corditis) as a benign chronic swelling of the superficial lamina propria (Reinke’s space) of the vocal cords, most commonly seen in chronic smokers, patients with voice abuse, and laryngopharyngeal reflux.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A skull specimen with a previous history of neurosurgery is shown in the image. The circular defect seen in the skull is most likely due to:
options: Gutter fracture caused by a bullet
Injury caused by a sharp-edged weapon
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Previous burr hole surgery

A burr hole is a circular opening drilled into the skull by a neurosurgeon to gain access to the intracranial cavity. It is commonly performed for:

• Evacuation of epidural hematoma (EDH)
• Evacuation of subdural hematoma (SDH)
• Placement of external ventricular drains (EVD)
• Intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring
• Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt insertion

The image shows a perfectly circular, smooth-edged defect in the skull, and the history of previous neurosurgery strongly indicates a burr hole.

Why not the other options?

• A. Gutter fracture caused by a bullet: Appears as a groove or tangential defect caused by a grazing bullet, not a smooth circular hole.
• B. Injury caused by a sharp-edged weapon: Produces cut/chop marks or linear defects, not a circular opening.
• D. Depressed skull fracture: Shows inward displacement of fractured bone fragments with irregular margins, unlike the smooth surgical defect.
questions.learning: Previous burr hole surgery — A burr hole is a circular opening drilled into the skull by a neurosurgeon to gain access to the intracranial cavity. It is commonly performed for: • Evacuation of epidural hematoma (EDH) • Evacuation of subdural hematoma (SDH)…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In Pringle Manoeuvre, clamping includes which of the following? 1. Common bile duct 2. Hepatic artery 3. Portal vein 4. Inferior vena cava Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The Pringle manoeuvre is a temporary vascular control technique used during liver surgery or hepatic trauma to reduce bleeding by clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament, thereby occluding the portal triad.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Common bile duct ✔️: Part of the portal triad.
• 2. Hepatic artery ✔️: Part of the portal triad.
• 3. Portal vein ✔️: Part of the portal triad.
• 4. Inferior vena cava ❌: Not clamped in the Pringle manoeuvre.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 The Pringle manoeuvre is a temporary vascular control technique used during liver surgery or hepatic trauma to reduce bleeding by clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament, thereby occluding the portal triad.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 18-year-old boy presents with a history of injury to the eye caused while climbing a tree 5 days ago, resulting in pain, photophobia, and redness of the eye for 2 days. Slit-lamp examination reveals a lesion as shown below. Which among the following is a feature of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Satellite lesion

The given clinical vignette and the image suggest that it is a fungal corneal ulcer. Satellite lesions are a feature of fungal ulcers.

A fungal corneal ulcer is usually caused by trauma with vegetative or organic matter. Signs are more pronounced than symptoms. The corneal ulcer appears dry.

Causative organisms :

* Aspergillus

* Fusarium

* Candida albicans

Signs of a fungal ulcer:

* Irregular margins of the ulcer.

* Presence of satellite lesions surrounding the ulcer.

* An immune ring (Wesseley) may be seen around the ulcer due to the deposition of the immune complexes.

* Slough is usually dry, with feathery borders surrounded by a yellow line of demarcation.

* Hypopyon may be present or absent. If present, it is thick, immobile due to the direct invasion of the fungal hyphae into the anterior chamber.

Treatment:

* Topical drugs: These include topical natamycin, voriconazole or amphotericin B drops which are effective against Aspergillus and Fusarium. Nystatin is effective against Candida.

* Systemic drugs: Severe ulcers with hypopyon, perforation or suspected endophthalmitis might warrant the use of oral antifungal agents such as ketoconazole or voriconazole.

Other options :

Option A: Reverse hypopyon is the collection of emulsified silicone oil in the anterior chamber. This can lead to complications such as glaucoma.

Option B: Dendritic ulcer is seen in epithelial keratitis caused by herpes simplex virus. An image of a dendritic ulcer with fluorescein dye is as shown below

Option C: Ring abscess is seen in helminthic keratitis, especially by acanthamoeba. There is gradual enlargement and coalescence of infiltrates which forms an abcess.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with pain along the lateral aspect of the thigh. What is the root value of this nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. L2-L3

Pain along the lateral aspect of the thigh with sensory symptoms indicates involvement of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

This nerve arises from L2–L3 roots, passes under the inguinal ligament near ASIS, and is commonly compressed causing meralgia paresthetica.

It is a purely sensory nerve, with no motor deficit, helping distinguish it from femoral or obturator nerve lesions.
