questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with visual disturbances has a past history of cataract surgery. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) findings are shown. Which syndrome is most likely associated with these findings?
questions.explanation: Irvine-Gass Syndrome is a specific form of cystoid macular edema (CME) that occurs as a complication following cataract surgery. The Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) finding characteristically shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and a loss of the normal foveal depression due to fluid accumulation. Posner-Schlossman Syndrome (Option A) involves recurrent episodes of high intraocular pressure and mild uveitis but is not associated with this pattern of macular edema. Central Serous Retinopathy (Option C) presents with neurosensory retinal detachment, often showing an "ink-blot" pattern on angiography, rather than the intraretinal cysts seen in CME. Elschnig Pearls (Option D) are clusters of epithelial cells on the posterior lens capsule that cause opacification, not retinal edema. Treatment for Irvine-Gass Syndrome often involves topical NSAIDs or steroids to reduce inflammation and promote fluid absorption. Most cases resolve within several months, but some require more aggressive intravitreal therapy

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the maneuver shown.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pringle's manoeuver

The given image depicts Pringle's maneuvre.

It is a technique where the free margin of the lesser omentum is compressed to obtain rapid control of the hepatic artery and portal vein in liver trauma and surgery.

The hepatoduodenal ligament is encircled with a vessel loop or vascular clamp to occlude hepatic blood flow from the hepatic artery and portal vein. This maneuver helps distinguish hepatic arterial and portal venous bleeding from hepatic vein bleeding, which will persist with the hepatoduodenal ligament clamped. In many cases, the liver laceration can then be explored and any actively bleeding vessels controlled with suture ligation.

4 P's in the management of liver injuries are:

* Push : compression of the edges of the laceration

* Pringle : applying pressure on the portal triad

* Plug: the defects with silicon tubes

* Pack : apply packs in and around the liver to arrest bleeding

Other options:

Option A: Mattox maneuver refers to left medial visceral mobilisation done to visualise and repair the vascular injury in case of retroperitoneal bleeds near the kidney.

Option C: Cattell braash maneuver refers to mobilisation of right viscera, namely the colon, to visualise the superior mesenteric artery and repair bleed in infrarenal region.

Option D: Liver hanging maneuver (LHM) is a method of liver resection by passing a tape between the inferior vena cava and liver to have adequate vascular control.

Pearl PF0630: Relations of Lesser sac and Foramen of Winslow (Important)

Relations of Epiploic foramen

Anterior

Hepatoduodenal ligament containing Hepatic artery, Portal vein, and Common bile duct

Posterior

IVC, Rt.suprarenal gland, and body of T12 vertebra

Superior

Caudate lobe of the liver

Inferior

1st part of duodenum

Relations of Lesser Sac

Anterior

Caudate lobe of liver, lesser omentum, stomach, first 2 layers of the greater omentum

Posterior

Structures forming the stomach bed (pancreas, splenic artery, left kidney and suprarenal gland, the commencement of abdominal aorta & coeliac artery, left crus of the diaphragm, splenic flexure of the colon, and the transverse mesocolon)

Upper Border

Reflection of the peritoneum from the esophagus to the diaphragm

Lower border

Continuation of 2nd and 3rd layers of the greater omentum

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 26-year-old female presents to the ER with menorrhagia. She mentions that her father and sister also suffer from bleeding disorders. Which of the following is an autosomal dominant bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Von Willebrand Disease

This patient's clinical features are suggestive of von-Willebrand disease. It is caused by a deficiency of the von-Willebrand factor.

They are present within cytoplasmic vesicles called Weibel-Palade bodies.

Normal Platelet count, Prolonged BT, Normal PT, and Prolonged aPTT are seen in von-Willebrand disease. Factor VIII is found bound to the Von-Willebrand factor (vWF)  in the blood. Deficiency of vWF results in Factor VIII deficiency and prolongation of aPTT in this disease. Prolonged BT is due to abnormal platelet-mediated hemostasis.

vWF is also found in

• Platelet granules (Less as compared to endothelial cells)
• Subendothelium, where it binds to collagen

Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder in humans. The bleeding tendency is usually mild and manifests during surgical or dental procedures. The most common presenting symptoms are spontaneous bleeding from mucous membranes (epistaxis), excessive bleeding from wounds, or menorrhagia.

It is usually transmitted as an autosomal dominant disorder, but rare autosomal recessive variants can be seen.

Three types are recognized, with phenotypic variations:

Type 1 and type 3 von-Willebrand disease are associated with quantitative defects in vWF.

Type 1 is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by a mild to moderate vWF deficiency, accounting for about 70% of all cases. It is associated with mild disease.

Type 3 disease is an autosomal disorder resulting in little to no vWF synthesis. Because vWF stabilizes factor VIII in the circulation, factor VIII levels are also reduced in type 3 disease and the associated bleeding disorder is often severe.

Type 2 von-Willebrand disease is characterized by qualitative defects in vWF. Type 2A is the most common. It is inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder.

Other options:

Factor X, VIII and IX deficiencies are all causes of hemophilias. These conditions manifest as prolonged bleeding after injuries, dental treatment and hemarthrosis. They are also additionally X-linked conditions so the presence of this condition in her father and sister makes X-linked transmission impossible.
questions.learning: Von Willebrand Disease — This patient's clinical features are suggestive of von-Willebrand disease. It is caused by a deficiency of the von-Willebrand factor.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient with diabetic nephropathy develops secondary hyperparathyroidism. Hyperparathyroidism is associated with all of the following conditions, EXCEPT which one?
questions.explanation: Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs as a compensatory response to chronic low serum calcium levels. In Chronic Renal Failure (Option D), the kidney's inability to excrete phosphate and activate Vitamin D leads to hypocalcemia, triggering the parathyroid glands to release more PTH. Similarly, Vitamin D deficiency in Rickets (Option C, children) and Osteomalacia (Option B, adults) results in poor calcium absorption, causing a secondary rise in PTH to pull calcium from the bones. Osteoporosis (Option A), however, is a disease of decreased bone density where serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH levels are typically completely normal. While primary hyperparathyroidism can lead to bone loss, osteoporosis itself is not a cause of elevated parathyroid hormone. Therefore, osteoporosis is the only condition among the choices where parathyroid dysfunction is not a standard physiological feature

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In patients with indications for warfarin usage, what is the recommended range of INR in a patient with mechanical heart valves ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2.5 – 3.5

The INR ratio recommended for the administration of warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves is around 2.5-3.5.

Warfarin therapy is usually monitored by measuring prothrombin time. Prothrombin time is sensitive to the reduction in levels of prothrombin, factor VII, and factor X.  International normalized ratio (INR) was developed to standardize the reporting of prothrombin time.

Other options:

Option B: In most of the patients on regular warfarin therapy,  the INR target is around 2.0-3.0

Option A: The range of 1.0-1.5 is too low for beneficial effects.

Option D: INR >3.5 can result in increased adverse effects and is not recommended for any condition.
questions.learning: 2.5 – 3.5 The INR ratio recommended for the administration of warfarin in patients with mechanical heart valves is around 2.5-3.5. Warfarin therapy is usually monitored by measuring prothrombin time.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the formula of crude birth rate?
options: (Total number of births / Estimated midyear Population) 1,000
(Number of live births / Estimated mid year women Population) 1,000
(Number of live births / Estimated midyear Population) 1,000
(Number of live births / Estimated midyear Population) 10,000
questions.explanation: The Crude Birth Rate (CBR) is a fundamental demographic measure used to quantify the fertility of a population. It is defined as the number of live births occurring in a given year per 1,000 of the estimated midyear population. Option A is incorrect because it uses "total number of births," which might include stillbirths; only live births are counted in CBR. Option B describes the General Fertility Rate, which restricts the denominator to the women of reproductive age. Option D is incorrect due to the use of 10,000 instead of the standard 1,000 multiplier. The midyear population is used as an estimate of the average population exposed to the risk of birth throughout the year. CBR is considered "crude" because it does not account for the age or sex structure of the population, but it is a vital starting point for evaluating demographic trends and population growth
questions.learning: The Crude Birth Rate (CBR) is a fundamental demographic measure used to quantify the fertility of a population. It is defined as the number of live births occurring in a given year per 1,000 of the estimated midyear population.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young patient presented with PND, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. However, the patient succumbed to her illness. On autopsy, the lungs showed hemosiderin-laden macrophages. In all of the following it can occur, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right heart failure

• Hemosiderin-laden macrophages (“heart failure cells”) result from chronic pulmonary congestion with RBC extravasation and breakdown.
• They are seen in left-sided heart failure, pulmonary venous obstruction, and volume overload states causing raised pulmonary capillary pressure.

These macrophages appear brown due to iron deposition. They indicate chronic pulmonary venous hypertension.

Analyzing Each Option

| Option | Causes Pulmonary Venous HTN? | Heart Failure Cells?

| ------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------

| A — Right heart failure | ❌ RHF → systemic venous congestion, NOT pulmonary | EXCEPT ✅

| B — Protein-losing enteropathy | ❌ No mechanism for pulmonary venous HTN | EXCEPT ✅

| C — Pulmonary venous obstruction | ✅ Directly raises pulmonary venous pressure | Yes ✅

| D — Volume overload | ✅ → Biventricular failure → pulmonary congestion | Yes ✅

The Controversy

This is genuinely controversial because both A and B are mechanistically correct "excepts."

Why A (Right heart failure) is the standard expected answer:

• Classic teaching: RHF causes systemic congestion (hepatomegaly, pedal edema, JVD), NOT pulmonary venous hypertension
• Therefore heart failure cells should NOT occur in isolated RHF
• Most Indian textbooks (Harsh Mohan, Robbins) frame it this way

Why B (Protein-losing enteropathy) could also be argued:

• PLE has absolutely no mechanism for pulmonary venous HTN
• It causes hypoalbuminemia → generalized edema, but not specifically pulmonary venous congestion
• Some argue B is a "cleaner" except than A
questions.learning: Right heart failure • Hemosiderin-laden macrophages (“heart failure cells”) result from chronic pulmonary congestion with RBC extravasation and breakdown. • They are seen in left-sided heart failure, pulmonary venous obstruction, and volume overload states…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What does the zero pressure indicate in the pressure-volume curve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Functional residual capacity

The zero pressure in the pressure-volume curve indicates the functional residual capacity.

The pressure-volume relationship is basic to the understanding of the fundamental relationship between the compliance of the lungs and the chest wall. It is measured by a spirometer.

The functional residual capacity is the volume of the air that remains in the lungs after normal expiration. The normal value is about 2.5 liters.

Other options:

Option A: Residual volume is the air left in the lungs after a maximal expiratory effort.

Option C: Tidal volume is the amount of air that moves in during each inspiration or the amount of air that moves out with each expiration, during quiet breathing. The normal tidal volume is 500–750 mL.

Option D: Inspiratory reserve volume is the air inspired with a maximal inspiratory effort in addition to the tidal volume.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the type of hernia in which the internal organ composes a portion of the wall of the hernia sac?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sliding hernia

* Sliding hernia occurs when an internal organ composes a portion of the wall of the hernia sac.

* The most common viscus involved are as follows:

* Left side: sigmoid colon and its mesentry

* Right side: cecum

* It is more common on the left side.

* Most sliding hernias are variants of indirect inguinal hernias.

* The primary danger associated with a sliding hernia is the failure to recognize the visceral component of the hernia sac before injury to the bowel or bladder.

Other options:

Option A: Lumbar hernia is a rare type of hernia occurring in the lumbar region

Option C: Spigelian hernia occurs along the Spigelian fascia

Option D: In Richter’s hernia only a part of the bowel wall (typically the antimesenteric border) is trapped, leading to strangulation without complete bowel obstruction.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following should be avoided by a patient of fish odour syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Choline

A fishy odor is seen in trimethylaminuria. Consumption of food products with choline should be avoided in fish odor syndrome.

Fish odor syndrome (trimethylaminuria) is an autosomal recessive disease where TMA(trimethylamine) is not converted to the non-odorous TMAO (TMA-N-oxide) in the liver. This is due to the deficiency of flavin-containing mono oxygenase 3 (FMO3). TMA then builds up in the body and is released in sweat, urine, and breath, giving off a strong odor of rotting fish from the body.

Choline, lecithin, and TMAO are precursors of trimethylamine which are found in food products. These food products are eggs, liver, peanuts, meat, poultry, fish, dairy foods, pasta, and rice.
questions.learning: Choline — A fishy odor is seen in trimethylaminuria. Consumption of food products with choline should be avoided in fish odor syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Five days after surgery requiring prolonged immobilization, a patient develops severe pain in one leg. On examination, Homan’s sign is positive. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT) is a common postoperative complication, particularly in patients who undergo prolonged immobilization, satisfying Virchow's triad of stasis. Homan's sign is a clinical test where the patient experiences calf pain upon passive dorsiflexion of the foot. While it is historically associated with DVT, its sensitivity and specificity are relatively low. Urinary sepsis (Option B) presents with fever, chills, and urinary symptoms, not localized leg pain. Peripheral vascular disease (Option C) typically causes chronic exertional pain (claudication) rather than acute postoperative swelling and pain. Lymphangitis (Option D) is an inflammation of the lymphatic channels, usually appearing as red streaks on the skin with associated lymphadenopathy. For a postoperative patient with leg pain and a positive Homan's sign, DVT must be the working diagnosis until ruled out by a Doppler ultrasound. Prophylaxis with anticoagulants and early mobilization are standard practices to prevent the potentially fatal sequel of DVT: pulmonary embolism
questions.learning: Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT) is a common postoperative complication, particularly in patients who undergo prolonged immobilization, satisfying Virchow's triad of stasis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 58-year-old male presents with a skull base malignancy, and his Glasgow Prognostic Score (GPS) is calculated using his C-reactive protein (CRP) value and serum albumin. As part of clinical evaluation, which of the following is least likely to be used for the prognosis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vertigo

Prognosis in skull base malignancies depends on tumor-related factors, cranial nerve involvement, systemic inflammatory status, and the patient’s functional performance. Important prognostic indicators include tumor extent, cranial nerve palsy (especially facial nerve involvement), Karnofsky Performance Score (KPS), and Glasgow Prognostic Score (GPS) based on CRP and serum albumin. Vertigo, although it may occur due to vestibular involvement, is not an established prognostic marker.

Why is C correct?

• Vertigo is a clinical symptom that may reflect involvement of the vestibular apparatus but does not independently predict prognosis.

Why not the other options?

• A. 7th cranial nerve palsy ✓: Indicates advanced local disease and is associated with a poorer prognosis.
• B. Extent of lesion ✓: Tumor size and local invasion are major determinants of prognosis and treatment planning.
• D. Karnofsky Performance Score ✓: A validated measure of functional status and an important predictor of survival and treatment tolerance.
questions.learning: Vertigo Prognosis in skull base malignancies depends on tumor-related factors, cranial nerve involvement, systemic inflammatory status, and the patient’s functional performance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Measles vaccine is classified under which type of vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Live vaccine

Measles vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine prepared from live or wild organisms grown in culture and attenuated to retain immunogenicity. It is available as a freeze-dried product and recommended only in the live attenuated form for safe and effective immunization.

The vaccine is supplied as a freeze-dried product, reconstituted with sterile diluent, and one dose of 0.5 ml contains ≥1000 viral infective units of the vaccine strain. The reconstituted vaccine is generally injected subcutaneously, but it is also effective when administered intramuscularly.

It should be stored at 2–8°C after reconstitution and used within 4 hours, since it loses about 50% potency after 1 hour at 20°C. When administered, measles vaccine induces seroconversion in 95–98% of recipients after a single dose, ensuring strong immunity.

The first dose (MCV1) is given at 9 completed months, with a second dose (MCV2) at 15–18 months to ensure full coverage.Reaching all children with 2 doses of measles containing vaccine (MCV) should be the standard for all national immunization programmes. In countries with high measles risk, MCV is also given as part of outbreak control or supplementary doses up to 5 years of age. It is often used in combination vaccines like MR (measles-rubella), MMR (measles-mumps-rubella), and MMRV (measles-mumps-rubella-varicella).

Adverse Reactions :

* After vaccination, a mild “measles-like illness” (fever and rash) may occur in 5–10 days, lasting for 1–2 days.

* Other reactions include minor upper respiratory infections, mild diarrhea, or fever that resolves in 1–3 days.

* Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) can occur if the vaccine vial is contaminated or used beyond 4 hours after reconstitution, leading to severe symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, high fever, and even death within 48 hours.

Contraindications:

* immunosuppression (e.g., HIV-infected persons with evidence of severe immunosuppression).

* Pregnancy – should be avoided for at least 4 weeks following MMR vaccination.

Persons with moderate or severe acute illness should postpone vaccination until recovery.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Assertion: Proteins destined for secretion into the extracellular space are tagged with a signal peptide and directed to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER). Reason: Signal Recognition Particle (SRP) recognizes the signal sequence emerging from the ribosome, transiently halts protein synthesis, and directs the ribosome to the rough ER.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

Proteins destined for secretion, lysosomes, or insertion into the plasma membrane are synthesized on ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER). Their translation begins on free ribosomes, but the presence of an N-terminal signal peptide targets them to the RER.

The Signal Recognition Particle (SRP) recognizes the emerging signal peptide, temporarily pauses translation, and directs the ribosome–mRNA complex to the SRP receptor on the rough ER. Translation then resumes, with the growing polypeptide translocated into the RER lumen for folding and post-translational modification.

Why is A correct?

• Both the assertion and reason are true.
• The reason correctly explains the mechanism by which signal peptide-containing proteins are targeted to the RER.
• Rough ER is specialized for: secretory proteins, membrane proteins, lysosomal proteins.
questions.learning: Both — A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A Proteins destined for secretion, lysosomes, or insertion into the plasma membrane are synthesized on ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER).

questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Perception of pain in an area that lacks sensation is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anesthesia dolorosa

Anesthesia dolorosa refers to pain perceived in an area that is otherwise numb or lacks normal sensation. It occurs due to damage to sensory pathways, especially after nerve injury or central nervous system lesions.

• Loss of normal sensory input (anesthesia)
• Simultaneous abnormal spontaneous pain signals from damaged nerves

Clinical examples:

• Trigeminal nerve injury after procedures for trigeminal neuralgia
• Thalamic lesions or other central sensory pathway injuries

Other terms:

B. Hyperalgesia: Increased response to a painful stimulus

C. Paresthesia: Abnormal sensations like tingling or “pins and needles”

D. Allodynia: Pain due to a normally non-painful stimulus

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During pregnancy, pyogenic granuloma, also called granuloma gravidarum, most commonly arises from which location? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gingival papillae

Pyogenic granuloma of pregnancy (granuloma gravidarum) is a benign vascular proliferative lesion that commonly develops during pregnancy due to hormonal influences and local irritation. Most common site: Gingival papillae, especially the interdental gingiva

Characteristics:

• Red, soft, highly vascular lesion
• Bleeds easily on touch
• Rapid growth during pregnancy
• Usually appears in the second or third trimester

Pathogenesis: Increased estrogen and progesterone enhance vascular response to local irritation and plaque

Despite the name, pyogenic granuloma is neither pyogenic nor a true granuloma.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The girl seen in the image has had history of severe sunburns after just a few minutes in the sun, severe freckling in the sun exposed areas. The most likely diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Xeroderma Pigementosum

The image shows a girl with Xeroderma Pigmentosum. It is characterized by Defective Nucleotide Excision repair that is transmitted autosomal recessively.

Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by defective DNA repair which leads to clinical and cellular hypersensitivity to ultraviolet radiation and other carcinogenic agents.

Important clinical features are:

* Child is asymptomatic at birth. Diffuse erythema, scaling, and freckle like areas over the sun exposed regions of the body at around 6 months of age.

* Poikiloderma is a characteristic feature of the second stage. Poikiloderma results in skin atrophy, telangiectasias with mottled hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation.

* In the third stage appearance of cutaneous malignancies like squamous cell carcinomas, malignant melanoma, basal cell carcinoma,  and fibrosarcoma.

The final diagnosis of XP can be confirmed by special laboratory tests by examining the DNA damage repair in cells from cultures exposed to ultraviolet radiation. The most common tests are skin biopsy and culture of skin fibroblasts.

There is no cure for XP. Treatment consists of minimizing exposure to sunlight and regular dermatological care, as well as surgery for recurrent tumors excision. Patients should be followed up every 3 months.

Genetic counseling is important in a family that has an affected child and is considering having more children.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A guy was playing in a garden. Suddenly, he collapsed and was rushed to the hospital. His friend who played with him in the garden informed the doctors that he ate one of the fruits in the garden post which he seemed to have developed these symptoms. He also had irritability, restlessness, dry hot skin, and was unable to pass urine and stools. Identify the poison and its appropriate antidote.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Datura, Physostigmine

The clinical vignette in the question is suggestive of Datura poisoning for which the appropriate antidote is physostigmine, a reversible acetylcholine esterase antagonist. It is an effective treatment for severe anticholinergic poisoning.

Datura poisoning:

The common names include thorn apple, Jimson weed, and Devil's trumpet. The active ingredients include the anticholinergic alkaloids atropine, scopolamine, and hyoscyamine. The seeds or other parts of the plant can be ingested or smoked.

Toxic manifestations of Datura:

• Mnemonic: "hot as a hare, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, and mad as a hatter"
• Also, remember the D's of Datura

• Dry hot skin (Temp rises up to 42 C, a scarlet rash may also be appreciated).
• Dilatation of pupils along with loss of accommodation
• Diplopia
• Dryness of the mouth and throat, unquenchable thirst
• Dysphagia
• Dilatation of cutaneous blood vessels
• Dysarthria (Difficulty in talking)
• Drunken gait
• Delirium
• Drowsiness
• Death due to respiratory or cardiac failure

Treatment

• Gastric lavage or decontamination with activated charcoal or tannic acid. Gastric emptying is often delayed, and the small, plentiful seeds can become trapped among the gastrointestinal folds after ingestion; thus gastric decontamination can be an important therapy.
• Physostigmine in severe toxicity given 1-2 mg IM/IV after every half hour as required. It is a physiological antidote. Pilocarpine may also be given.

Medico-legal importance:

In India, datura is used as a stupefying poison prior to robbery, kidnapping, and rape. It is also known as a rail-road poison, as it is commonly encountered during a journey. Robbers disguised as saints may offer ‘prasad’ mixed with datura seeds and rob the passengers.

Yellow oleander:

All parts of the plant are poisonous. The active principles are thevatin, and thevatoxin, which are cardiac glycosides. The nectar of the flower yields poisonous honey. Symptoms include burning sensation in the mouth, tingling of the tongue, dryness of throat, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, dilated pupils, irregular action of heart followed by drowsiness, coma, collapse, and death.

The given image shows the flowers of Cerebra thevatia.
questions.learning: Datura, Physostigmine — The clinical vignette in the question is suggestive of Datura poisoning for which the appropriate antidote is physostigmine, a reversible acetylcholine esterase antagonist.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 40-year-old nurse presents to the clinic requesting an HIV test. She had a needle prick injury while at work from an HIV positive patient. Antibodies against which of the following will be detected first by ELISA or Western blot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. gp 41

Antibodies against gp41 will be detected first by ELISA or Western blot.

Antibodies to HIV usually appear within 3–6 weeks of primary infection. The appearance of HIV-binding antibodies occurs prior to the appearance of neutralizing antibodies. The only viral proteins that elicit neutralizing antibodies are the envelope proteins gp120 and gp41.

The order of appearance of antibodies is as follows:

Antibody to envelope gp41 > Antibodies to gag protein (p24 and p55) > Antibodies to envelope gp120 > Antibodies to gag protein p17 > Antibodies to pol gene products (p31 and p66).

Note: The earliest antigen to appear in the blood following HIV infection is p24.
questions.learning: gp 41 Antibodies against gp41 will be detected first by ELISA or Western blot. Antibodies to HIV usually appear within 3–6 weeks of primary infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The investigation of choice for early follow-up in patients treated for anti-H. pylori drugs is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urea breath test

The urea breath test (UBT) is the investigation of choice for confirming eradication of Helicobacter pylori after completion of therapy. It is non-invasive, has high sensitivity and specificity, and detects active infection, making it ideal for early follow-up.

Why not the other options?

• B. Rapid urease test: Requires endoscopy and is not routinely used for follow-up.
• C. Stool H. pylori antigen test: Also detects active infection and is an acceptable alternative, but UBT is considered the preferred test.
• D. Serology for H. pylori: Not useful for follow-up, as antibodies may remain positive for months to years after successful eradication.
questions.learning: Urea breath test — The urea breath test (UBT) is the investigation of choice for confirming eradication of Helicobacter pylori after completion of therapy.

Among the given options, maximum thermic effect is seen with proteins

Specific dynamic allowance (previously called as thermic effect of food): This refers to the increased heat production or increased metabolic rate following the intake of food (diet-induced thermogenesis).

The values of SDA are:

• 30% for proteins: This means that out of every 100 grams of proteins consumed, the energy available for doing useful work is 30% less than the calculated value.
• 15% for lipids, and
• 5% for carbohydrates.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: You are a junior resident in the ICU. A senior doctor asks you to manage a mechanically ventilated patient whose arterial blood gases showed features of hypoventilation with respiratory acidosis. Which of the following parameters can you modulate to improve the condition of the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increase Respiratory Rate

Since this patient has features of hypoventilation and respiratory acidosis this is a case of type 2 respiratory failure and needs correction of hypoxia and hypercapnia. Thus, the respiratory rate should be increased, which increases ventilation and decreases the CO2 content, leading to improvement in the condition of this patient.

The most common ventilator mode to use in a newly intubated patient is ACMV(Assist Control Mode Ventilation).

The common terms used in association with a ventilator:

* Ventilation/minute ventilation is calculated as respiratory rate (RR) times tidal volume (Vt). In a mechanically ventilated patient, the CO2 content of the blood can be modified by changing the tidal volume or the respiratory rate.

* Tidal volume is the volume of air moved in and outside the lungs in each respiratory cycle.

* Oxygenation of the lungs can be changed by altering the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2%) or the positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP).

*

FiO2 is the percentage of oxygen in the air mixture that is delivered to the patient.

* PEEP: The positive pressure that will remain in the airways at the end of the respiratory cycle.

* Peak pressure is a measure of airway resistance as well as compliance and includes the tubing and bronchial tree.

* Plateau pressures are a reflection of alveolar pressure and thus of lung compliance.

Initial ventilatory settings are as given below:

* Tidal volume - 4-6 ml/kg of IBW (Ideal Body Weight)

* Respiratory rate - 12 Breaths/ min

* FiO2 - 100% to begin with and titrated to lesser values to prevent oxygen toxicity

* PEEP - Begin with 5 cm H2O, titrate to 10 cm H2O (Carefully increased as high PEEP may impair ventricular filling in a patient with blunt chest trauma)

An ABG should be obtained 30 minutes after intubation and changes to the ventilator settings should be made in accordance with ABG findings. Peak and plateau pressures should be checked on the vent to assure there are no problems with airway resistance or alveolar pressure in order to prevent ventilator-induced lung injury.

Based on the ABG, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and hyperventilation can be corrected by altering some ventilator settings.

* To increase the oxygenation either FiO2% or PEEP has to be increased. Raising the PEEP has a risk of barotrauma and hypotension while increased FiO2 can cause oxidative damage in the alveoli. A target of 92-94% should be maintained. A sudden drop of saturation can be caused by tube misplacement, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, or the development of mucus plugs.

* Hypercapnia can be managed by modifying alveolar ventilation which is dependent on tidal volume or the respiratory rate. Raising the rate or the tidal volume, will increase ventilation and decrease CO2. While increasing the rate, it will also increase the amount of dead space and can lead to the development of auto-PEEP.

Dynamic hyperinflation or auto-PEEP is a process in which some of the inhaled air is not fully exhaled at the end of the respiratory cycle. The accumulation of trapped air will increase pulmonary pressures and cause barotrauma and hypotension. To prevent and resolve auto-PEEP, enough time should be given for the air to leave the lungs during exhalation.

Note:

Causes of elevated peak pressure and normal plateau pressure: Kinked ET tube, Mucus plug, Bronchospasm.

Causes of elevated peak and elevated plateau pressure: Mainstem intubation, Pneumothorax, Atelectasis, Pulmonary edema, ARDS.
questions.learning: Increase Respiratory Rate Since this patient has features of hypoventilation and respiratory acidosis this is a case of type 2 respiratory failure and needs correction of hypoxia and hypercapnia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the current scenario treatment for urea cycle disorder is available. Administration of amino acid phenylbutyrate can decrease ammonia formation. Which amino acid provides phenylbutyrate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutamate

The amino acid that provides phenylbutyrate in the treatment of urea cycle disorders is glutamate.

Ammonia to Urea cycle: Ammonia gets converted to glutamate (non toxic form) through transamination.  Glutamate is transported to the liver as glutamine (by glutamine synthase). In the liver, ammonia is released from glutamine, converting it to alpha keto glutatamte. The released ammonia enters the urea cycle.

In acetylation therapy, Phenylbutyrate (a prodrug) which is metabolized to phenylacetate. Phenylacetate combines with glutamine (a nitrogen-rich amino acid) to form phenylacetylglutamine. Phenylacetylglutamine is water-soluble and is excreted in the urine. This process helps trap excess nitrogen, bypassing the urea cycle.

Other drugs that can be used to achieve the same outcome (ammonia scavengers) include:

• Phenylacetate
• Benzoate

Other Options:

Option A and C: Arginine and Aspartate do not play a role in this specific reaction.

Option D: Glycine: The combination of benzoate and glycine forms hippuric acid, a non-toxic compound. When Benzoate is administered to the body, it acts as a nitrogen-scavenging agent. Hippuric acid is water-soluble and is excreted in the urine, effectively removing one nitrogen molecule from the body per molecule of hippuric acid formed. This mechanism is similar to how phenylacetate acts as a scavenger for glutamate.
questions.learning: Glutamate — The amino acid that provides phenylbutyrate in the treatment of urea cycle disorders is glutamate. Ammonia to Urea cycle: Ammonia gets converted to glutamate (non toxic form) through transamination.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the maximum duration for TRALI to occur after blood transfusion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 6 hours

The maximum duration for TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) to occur after blood transfusion is upto 6 hours. TRALI is sudden-onset respiratory failure that occurs during or soon after blood transfusion.

The pathogenesis involves a two-hit hypothesis:

• Priming event - increased sequestration and sensitization of neutrophils in the microvasculature of the lung
• Second hit - the factor (most commonly MHC class I antigens) present in the transfused blood product activates the primed neutrophils

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A Calabar swelling, which is a short-lived, inflammatory, oedematous swelling close to a limb joint, is characteristically seen in infection caused by which of the following nematodes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loa loa

Loiasis is a filarial infection caused by Loa loa, transmitted by the Chrysops (deer fly or mango fly). It is characterized by transient, localized, non-pitting subcutaneous edema (Calabar swellings), which result from a hypersensitivity reaction to migrating adult worms. Migration of the adult worm across the conjunctiva (“African eye worm”) is a classic clinical feature.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Onchocerca volvulus: Causes river blindness, subcutaneous nodules, and dermatitis; transmitted by the blackfly (Simulium).
• B. Mansonella perstans: Usually causes mild or asymptomatic filariasis without characteristic Calabar swellings.
• D. Brugia malayi: Causes lymphatic filariasis with recurrent lymphangitis and lymphedema/elephantiasis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with low-grade fever and cough. Based on the provided chest X-ray, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The Chest X-ray demonstrates numerous tiny, uniform, 1-2 mm nodules scattered symmetrically throughout both lung fields, resembling millet seeds. This is the classic radiological presentation of Miliary Tuberculosis, a form of disseminated TB resulting from hematogenous spread of the bacilli. Lung cancer (Option A) typically presents as one or more larger, irregular masses. ARDS (Option C) shows diffuse "white-out" or bilateral alveolar infiltrates rather than discrete miliary nodules. Aspergilloma (Option D) is a solid ball of fungus that typically resides in a pre-existing cavity. Miliary TB can be a life-threatening emergency, particularly in young adults or immuno compromised individuals, and may involve multiple organ systems including the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Diagnosis is often difficult and may require high-resolution CT (HRCT) or sputum/tissue cultures. Prompt initiation of standard four-drug antitubercular therapy (ATT) is essential

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man develops sudden onset of profuse vomiting and diarrhea within three hours of consuming pre-packaged salad and milk at a picnic. He does not have fever. Which organism is the most likely cause of this illness?
questions.explanation: A very short incubation period of 1–6 hours (specifically 3 hours here) combined with profuse vomiting and the absence of fever is highly suggestive of food poisoning caused by preformed enterotoxins of Staphylococcus aureus. These heat-stable toxins are often found in contaminated dairy products or salads and cause a rapid onset of symptoms that typically resolve within 24–48 hours. Clostridium perfringens (Option A) has a longer incubation (8–16 hours) and is associated with meat dishes. Salmonella enterica (Option B) typically presents with fever and a longer incubation period (6–72 hours) due to invasive infection. Bacillus cereus (Option D) can cause an emetic syndrome with a short incubation (1–5 hours), but it is most frequently linked to contaminated fried rice rather than the salad and milk mentioned here
questions.learning: A very short incubation period of 1–6 hours (specifically 3 hours here) combined with profuse vomiting and the absence of fever is highly suggestive of food poisoning caused by preformed enterotoxins of Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The sulcus located deep to the marked structure is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stem of the lateral sulcus

The area marked by an arrow in the given image is pterion and the stem of the lateral sulcus lies under it.

The pterion is an H-shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull:

• Frontal bone
• Squamous part of the temporal bone
• Greater wing of the sphenoid bone
• Parietal bone.

The surface of the cerebrum consists of folds called gyri separated by fissures called sulci. The lateral sulcus, also called the Sylvian Fissure, is present on the infero-lateral surface of each cerebral hemisphere and separates the frontal lobe from the temporal lobe. The lateral sulcus consists of a stem which divides into three rami, which are, the anterior horizontal, anterior ascending, and the posterior rami.

The structures lying deep to the pterion are:

• The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery
• The middle meningeal vein
• The stem of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure)

The bone in this area is thin and an injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Countercurrent mechanism is present in which of the following parts of the body?

1. Eye
2. Testes
3. Kidney
4. Gut
5. Lungs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2,3,4,5 are correct

The countercurrent mechanism is present in the testis, kidney, gut, and lungs.  When the inflow runs parallel to, counter to, and in close proximity to the outflow for some distance it is called as the counter current mechanism.

Spermatogenesis requires a temperature considerably lower than that of the interior of the body. The testes are kept cool by heat exchange in a countercurrent manner between the spermatic arteries and veins.

The concentration of the urine by the kidney requires an osmolality gradient. This gradient is produced by the loop of Henle as counter-current multipliers and maintained by vasa recta as counter-current exchangers.
The functioning of the loop of Henle depends upon:

1. The high permeability of the thin descending limb to water ( via aquaporin-1)
2. Active transport of Na+ and Cl- from the thick ascending limb, thereby diluting the tubular fluid.
3. The inflow of tubular fluid from proximal tubule and outflow to the distal tubule.

The countercurrent mechanism is used in the villi to decrease the oxygen availability for local metabolic reactions of the gut. Hence this will increase the blood flow in the intestine during gastrointestinal activity.

Countercurrent exchange of oxygen is seen in the lungs as well.
questions.learning: 2,3,4,5 are correct The countercurrent mechanism is present in the testis, kidney, gut, and lungs. When the inflow runs parallel to, counter to, and in close proximity to the outflow for some distance it is called as the counter current mechanism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young patient presents with a severe headache. He has never experienced a headache of this severity before. He has hypertension and nuchal rigidity on examination. Which of the following could be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache (like never before) suggests a diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is the bleeding into the subarachnoid space, which is the area between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater surrounding the brain. The diagnosis is suspected when a hyperattenuating material is seen filling the subarachnoid space. Most commonly this is apparent around the circle of Willis, on account of the majority of berry aneurysms occurring in this region, or in the Sylvian fissure.

Young males with a history of spontaneous sudden onset severe headaches with seizures should raise suspicion for subarachnoid hemorrhage (aneurysmal). The most common cause of SAH is head trauma and the second common cause is the rupture of a saccular aneurysm.

Symptoms include:

* Severe headache (thunderclap headache)

* Rapid onset vomiting

* Confusion or a lowered level of consciousness

* Seizures

* Neck stiffness or neck pain

Other options:

Cluster headache is a rare form of primary headache. It is characterized by deep excruciating pain that is usually retroorbital, and unilateral. It usually lasts for short duration of 8-10 weeks a year followed by a pain-free interval. It is associated with lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, and ptosis. In acute cases, oxygen therapy is useful. Subcutaneous and nasal sumatriptan can be used.

The classic clinical triad of fever, headache, and neck rigidity is suggestive of meningitis. Other common complaints are nausea, vomiting, and photophobia. Nuchal rigidity (“stiff neck”) is the pathognomonic sign of meningitis. Hip and knee flexion on passive flexion of the neck is called Brudzinsky's sign.

Encephalitis presents similar to meningitis with fever, altered mental status, and focal or diffuse neurological symptoms.

Pearl PF1866: Intracranial haemorrhage
questions.learning: Subarachnoid hemorrhage — The clinical manifestations of neck stiffness and severe headache (like never before) suggests a diagnosis of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A homogenous sample of 4 groups was taken as shown below. The height and weight of each group had a correlation coefficient of 0.6. What will be the total coefficient of correlation of the whole group?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Equal to 0.6

In a homogenous sample or population, the total coefficient of correlation (r) will be the average of the individual correlation coefficients. Therefore in the given condition, it will be the same as 0.6

The given scattergram shows the correlation coefficient of height and weight of 4 homogenous samples. Averaging methods are appropriate when several different samples are independently drawn from the same or a homogenous population and the interest is in aggregating those values.

Therefore the total correlation coefficient of the whole group will be:

r = (sum of correlation coeffiecient of each sample) ÷ (total no. of samples)

= (0.6 + 0.6  + 0.6 + 0.6) ÷ 4 = 2.4 ÷ 4

= 0.6

Note: A correlation between 2 variables does not demonstrate any causal relationship between those variables, no matter how strong it is. Correlation is merely a measure of a statistical association between the variables. Therefore inferring a causal relationship between two variables on the basis of a correlation is a common and fundamental error.
questions.learning: Equal to 0.6 In a homogenous sample or population, the total coefficient of correlation (r) will be the average of the individual correlation coefficients.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman at 28 weeks of gestation presents for a routine checkup and is asymptomatic. On examination, a soft early to mid-systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border, with no associated thrills, heaves, or other abnormal findings. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Physiological murmur of pregnancy

During pregnancy, increased plasma volume and cardiac output produce a physiological flow murmur, typically heard as a soft (grade I–II), early-to-mid systolic ejection murmur along the left sternal border or pulmonary area. It is not associated with thrills, heaves, or other abnormal cardiac findings and requires no treatment.

Why not the other options?

• A. Mitral stenosis: Characterized by a mid-diastolic murmur with an opening snap, not a systolic murmur.
• B. Aortic stenosis: Produces a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, often with a thrill.
• D. Ventricular septal defect: Causes a loud pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, frequently associated with a palpable thrill.
questions.learning: Physiological murmur of pregnancy During pregnancy, increased plasma volume and cardiac output produce a physiological flow murmur, typically heard as a soft (grade I–II), early-to-mid systolic ejection murmur along the left sternal border or pulmonary area.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a patient with Wilson's disease which of the following is decreased in urine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 3-methylhistidine

Urinary levels of 3-methylhistidine are decreased in patients with Wilson disease.

Amino acids in urine exist either in conjugated form (most) or in free form. In Wilson's disease the amount of conjugated amino acids far exceeds the amount of free amino acids. Methyl Histidine largely exists in free form and does not increase in amount on hydrolysis of acids in urine. Hence low amounts is seen in Wilson's disease.

Wilson disease is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by mutation of the ATP7B gene located on chromosome 13. The ATP7B gene, encodes a transmembrane copper-transporting ATPase, expressed on the hepatocyte canalicular membrane.

Deficiency in the ATP7B protein causes a decrease in copper excretion into the bile, impairs its incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and inhibits ceruloplasmin secretion into the blood, leading to the accumulation of toxic levels of copper in the liver, brain, and eye.
questions.learning: 3-methylhistidine Urinary levels of 3-methylhistidine are decreased in patients with Wilson disease. Amino acids in urine exist either in conjugated form (most) or in free form.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old chronic smoker presents with bluish discoloration of the toe along with intermittent claudication. Which of the following will be the next appropriate investigation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Duplex scan

Chronic smoker presenting with bluish discoloration of the toe along with intermittent claudication is suggestive of peripheral arterial disease and duplex scanning will be the next appropriate investigation.

Duplex Scanning is a major non-invasive technique that uses B-mode ultrasound to provide an image of the vessel. Most scanners now have color coding, which allows detailed visualization of blood flow in a vessel. Different colors indicate changes in the direction and velocity of flow, with areas of high flow usually indicating stenotic lesions.

Other options:

Option A: CT Angiography (CTA) is more useful in the evaluation of visceral arterial disease (eg. mesenteric ischemia). It can be beneficial in peripheral artery diseases where a duplex scan shows poor images (aortoiliac segment involvement). CTA is not routinely recommended in peripheral artery disease because of concomitant renal dysfunction in these patients which can lead to contrast-induced nephropathy.

Option B: MR Angiography is time-consuming and expensive, hence not done as the next investigation. It is contraindicated in patients with claustrophobia and metallic implants.

Option C: Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) is an invasive and expensive procedure compared to other investigations. The benefits of DSA are that it provides dynamic arterial flow information and can be combined with a definitive endovascular intervention when indicated. DSA is indicated only when there is a discrepancy in diagnosis or intervention is planned. Complications associated with DSA include bleeding, hematoma, false aneurysm formation, thrombosis, arterial dissection, distal embolisation, renal dysfunction, and allergic reaction.
questions.learning: Duplex scan Chronic smoker presenting with bluish discoloration of the toe along with intermittent claudication is suggestive of peripheral arterial disease and duplex scanning will be the next appropriate investigation.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 38-year-old lady, who was recently started on OCPs is referred to the dermatology OPD with hyperpigmented macules on the upper lip, malar region, and forehead as shown below. It is exacerbated by sun exposure. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Melasma

The given clinical scenario of a woman on OCPs, who has hyperpigmented macules on her face, exacerbated by sun exposure is suggestive of melasma.

Melasma is the most common cause of facial melanosis that manifests as hyperpigmented macules on the face. It is exacerbated by sun exposure and oral contraceptive pills. The condition is predominantly seen in females. Melasma presents as hypermelanosis of the upper lip, malar regions, forehead, and chin. There may also be darkening of the nipples, linea alba, and groin. The lesions are usually bilateral and symmetrical.

In a pregnant woman, melasma is called chloasma (also known as mask of pregnancy). Chloasma is very common in the 3rd trimester of pregnancy. The pigmentation usually fades after parturition, but the course is variable.

Treatment for melasma:

* First-line - Sun protection, changing oral contraceptives to low estrogen formulation, or triple therapy with topical hydroquinone, tretinoin, and corticosteroid cream.

* Second-line - Chemical peels, azelaic acid alone or in combination with tretinoin.

* Third line - Laser therapy, pulsed light therapy, dermabrasion, topical liquiritin, topical rucinol, kojic acid, and hydroquinone.

* Melasma

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 62-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease presents for routine follow-up. His blood glucose and lipid profile are normal, but laboratory testing reveals an elevated homocysteine level above the normal range. Based on these findings, deficiency of which enzyme is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: A elevated homocysteine level is a significant risk factor for cardiovascular disease and premature atherosclerosis. The most common enzyme deficiency leading to hyperhomocysteinemia is Cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS). CBS is responsible for the conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine in the transsulfuration pathway; its lack causes homocysteine to accumulate in the blood. Homogentisate oxidase (Option A) deficiency causes Alkaptonuria (dark urine/ochronosis). Cystathionine gamma-synthase (Option C) is not a primary human enzyme defect associated with this clinical presentation. HGPRTase (Option D) deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, which results in hyperuricemia and self-mutilation, not homocysteinemia. Patients with homocystinuria often present with early-onset CAD, lens subluxation, and tall stature. While vitamin deficiencies (B6, B12, folate) are common causes of mild elevation, a primary genetic enzyme defect like CBS deficiency is the most probable cause for significant, unexplained hyperhomocysteinemia in a patient with established vascular disease
questions.learning: A elevated homocysteine level is a significant risk factor for cardiovascular disease and premature atherosclerosis. The most common enzyme deficiency leading to hyperhomocysteinemia is Cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS).

questions.text: A phlebotomist has been asked to take samples from a patient for multiple tests. Which of the following order of blood collection for testing will not contaminate the sample based on the additives present in the collecting tubes?
questions.explanation:

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man develops sudden difficulty breathing and is unable to speak while eating. Based on the image shown, the most appropriate immediate management is:
options: Direct laryngoscopy and removal of the foreign body
Back blows followed by chest thrusts
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Heimlich maneuver

The image shows the universal choking sign (hands clutching the neck), indicating severe foreign body airway obstruction (FBAO). In a conscious adult who cannot speak, cough, or breathe, the immediate management is the Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts) to expel the obstructing object.

These findings indicate complete airway obstruction in a conscious adult. The first-line treatment is the Heimlich maneuver.

Why not the other options?

• B. Direct laryngoscopy and removal of the foreign body: Performed only if basic life support maneuvers fail or in a hospital setting with a visible foreign body.
• C. Back blows followed by chest thrusts: Recommended for infants (<1 year), not conscious adults.
• D. Initiate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR): Indicated only if the patient becomes unconscious.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis for the ocular lesion observed in a 21-year-old male patient?
questions.explanation: The image displays follicular conjunctivitis, which is characteristic of infections caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (Serotypes D-K). In adults, this is known as "Inclusion Conjunctivitis" and is typically acquired from genital secretions. It features large, pale follicles most prominent in the lower tarsal conjunctiva. Option B (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) causes hyperacute, severe purulent conjunctivitis with massive lid swelling. Option C (Haemophilus influenzae) typically causes acute bacterial conjunctivitis in children, characterized by crusting and redness. Option D (Vitamin A deficiency) causes xerosis and Bitot's spots rather than follicles. Chlamydial infection can also cause Trachoma (Serotypes A-C), the leading infectious cause of blindness, which features follicles on the upper tarsal conjunctiva. Treatment for inclusion conjunctivitis involves oral azithromycin or doxycycline, and it is essential to treat sexual partners simultaneously to prevent reinfection and systemic complications

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient presents with colicky abdominal pain, joint pain, and palpable purpura. Urinalysis reveals only red blood cells without other significant findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of colicky abdominal pain, joint pain, and palpable purpura in a 35-year-old patient is highly characteristic of IgA vasculitis, formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura. This small-vessel vasculitis often presents with a tetrad of symptoms: palpable purpura (typically on lower extremities), arthralgia/arthritis, abdominal pain (often colicky), and renal involvement. The presence of red blood cells in the urinalysis indicates glomerulonephritis, a common complication of this condition. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Option B) usually involves the respiratory tract and is associated with c-ANCA. Microscopic polyangiitis (Option C) also causes glomerulonephritis but lacks the characteristic palpable purpura and abdominal findings of IgA vasculitis. Behçet's disease (Option D) typically presents with recurrent oral and genital ulcers and uveitis. Therefore, given the specific combination of systemic symptoms and the age of the patient, IgA vasculitis is the most likely diagnosis. The pathology involves the deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes in vessel walls
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of colicky abdominal pain, joint pain, and palpable purpura in a 35-year-old patient is highly characteristic of IgA vasculitis, formerly known as Henoch-Schönlein purpura.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy has non-blanching rashes on the legs and buttocks as seen in the picture. He also complains of joint pains, abdominal pain, vomiting, and blood in the stool. Lab investigations revealed normal platelet count and urine analysis shows haematuria +++ and proteinuria +. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP)

This clinical scenario describes Henoch Schonlein purpura.

Features of Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP):

* Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) is a common small vessel vasculitis in childhood.

* It is characterized by a purpuric rash and commonly accompanied by arthritis and abdominal pain.

* About half of the patients with HSP develop renal manifestations, which vary from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria to severe, progressive glomerulonephritis: The pathogenesis of HSP nephritis appears to be mediated by the deposition of polymeric immunoglobulin A (IgA) in glomeruli.

* Laboratory studies generally show a mild leukocytosis, a normal platelet count, and occasionally eosinophilia. Serum complement components are normal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with cheilitis, stomatitis, and a glove and stocking pattern of neuropathy. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B12

The clinical presentation described, including cheilitis, stomatitis, and glove and stocking pattern neuropathy, is most consistent with Vitamin B12 deficiency. This deficiency can lead to a condition known as pernicious anemia which presents with a variety of symptoms including those described.

Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause a wide range of symptoms, including neurological manifestations such as peripheral neuropathy (glove and stocking pattern), as well as gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea. Additionally, vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to megaloblastic anemia, which may present with cheilitis and stomatitis.

Other options:

(a) Niacin (B3) deficiency: Niacin deficiency can lead to a condition called pellagra, which is characterized by the "3 Ds": dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Cheilitis and stomatitis are common manifestations of pellagra, but glove and stocking pattern neuropathy are not typically associated with niacin deficiency.

(b) Thiamine (B1) deficiency: Thiamine deficiency can cause a condition known as beriberi, which can manifest with neurological symptoms such as peripheral neuropathy, but it usually does not present with dermatological symptoms like cheilitis and stomatitis.

(d) Riboflavin (B2) deficiency: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency can cause glossitis (inflammation of the tongue) and cheilosis (cracks or sores at the corners of the mouth). While riboflavin deficiency can cause dermatological symptoms, it is less likely to cause rashes in sun-exposed areas and peripheral neuropathy.
questions.learning: Vitamin B12 — The clinical presentation described, including cheilitis, stomatitis, and glove and stocking pattern neuropathy, is most consistent with Vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is not treated with high-ceiling diuretics?
questions.explanation: High-ceiling diuretics, such as Furosemide (Lasix), are potent loop diuretics used to manage states of severe fluid overload. They are the mainstay of treatment for generalized edema (Option A), acute pulmonary edema (Option C) in congestive heart failure, and are sometimes used as adjuncts in the management of cerebral edema (Option B) to reduce intracranial volume. However, they are NOT used to treat pulmonary hypertension (Option D). Pulmonary hypertension is a condition of high pressure in the lung's arteries, requiring specialized vasodilators like sildenafil or bosentan to lower the vascular resistance. While diuretics may be used in right-sided heart failure resulting from pulmonary hypertension, they do not treat the underlying hypertensive vascular condition itself. Therefore, pulmonary hypertension is the correct "except" choice as its primary pathology is vascular resistance rather than simple fluid retention

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following are the core clinical features for the diagnosis of Lewy body dementia except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Orthostatic hypotension

Orthostatic hypotension is not a core clinical feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) as per DSM-5.

LBD also known as dementia with Lewy bodies is the second most type of progressive dementia after Alzheimer’s disease. Protein deposits, called Lewy bodies, deposit in nerve cells in the brain region involved in thinking, memory, and movement (motor control)

Core features of LBD as per DSM-5 are fluctuating cognition, attention, alertness, recurrent visual hallucination, and Parkinsonian symptoms. Suggestive features are REM sleep behavior disorder and severe neuroleptic sensitivity.
Orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction, and constipation are other features of LBD.

Treatment of LBD includes rivastigmine and donepezil which may improve cognition, and reduce hallucinosis and delusion. Pimavanserin may be used to treat psychosis.
questions.learning: Orthostatic hypotension Orthostatic hypotension is not a core clinical feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) as per DSM-5. LBD also known as dementia with Lewy bodies is the second most type of progressive dementia after Alzheimer’s disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following vaccines produces seroconversion more rapidly than the incubation period of the disease it is meant to prevent?
questions.explanation: In public health and immunology, certain vaccines can be used for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) because the immune system can mount a protective response faster than the virus can complete its incubation period. Measles (Option B) is the classic example of this. The incubation period for measles is approximately 10-14 days, whereas the live-attenuated measles vaccine induces protective antibodies within 3-5 days of administration. Therefore, if a susceptible individual is vaccinated within 72 hours of exposure, the infection can often be prevented or significantly modified. Coronavirus (Option A), Polio (Option C), and Mumps (Option D) have varying incubation periods and seroconversion rates, but they are not the standard examples used to illustrate this specific epidemiological concept as effectively as measles. This property makes measles vaccination a critical emergency response tool during outbreaks in refugee camps or schools. Susceptible contacts of a measles case should always be prioritized for immediate vaccination
questions.learning: In public health and immunology, certain vaccines can be used for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) because the immune system can mount a protective response faster than the virus can complete its incubation period.

• This is a health outcome indicator reflecting improvement in the overall health status of the population.

2. Health Systems Performance → More than 90% of newborns fully immunized by one year of age by 2025 ✓

• Immunization coverage is a health system performance indicator, reflecting the effectiveness of service delivery.

3. Health Systems Strengthening → Increase State sector health spending to more than 8% of their budget by 2020 ✓

• Increasing government health expenditure strengthens infrastructure, workforce, and service delivery, making it a health systems strengthening target.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old homeless man comes to the emergency department due to a "pins-and-needles" sensation in his legs. He also has painful lesions on his lips and corners of his mouth. Abdominal examination reveals hepatomegaly. Laboratory evaluation shows very low urinary riboflavin excretion. Activity of which of the following enzymes is most likely directly impaired in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Succinate dehydrogenase

Riboflavin (vitamin B₂) is the precursor for FAD and FMN, which are essential cofactors for flavoproteins. Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II of the ETC) is an FAD-dependent enzyme, and its activity is directly impaired in riboflavin deficiency. This leads to defects in oxidative phosphorylation and energy metabolism, which contributes to neuropathy and muscle weakness seen in this patient.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase: NADP⁺-dependent; indirectly affected by riboflavin deficiency but not directly FAD-dependent.

B. HMG-CoA reductase: Requires NADPH, not FAD/FMN.

C. Isocitrate dehydrogenase: Uses NAD⁺ or NADP⁺, not FAD/FMN.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A couple brings their 4-year-old child to the outpatient department due to self-mutilating behavior and poor growth. Which condition and associated enzyme deficiency could explain these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Self-mutilation (such as biting lips and fingers) combined with poor growth and neurological symptoms like dystonia is the hallmark of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. This X-linked recessive disorder is caused by a near-complete deficiency of the enzyme Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). HGPRT is essential for the purine salvage pathway; its absence leads to massive overproduction of uric acid. This results in hyperuricemia, gouty arthritis, and severe neurological dysfunction. Homogentisic Aciduria (Option B) is Alkaptonuria, which causes dark urine and joint cartilage damage but not self-mutilation. Phenylalanine Hydroxylase deficiency (Option C) causes Phenylketonuria (PKU), leading to intellectual disability and a "mousy" odor, but not the specific aggressive self-harm seen in Lesch-Nyhan. Benzoyl Acidase deficiency (Option D) is not a standard clinical metabolic disorder associated with these symptoms. Therefore, HGPRT deficiency is the definitive enzymatic diagnosis for a child presenting with this unique behavioral phenotype
questions.learning: Self-mutilation (such as biting lips and fingers) combined with poor growth and neurological symptoms like dystonia is the hallmark of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a COPD patient what is the critical value of FEV1 for patients to develop resting hypoxemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 30%

COPD + FEV₁ < 30% predicted → resting hypoxemia begins to appear.

• FEV₁ (Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second)

→ Measures severity of airflow obstruction

In COPD, as FEV₁ falls:

• Air trapping ↑
• V/Q mismatch ↑
• Gas exchange ↓

Eventually → hypoxemia at rest

| GOLD Stage | FEV₁ (% predicted) | Severity | Clinical Impact

| ---------- | ------------------ | -------- | ---------------

| GOLD 1 | ≥80% | Mild | Minimal symptoms

| GOLD 2 | 50–79% | Moderate | Dyspnea on exertion

| GOLD 3 | 30–49% | Severe | Marked limitation

| GOLD 4 | <30% | Very severe | Resting hypoxemia

Mechanisms:

1. V/Q mismatch (MOST IMPORTANT)

• Some areas ventilated but not perfused properly

2. Alveolar hypoventilation

• Leads to CO₂ retention (Type II RF)

3.

Loss of alveolar surface area (emphysema)

4.

FEV₁ <30% = critical threshold

5. First: exertional hypoxemia
6. Later: resting hypoxemia
7. COPD death often due to:

• Respiratory failure
• Cor pulmonale
