questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 3-year-old child is brought with extensive burn injuries affecting the entire head, neck, and upper limb. Based on this distribution, what is the estimated percentage of total body surface area burned?
questions.explanation: Burn area in children is calculated differently than in adults due to their larger head-to-body ratio. According to the adjusted Rule of Nines, the entire head and neck of a child account for approximately 18% of the total body surface area (TBSA). Each individual upper limb accounts for 9% of the TBSA. In this case, adding the 18% for the head and neck to the 9% for one upper limb results in a total of 27%. This value falls within the 25–30% range provided in Option A. Option B (40–44%) would imply much more extensive injuries, such as both arms or parts of the trunk. Option C (18–20%) only accounts for the head and neck without the upper limb. Option D (5–10%) is a severe underestimation. Therefore, 27% (rounded to the 25–30% range) is the accurate clinical estimation for this 3-year-old child
questions.learning: Burn area in children is calculated differently than in adults due to their larger head-to-body ratio. According to the adjusted Rule of Nines, the entire head and neck of a child account for approximately 18% of the total body surface area (TBSA).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following health programmes supports DANIDA?
questions.explanation: The Danish International Development Agency (DANIDA) specifically supports the National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB) in India. Its assistance focuses on providing high-quality eye care services, particularly cataract surgeries, and developing the necessary infrastructure and professional training to reduce preventable blindness. Regarding the distractors, the TB control program (Option A) has historically been assisted by SIDA (Swedish International Development Agency) and the World Bank. Malaria eradication efforts (Option C) are primarily supported by USAID and the Global Fund. HIV/AIDS programs (Option D) receive significant backing from NACO and international agencies like UNAIDS and the Global Fund, rather than DANIDA. Therefore, DANIDA’s primary contribution to India’s public health landscape is through the NPCB

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the condition depicted in the given image, and what is the next investigation required for management?
questions.explanation: The image shows a well-defined red patch on the oral mucosa, consistent with erythroplakia. Erythroplakia is a premalignant lesion characterized by a velvety red appearance and is clinically more significant than leukoplakia because it has a much higher risk of malignant transformation. Histologically, a large proportion of erythroplakic lesions show severe epithelial dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, or even invasive carcinoma at the time of diagnosis. Therefore, the next step in management is an immediate biopsy to establish a definitive diagnosis and assess the degree of dysplasia or malignancy. Early detection is crucial for appropriate treatment and improved prognosis. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Erythroplakia and observation: Not appropriate due to high malignant potential; delay can be dangerous. (C) Leukoplakia and biopsy: Leukoplakia appears as a white patch, unlike this red lesion. (D) Leukoplakia and observation: Incorrect diagnosis and inappropriate management. Hence, erythroplakia always warrants prompt biopsy

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is a true statement about congenital CMV infection?
options: About 20-30% of the infections are symptomatic
Triad of SNHL, periventricular calcification and enamel hypoplasia
Most children asymptomatic at birth can develop conductive hearing loss later in life
If mother is IgG positive for CMV, the child is unlikely to develop infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. If mother is IgG positive for CMV, the child is unlikely to develop infection

If the mother is IgG positive for CMV, then the child is unlikely to develop the infection.

In one-third of mothers who develop a primary infection during pregnancy, the virus gets transmitted to the fetus. In previously infected mothers with IgG antibodies, only 1-3% would transmit the virus to the fetus.

Most CMV transmission occurs in the first trimester. The risk of transmission is high in the third trimester. Only 10% of infants with congenital CMV infection are symptomatic (option A).

Hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, and petechiae constitute the clinical triad (option B) in congenital CMV. Neuroimaging shows intracranial periventricular calcifications. Other manifestations include IUGR, hydrops, microcephaly, pneumonitis, chorioretinitis, seizures, sensorineural hearing loss, abnormal dentition, and hypocalcified enamel.

About half of the symptomatic infants develop long-term sequelae which include sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), vision loss, seizure disorders, mental retardation, and developmental delay. But in asymptomatic infants, only about 13.5% develop long-term sequelae which is commonly SNHL (option C).

The investigation of choice is PCR or viral culture. It should be done within the first two to three weeks of life. After this period, it is difficult to distinguish between a congenital and an acquired infection. Since not all affected infants are viremic at birth, urine and/or saliva are more reliable samples than blood.

There is no definitive treatment for congenital CMV infection. Treatment with ganciclovir is indicated only in patients with progressive neurologic disease and deafness.
questions.learning: If mother is IgG positive for CMV, the child is unlikely to develop infection If the mother is IgG positive for CMV, then the child is unlikely to develop the infection.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The investigation of choice for ovarian torsion is?
questions.explanation: Ovarian torsion—the twisting of the ovary on its vascular pedicle—is a surgical emergency. The investigation of choice for rapid bedside diagnosis is Color Doppler Ultrasonography. The hallmark finding is the partial or complete absence of blood flow to the ovary, often accompanied by an enlarged, edematous ovary with peripheral follicles (the "string of pearls" sign). While the diagnosis must be clinically correlated (Option B) with severe, acute pelvic pain and nausea, USG Doppler provides the objective evidence needed to proceed to surgery. MRI (Option C) and CT (Option D) are less appropriate in an acute setting due to the time and cost involved, though they may show ovarian enlargement. It is important to note that the presence of some blood flow on Doppler does not rule out torsion if the clinical suspicion is high. Immediate laparoscopy is required to untwist (detorse) the ovary and restore blood flow to prevent irreversible infarction and loss of the gonad
questions.learning: Ovarian torsion—the twisting of the ovary on its vascular pedicle—is a surgical emergency. The investigation of choice for rapid bedside diagnosis is Color Doppler Ultrasonography.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the most likely cause when a patient under general anaesthesia develops left lung collapse after intubation, with breath sounds heard only on the right side during auscultation? PPV-Positive pressure ventillation
options: Mucus secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube
Pneumothorax on the left side due to PPV
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right endobronchial intubation

The most likely cause of left lung collapse after intubation, with breath sounds heard only on the right side, is endobronchial intubation of the right main bronchus.

Endobronchial intubation is first indicated by a sudden rise in peak inspiratory pressure.
Capnography and detection of end-tidal CO2 is the confirmation for an advanced airway placement, but it does not differentiate endotracheal from endobronchial intubation.

Signs of endobronchial intubation:

* Elevated peak inspiratory pressure (first sign)

* Asymmetric chest expansion

* Unilateral breath sounds

* Drop in oxygen saturation (hypoxemia)

Other options:

Option A: Mucus secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube- will lead to diminished breath on both sides.

Option B: Pneumothorax on the left side due to PPV- less likely to occur immediately after intubation. It may be seen after prolonged PPV, post-intubation. It is a serious complication of mechanical ventilation. It is rare in intubated patients with normal lungs and most patients with pneumothorax related to mechanical ventilation (PRMV) have underlying lung diseases that range from primary obstructive lung disease to secondary pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Excessive airway pressure during mechanical ventilation can rupture alveoli, leading to air leakage into the pleural space → pneumothorax.

Option C: Intraoperative bronchospasm is usually manifested as wheezing, increasing peak airway pressure, and a slowly rising waveform on the capnograph.
questions.learning: Right endobronchial intubation — The most likely cause of left lung collapse after intubation, with breath sounds heard only on the right side, is endobronchial intubation of the right main bronchus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure marked as 'X' in image A has a direct connection with which of the following structures marked in image B?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1

Image A shows a section of the cerebellum and image B shows a section of the midbrain. The structure labeled as 'X' represents the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum, which has a direct connection with the structure marked as '1', which is the red nucleus.

The dentate nucleus is the largest of the cerebellar nuclei. It has the shape of a crumpled bag with the opening facing medially. The interior of the bag is filled with white matter made up of efferent fibers that leave the nucleus through the opening to form a large part of the superior cerebellar peduncle.

The efferent pathways from the dentate nucleus connect to the thalamus and the red nucleus, via the dentato- rubro -thalamic pathway.

Other structures in the image B :

2 - Represents superior colliculus, which receives afferents from the retina and the occipital cortex.

3 - Represents substantia nigra, which receives afferents mainly from the caudate nucleus

4 - Represents the crus cerebri, which contains fibers from the cerebral cortex.
questions.learning: 1 Image A shows a section of the cerebellum and image B shows a section of the midbrain. The structure labeled as 'X' represents the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum, which has a direct connection with the structure marked as '1', which is the red nucleus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A female patient presented with fatigue. Routine complete blood count analysis showed hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, MCV 60fL, and RBC count of 5.2 million. A peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia. Which of the following is the next best investigation for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HbA2 levels

The next best investigation for this patient would be determining the HbA2 levels, as the history of reduced hemoglobin, reduced MCV (microcytic anemia) and normal to high RBC count is suggestive of thalassemia.

The MCV count divided by the RBC count is called the Mentzer index, which is lower than 13 in thalassemia due to the normal to high RBC count in the denominator. In iron deficiency anemia, it is higher than 13 as the MCV and the RBC count both are reduced.

Alpha- and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively. This leads to precipitation of the excess (unpaired) chains, interfering with red blood cell (RBC) production and survival.

Clinical features in thalassemia include anemia, jaundice, skeletal deformities including facial deformities, changes in body habitus, growth impairment, and hepatosplenomegaly. Due to frequent blood transfusions, iron overload is also seen.

Peripheral smear is likely to show microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, teardrop cells, and some coarse basophilic stippling in certain cases.

The image given below shows peripheral smear findings in thalassemia.

An X-ray of the skull shows a crewcut appearance due to expansion of hematopoetically active marrow.

Thalassemia is usually managed by blood transfusions every 2-4 weeks and chelation therapy with deferoxamine, deferasirox, and deferiprone for iron chelation. Splenectomy is indicated when the transfusion requirement to maintain ideal hemoglobin increases. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the only known curative treatment for thalassemia.

Other options:

Option A: Serum ferritin level is used to diagnose iron-deficiency anemia (IDA). They are usually low in IDA.

Option C: Serum folate level is used to diagnose macrocytic anemia due to a deficiency of folic acid.

Option D: Serum homocysteine levels are increased in vitamin B12–deficient macrocytic anemia.
questions.learning: HbA2 levels — The next best investigation for this patient would be determining the HbA2 levels, as the history of reduced hemoglobin, reduced MCV (microcytic anemia) and normal to high RBC count is suggestive of thalassemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids primarily acts as a buffer in blood due to its ability to accept and donate protons at physiological pH?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histidine

At physiological pH, buffering action in blood is caused by histidine.

The imidazole group of histidine has a pKa value of 6.5-7.4, which is close to physiological pH.

Histidine is a positively charged amino acid that can exist in both its protonated (positively charged) and deprotonated (neutral) forms. It acts as a buffer by accepting or donating protons (H+ ions) in response to changes in pH, helping to maintain the blood's pH within a narrow physiological range.

Hence, histidine has the maximum buffering capacity at physiological pH.

Other options:

Option B: Arginine is a semi-essential amino acid involved in protein synthesis, wound healing, and immune function. It also serves as a precursor for nitric oxide, which regulates blood flow and vascular health.

Option C: Tryptophan is an essential amino acid that serves as a precursor for serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in mood regulation. It is also a precursor for melatonin, which plays a key role in regulating sleep-wake cycles.

Option D: Tyrosine is a non-essential amino acid that plays a crucial role in the synthesis of neurotransmitters such as dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. It also contributes to the production of thyroid hormones and melanin.
questions.learning: Histidine At physiological pH, buffering action in blood is caused by histidine. The imidazole group of histidine has a pKa value of 6.5-7.4, which is close to physiological pH.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under which provision of the Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) Act are beneficiaries entitled to receive 70% of their wages for a period of three months?
questions.explanation: Under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act, the Sickness Benefit provides cash compensation to insured workers during periods of certified illness. Eligible beneficiaries receive approximately 70% of their average daily wages for a maximum duration of 91 days (roughly 3 months) in two consecutive benefit periods. Medical benefit (Option B) refers to the direct provision of medical care and treatment to the worker and their family but does not involve cash wage compensation. Maternity benefit (Option C) provides full wages (100%) for 26 weeks for pregnancy. Dependent's benefit (Option D) involves a monthly pension for family members if the worker dies due to an employment-related injury. The 70% wage replacement for 3 months is the characteristic financial structure of the standard sickness cash benefit. This social security measure ensures that workers do not face total income loss due to temporary physical incapacity, provided they have met the contribution requirements
questions.learning: Under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act, the Sickness Benefit provides cash compensation to insured workers during periods of certified illness.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young woman came to the clinic requesting a post-coital pill. Which of the following would you prescribe?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Levonorgestrel

Levonorgestrel can be prescribed to a young woman requesting a post-coital pill.

Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, can be used for emergency contraception. Alternatively, it can also be administered in two doses of 0.75 mg. The first dose is taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, and the 2nd dose is taken 12 hours apart. The tablets can be offered up to 120 hours but the efficacy decreases with the longer coital-drug interval.

Advantages of LNG tablets:

* It has no estrogen and its associated side effects.

* It can be offered to hypertensive, cardiac and diabetic women.

* It can be offered to a lactating woman.

* It can be given as late as 120 hours after unprotected intercourse (but efficacy decreases).

* Single-dose therapy is an advantage.

Combined oral pills consisting of both estrogen and progesterone act on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to inhibit the release of GnRH (and thus subsequently LH and FSH) and thus inhibit ovulation.

Emergency contraception refers to backup methods for contraceptive emergencies that women can use within the first few days after unprotected intercourse to prevent an unwanted pregnancy. Administration of postcoital contraceptive agents that interfere with postovulatory events that can lead to pregnancy.

The various emergency contraceptive methods, along with their mechanism of action have been described below:

* Ethinyl estradiol 50 μg + norgestrel 0.25 mg is administered as two tablets within 72 hours of coitus, followed by the 2 tablets after 12 hours. The hormone may delay ovulation if taken soon after intercourse.

* Ulipristal is given as a 30 mg tablet and should be taken within 5 days. It is a synthetic progesterone hormone receptor modulator. The drug attaches to the progesterone receptor, delays ovulation, and suppresses endometrium, thereby preventing implantation.

* IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device) prevents the implantation of a fertilized ovum. It does so by acting as a foreign body within the uterine cavity. This leads to increased contractility, tubal peristalsis, and leukocytic infiltration in the endometrium.

* Centchroman is administered as two tablets of 60 mg, taken twice over a duration of 24 hours and within 24 hours of intercourse. It acts by preventing the implantation of the blastocyst in the endometrium.

Pearl PF1657: Hormonal contraceptives

Oral pills:

* Combined oral contraceptive pills (COC)

* Mala D - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate

* Mala N - Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg + Ethinyl estradiol  0.03 mg + Ferrous fumarate (Govt. supply, free of cost)

* Progesterone only pills (POP) - suitable for lactating women

* Norethisterone 350 μg

* Norgestrel 75 μg

* Levonorgestrel (LNG) 30 μg

* Once a month or long-acting pills - highly disappointing results

* Quinestrol (long-acting estrogen) + short-acting progesterone

* Gossypol - male pill : Cottonseed derivative and causes azoospermia and severe oligospermia

* Post-coital pills or interceptive

* Levonorgestrel 0.75 mg, 2 doses, 12 hours apart

* Mifepristone 10-600 mg

* Ulipristal 30 mg, within 5 days of intercourse

* Centchroman 60 mg, 2 tablets, within 24 hrs of intercourse

* GnRH agonists

* CuT IUCD, inserted within 5 days

Injectable contraceptives

* Progesterone only injectables

* DMPA 150 mg IM every 3 months

* NET-EN 200 mg IM every 2 months

* Combined injectables

* Cyclofem - DMPA 25 mg + Estradiol cypionate 5 mg

* Mesigyna - NET-EN 50 mg  + Estradiol valerate 5 mg

Subdermal implants

* Norplant I - Levonorgestrel 35 mg

* Norplant II or Jadelle - 2 rods with levonorgestrel 70 mg in each and released at a rate of 50 μg/day

Others

* Hormonal IUCD - Mirena which contains LNG 52 mg with release rate of 20 μg/day

* Orthoevra patch - Norelgestomin + Ethinyl estradiol weekly for 3 weeks, then patch free for 1 week

* Vaginal ring or Nuvaring - Etonogestrel + ethinyl estradiol daily release, use for 3 weeks with withdrawal for 1 week
questions.learning: Levonorgestrel Levonorgestrel can be prescribed to a young woman requesting a post-coital pill. Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse, can be used for emergency contraception.

questions.explanation:

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A full-term neonate develops tachypnea and central cyanosis within a few hours of birth. Pulse oximetry reveals an oxygen saturation of 96% in the right hand and 84% in the left foot. Femoral pulses are palpable with no brachiofemoral delay. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal heart but markedly elevated pulmonary artery pressures. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)

In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), the normal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) after birth fails to occur. As a result:

• Pulmonary artery pressure remains abnormally high.
• Blood is shunted right-to-left through the patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and/or foramen ovale.
• The right upper limb (preductal) receives blood before it mixes with deoxygenated blood at the ductus, resulting in a higher oxygen saturation than the lower limbs (postductal).

This produces the characteristic finding of: Preductal SpO₂ > Postductal SpO₂

The presence of a structurally normal heart with elevated pulmonary pressures strongly supports the diagnosis of PPHN.

Why not the other options?

• A. Coarctation of the aorta: Typically presents with weak femoral pulses and radiofemoral/brachiofemoral delay, which are absent in this infant.
• B. Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR): Causes cyanosis but echocardiography would demonstrate anomalous pulmonary venous drainage rather than a structurally normal heart.
• D. Eisenmenger syndrome: Develops over years as a consequence of long-standing congenital left-to-right shunts and does not occur in the neonatal period.
questions.learning: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), the normal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) after birth fails to occur.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All of the following variables are measured on nominal scale, except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Severity of disease

A nominal scale classifies data into distinct categories without any inherent order, such as gender or vaccine status.

| Scale | Characteristics | Example

| ----- | --------------- | -------

| Nominal | Categories without order | Gender, blood group

| Ordinal | Categories with order | Disease severity

| Interval | Numeric scale with equal intervals | Temperature (°C)

| Ratio | Numeric with true zero | Height, weight

Pain (present/absent) can also be treated as nominal when not graded.

Severity of disease implies an ordered progression (mild, moderate, severe), which places it on an ordinal scale, not nominal.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the principle behind the wound-healing procedure shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Negative pressure wound therapy

The given image shows negative pressure wound therapy using a vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) device to promote healing in chronic wounds.

Principle: An intermittent negative pressure of -125 mmHg hastens debridement and formation of granulation tissue in chronic wounds.

Indications: Chronic wounds (such as diabetic foot ulcers, stage III and IV pressure ulcers), traumatic wounds, flaps and grafts, and dehisced incisions.

Contraindications:

1. Exposed vital structures (organs, blood vessels, or vascular grafts)
2. Preexisting infection
3. Inadequate debridement of devitalized soft tissue or bone increases the risk of infection.
4. The presence of malignancy (Marjolin’s ulcer).
5. An allergic reaction towards the adhesive used to maintain the vacuum seal.

Though not an absolute contraindication, there is no appreciable benefit for ischemic wounds.
questions.learning: Negative pressure wound therapy — The given image shows negative pressure wound therapy using a vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) device to promote healing in chronic wounds.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a contraindication of Renal Biopsy?
options: Acute renal injury of uncertain etiology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Uncontrolled hypertension

Uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication to percutaneous renal biopsy because markedly elevated blood pressure significantly increases the risk of severe bleeding and perirenal hematoma following the procedure. Blood pressure should be adequately controlled before performing the biopsy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Nephritic syndrome: Often an indication for renal biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain or histological classification will guide treatment.
• B. Acute renal injury of uncertain etiology: Renal biopsy may be indicated when the cause remains unclear after initial evaluation.
• D. Renal transplant dysfunction: Allograft biopsy is commonly performed to evaluate causes such as acute rejection, drug toxicity, recurrent disease, or infection.
questions.learning: Uncontrolled hypertension Uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication to percutaneous renal biopsy because markedly elevated blood pressure significantly increases the risk of severe bleeding and perirenal hematoma following the procedure.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with diffuse abdominal pain, and on examination, there is generalised tenderness along with board-like abdominal rigidity. An X-ray of the abdomen is provided. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Perforation peritonitis

The given clinical scenario and the chest radiograph showing air under the diaphragm are suggestive of a hollow viscus perforation resulting in perforation peritonitis.

Perforation of a viscus is a life-threatening condition that occurs following the rupture of the alimentary tract. This leads to the leakage of the enteric contents, thereby leading to acute bacterial peritonitis. Peritonitis is the generalized or localized inflammation of the peritoneum either due to the free spillage of fluids into the peritoneal cavity or secondary bacterial infection.

Clinical features of hollow viscous perforation occur due to the developed peritonitis and the features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Sometimes, features of septic shock can be seen at later stages.

Investigations include estimating the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus. The below image shows a hollow viscus perforation.

Management of a hollow viscous perforation is mainly resuscitation, analgesics, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency laparotomy. Peritonitis is managed by nutritional support, pain relief, correction of fluid loss and circulating volume, urinary catheterization with or without gastrointestinal compression, antibiotics, analgesics, and specific surgical treatment of the cause.

Other Options:

Option A: Clinical presentation of acute pancreatitis is characterized by epigastric pain radiating to the back which is relieved by bending forward, nausea, and vomiting.

Option C: Duodenal ulcer pain occurs 1.5 to 3 hours after a meal and is frequently relieved by antacids or food. Gastric Ulcer pain/discomfort may be precipitated by food. Nausea and weight loss are common.

Option D: A hiatal hernia occurs when a portion of the stomach pushes through the diaphragm into the chest cavity. It can cause symptoms such as heartburn, regurgitation, and chest pain, and may require medical or surgical treatment.
questions.learning: Perforation peritonitis — The given clinical scenario and the chest radiograph showing air under the diaphragm are suggestive of a hollow viscus perforation resulting in perforation peritonitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly lady was diagnosed to have a gallbladder polyp. She was told that she has a risk for gallbladder cancer. Which of the following is not a risk factor for gallbladder cancer?
options: A single gall bladder polyp < 1 cm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A single gall bladder polyp < 1 cm

A single gallbladder polyp <1 cm is not a risk factor for carcinoma gallbladder. Gallbladder polyps >10mm have malignant potential.

Risk factors for carcinoma gallbladder:

• Gallstones of size >3 cm (most important risk factor)
• Porcelain gallbladder
• Anomalous pancreato-biliary junction
• Choledochal cyst
• Adenomatous polyps
• Primary sclerosing cholangitis
• Obesity
• Salmonella typhii infection.

Gallbladder carcinoma is a rare malignancy that is seen in the elderly. It is associated with a poor prognosis and is indistinguishable from cholecystitis or cholelithiasis. It is usually diagnosed when patients undergo cholecystectomy for gallstones.

Its clinical features include right upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Jaundice is a late feature. CA 19-9 is elevated in the carcinoma gallbladder and is used for monitoring.

The preoperative diagnosis is often made on ultrasonography and followed up by a CT scan or MRI/Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography.

A percutaneous biopsy under radiological guidance is done for pathological examination. PET scanning helps in detecting metastatic disease.

In select cases, a laparoscopic examination is useful in staging the disease. Laparoscopy can also detect peritoneal or liver metastases. The most important prognostic factor is the depth of invasion (T-stage).
questions.learning: A single gall bladder polyp 10mm have malignant potential. Risk factors for carcinoma gallbladder: • Gallstones of size >3 cm (most important risk factor) • Porcelain gallbladder • Anomalous pancreato-biliary junction • Choledochal cyst • Adenomatous…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Marked structure is derived from the______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endocardial cushions

The structure marked is the membranous part of the interventricular septum. It is derived from endocardial cushions.

Endocardial cushions are soft tissue masses that protrude in the atrioventricular and conotruncal regions.

• Atrioventricular cushions are derived from overlying endocardial cells.
• The conotruncal cushions are derived from the neural crest cells.

Endocardial cushions contribute to the formation of:

• Atrial septa
• Ventricular septa (membranous portion)
• Atrioventricular canals
• Atrioventricular valves
• Aortic and pulmonary channels

Defects in endocardial cushion formation can result in cardiac malformations, including ASDs, VSDs, and defects involving the great vessels (transposition of the great vessels, common truncus arteriosus, and tetralogy of Fallot).
questions.learning: Endocardial cushions — The structure marked is the membranous part of the interventricular septum. It is derived from endocardial cushions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient who has taken the first COVID vaccine comes for the second dose. An astute nurse noticed that the shoulder was flabby, flat, and was asymmetrical. There was an associated loss of contour of the shoulder joint. Injury to which of the structures might have resulted and was avoidable?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Axillary nerve

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of injury to axillary nerve which leads to deltoid muscle palsy.

The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid muscle. Iatrogenic injuries of the axillary nerve can occur due to incorrectly administered IM injection or while performing transaxillary operations on the shoulder with lateral deltoid-splitting incisions. But, note that this nerve is commonly injured during shoulder dislocation (most commonly anterior type) or fractures of the humeral neck as both the nerve and the posterior circumflex vessels (Option-B) pass horizontally and posterior to the neck of the humerus.

Injury to the axillary nerve can lead to:

• Weakness of abduction and lateral rotation of the arm
• Retropulsion (extension of the shoulder with the arm abducted to 90 degrees) is impossible.
• Atrophy of the Deltoid muscle leading to the loss of muscle contours of the shoulder
• Loss of sensation in the Regimental badge area

Note:

Upper (superior) lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm (Option-C) that innervates the skin over the lower deltoid (regimental badge area). Thus, this is not the best of the given four options.

The images below show the Seargent/regimental badge sign and the various anatomical structures that can be appreciated in the transverse section of the shoulder joint respectively.

Vaccine administration in the deltoid can sometimes injure the axillary and the radial nerve.
questions.learning: Axillary nerve — The given clinical vignette is suggestive of injury to axillary nerve which leads to deltoid muscle palsy. The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid muscle.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: From the X-ray given, pick out the probable diagnosis:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pneumoperitoneum

The above X-ray clearly shows the presence of subdiaphragmatic free gas in the right upper quadrant. This indicates pneumoperitoneum.

Pneumoperitoneum is the presence of free gas within the peritoneal cavity but outside the viscera. The most common cause of pneumoperitoneum is bowel perforation.

• Gastric and posterior duodenal perforations are seen in long-standing cases of peptic ulcers.
• Intestinal perforations are seen with ischemia, inflammation, diverticula, or obstruction.
• Other causes also include iatrogenic, penetrating injuries, prolonged mechanical ventilation, peritoneal dialysis, etc.

Signs of pneumoperitoneum:

• Bowel-related signs

• Double wall sign/Rigler's sign/gas-relief sign- Air is seen on both sides of the bowel wall.
• Telltale triangle sign/triangle sign - Triangle of gas formed between three loops of the bowel or between the abdominal wall and two loops of the bowel.

• Peritoneal ligament-related signs

• Football sign- Air outlines the confines of the peritoneal cavity
• Falciform ligament sign-  Air outlines the falciform ligament
• Lateral umbilical ligament sign/inverted "V" sign- Air outlines the lateral umbilical ligament
• Urachus sign - Air outlines the urachus

• Right upper quadrant signs

• Cupola sign- Air outlines the median subphrenic space
• Fissure for ligamentum teres sign- Air outlines the ligamentum teres
• Hepatic edge sign- Cigar-shaped free-air pocket in the subhepatic region. It tracks superomedial following the contours of the liver
• Lucent liver sign - Reduction of hepatic radiodensity due to accumulation of free gas anterior to the liver
• Morison's pouch sign / Doge cap sign - Triangular/ crescentic gas lucency bound by the 11th rib
• Periportal free gas sign.
questions.learning: Pneumoperitoneum — The above X-ray clearly shows the presence of subdiaphragmatic free gas in the right upper quadrant. Pneumoperitoneum is the presence of free gas within the peritoneal cavity but outside the viscera.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: During isometric (static) exercise, which of the following hemodynamic changes is most characteristic?
options: Increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure
Increase in stroke volume with fall in heart rate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure

During isometric (static) exercise (e.g., handgrip, weight holding), sustained muscle contraction compresses blood vessels within the muscle, increasing total peripheral resistance (TPR). Hemodynamic effects:

• Sympathetic activation
• Increased heart rate and cardiac output
• Increased total peripheral resistance

As a result, both systolic and diastolic blood pressure rise.

Contrast with dynamic exercise:

• Dynamic exercise (running, cycling): ↓ TPR due to vasodilation → SBP ↑ but DBP normal or ↓.
• Isometric exercise: ↑ TPR → both SBP and DBP increase.
questions.learning: Increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure During isometric (static) exercise (e.g., handgrip, weight holding), sustained muscle contraction compresses blood vessels within the muscle, increasing total peripheral resistance (TPR).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with progressively worsening shortness of breath over the past six months, along with a dry cough. On auscultation, bilateral basal end-inspiratory crepitations are heard. There is no history of fever, joint pain, or occupational exposure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive fibrosing lung disease typically seen in older adults. The clinical presentation of worsening exertional dyspnea and a nonproductive cough over several months is classic. The most characteristic physical finding on auscultation is bilateral basal end-inspiratory "Velcro" crackles (crepitations). The diagnosis of "idiopathic" is supported by the absence of systemic symptoms like fever, joint pain, or any known occupational exposures. Cor-pulmonale (Option A) refers to right heart failure resulting from chronic lung disease, not the primary lung disease itself. Sarcoidosis (Option B) usually presents with systemic features and hilar lymphadenopathy. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Option D) is typically linked to a clear history of organic dust exposure (e.g., birds or mold) and often has a more acute or subacute onset. Therefore, the described presentation is most consistent with IPF
questions.learning: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive fibrosing lung disease typically seen in older adults. The clinical presentation of worsening exertional dyspnea and a nonproductive cough over several months is classic.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents to you with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. A trephine biopsy aspirate shows the following finding. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glucocerebrosidase

The given clinical scenario of a child with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and trephine biopsy showing Gaucher's cell with a characteristic crumpled tissue paper appearance is suggestive of Gaucher's disease. The deficient enzyme is glucocerebrosidase (also known as beta-glucosidase).

Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues.

There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype.

Gaucher's cells are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance.
questions.learning: Glucocerebrosidase — The given clinical scenario of a child with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and trephine biopsy showing Gaucher's cell with a characteristic crumpled tissue paper appearance is suggestive of Gaucher's disease.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: The General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) primarily describes the body's response to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stressful situations

The General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) is a model developed by Hans Selye that describes the body's physiological response to stress. It outlines how the body responds to any demand (stressor) placed upon it, regardless of whether the stressor is physical, psychological, or environmental.

| Stage of GAS | Description | Physiological Changes

| ------------ | ----------- | ---------------------

| Alarm Reaction | Initial response to stressor | Activation of sympathetic nervous system, release of adrenaline and cortisol

| Resistance | Body's attempt to adapt to continued stress | Continued hormone secretion but at more sustainable levels

| Exhaustion | Resources depleted after prolonged stress | Inability to maintain adaptation, vulnerability to illness
questions.learning: Stressful situations — The General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) is a model developed by Hans Selye that describes the body's physiological response to stress.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with recurrent headaches and is found to have raised intracranial pressure. Imaging reveals a tumor arising from the dura. Which histopathological feature is most characteristic of her condition?
options: Psammoma bodies with whorling of tumor cells
questions.explanation: The clinical description of a middle-aged female with a dura-based tumor and signs of raised intracranial pressure is highly classic for a Meningioma. Meningiomas are the most common primary brain tumors in adults and are typically benign. The hallmark histological findings include tumor cells arranged in concentric, "onion-skin" whorls and the presence of Psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concretions). A "fried egg appearance" (Option A) is characteristic of oligodendrogliomas (due to perinuclear halos). Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (Option B) are seen in retinoblastomas. Homer Wright rosettes (Option D) are found in primitive neuroectodermal tumors like medulloblastomas or neuroblastomas. Because meningiomas grow from the arachnoid cap cells, they are typically found on the surface of the brain attached to the dura, often causing symptoms through compression. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice and is usually curative. Recognizing the specific whorled pattern and calcified Psammoma bodies is essential for the pathological diagnosis of this common intracranial neoplasm
questions.learning: The clinical description of a middle-aged female with a dura-based tumor and signs of raised intracranial pressure is highly classic for a Meningioma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Vessel A has a length of L and diameter of D and vessel B has 2L and 2D. Considering the flow is laminar through both the cylinders, the flow through B is how many times as much as the flow through A?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 8 times

Flow through B will be 8 times more than the flow through A.

According to Poiseuille Hagen formula,

F= ΔP x π/8 x 1/n x r4/L

F = flow

ΔP = pressure difference between two ends of the tube

η = viscosity

r = radius of the tube

L = length of the tube

Hence flow directly varies to the 4th power of radius and inversely varies to length.

Flow through B = (2r)4/2L = 8 times

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is true about nicotine replacement therapy?
options: Nicotine gums are better than lozenges
Patient is instructed not to take liquids (tea/coffee) before taking the gum and for 15 minutes after taking the gum
Varenicline used for nicotine replacement therapy comes with a black box warning for cardiovascular side effects
Nicotine is delivered by the gastrointestinal route
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Patient is instructed not to take liquids (tea/coffee) before taking the gum and for 15 minutes after taking the gum

Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT) is a first-line treatment for tobacco dependence. It relieves nicotine withdrawal symptoms by delivering controlled doses of nicotine without the harmful toxins present in tobacco smoke. Nicotine gum is absorbed through the buccal mucosa, and acidic beverages (tea, coffee, soft drinks, fruit juices) should be avoided 15 minutes before and during use, as they reduce nicotine absorption.

Why not the other options?

• A. Nicotine gums are better than lozenges: Incorrect. Both are effective; the choice depends on patient preference and adherence.
• C. Varenicline used for nicotine replacement therapy comes with a black box warning for cardiovascular side effects: Incorrect. Varenicline is not a nicotine replacement product; it is a partial nicotinic (α4β2) receptor agonist. The previous boxed warning for neuropsychiatric adverse effects has been removed.
• D. Nicotine is delivered by the gastrointestinal route: Incorrect. NRT nicotine is primarily absorbed through the buccal mucosa (gum/lozenge), skin (patch), nasal mucosa (spray), or lungs (inhaler), not via the gastrointestinal tract.
questions.learning: Patient is instructed not to take liquids (tea/coffee) before taking the gum and for 15 minutes after taking the gum Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT) is a first-line treatment for tobacco dependence.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the average duration of lochial discharge in a puerperal woman?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 24-36 days

The average duration of lochial discharge in a puerperal woman is about 24-36 days. The average amount of discharge for the first week is 250 mL.

During early puerperium, sloughing of the decidual tissue causes vaginal discharge which is known as lochia. Most women experience an increase in the amount of bleeding at 7-14 days secondary to the sloughing of the eschar on the placental site. But the average duration of lochial discharge ranges from 24 to 36 days.

The lochial discharge appears as follows:

Name
Colour
Timing after delivery
Content

Lochia rubra
Red
First few days
Blood, decidua, fetal membranes, vernix, lanugo, meconium

Lochia serosa
Yellowish/Pink
After 3-4 days

WBC, cervical mucus, microorganisms

Lochia alba
Pale White
After 10th day
Decidua, cells, WBC, mucin, cholesterol crystals, and fat cells

The persistence of red lochia beyond one week might be an indicator of uterine subinvolution. The presence of an offensive odour, large pieces of tissue or blood clots in lochia, excessive or absence of lochia might be a sign of infection.
questions.learning: 24-36 days The average duration of lochial discharge in a puerperal woman is about 24-36 days. The average amount of discharge for the first week is 250 mL.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about laryngomalacia?
options: Patient will present with an inspiratory stridor.
It is the most common congenital cause of stridor in children.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stridor improves in supine position.

In laryngomalacia, stridor improves in prone position.

Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital cause of stridor. It is characterized by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic larynx which is sucked in during inspiration producing stridor and sometimes cyanosis.  It presents just after birth and subsides by 2 years of age. Stridor is increased on crying but improves (decreases) in the prone position, and worsens during feeding. The cry is normal.

Direct laryngoscopy shows -

* Elongated epiglottis, curled upon itself (omega-shaped)

* Floppy aryepiglottic folds, and

* Prominent arytenoids

A flexible laryngoscope is very useful to make the diagnosis. Laryngomalacia cannot be visualized in a paralyzed patient.

The below image shows the omega-shaped epiglottis:

Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. Stridor may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both

* Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

* Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis.

* Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g. laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

Treatment of Laryngomalacia:

* Mostly, it self corrects by 2 years of age.

* Tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction.

* Supraglottoplasty is required in cases of severe laryngomalacia.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

Important differentials:

Condition
Findings

Croup

Non-toxic, viral prodrome, barking cough

X-ray neck shows steeple sign

Epiglottitis

Toxic child, drooling saliva

Lateral X-ray neck shows thumb sign

Diphtheria
Cervical lymph nodes (bull neck), dirty grey/ white membrane, and un-immunized

Foreign body aspiration
Choking, decreased air entry, unilateral hyperinflation
questions.learning: Stridor improves in supine position. In laryngomalacia, stridor improves in prone position.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following staging systems is used in Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fisch staging system

The Fisch staging system is used in the case of Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibromas.

Type
Details

1
Tumour limited to the nasopharyngeal cavity; bone destruction negligible or limited to the sphenopalatine foramen

2
Tumour invading the pterygopalatine fossa or the maxillary, ethmoid, or sphenoid sinus with bone destruction

3
A: Tumour invading the infratemporal fossa or orbital region without intracranial involvement
B: Tumour invading the infratemporal fossa or orbital region with intracranial extradural (parasellar) involvement

4
A: Intracranial intradural tumor without infiltration of the cavernous sinus, pituitary fossa, or optic chiasm
B: Intracranial intradural tumor with infiltration of the cavernous sinus, pituitary fossa, or optic chiasm

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumor seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality.

Other options:

Option A: Duke staging system is done in cases of colorectal cancer

Option C: Ann arbor staging system is used in Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

Option D: TNM staging system is used to classify malignancies. It is most commonly utilized in solid tumors and can help with prognostic cancer staging. The system evaluates the tumor size, regional lymph nodes, and distant metastases.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to the biomedical waste management guidelines, a cotton swab used for cleaning should be discarded in which type of bag?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Yellow non-chlorinated

Under Biomedical Waste Management Rules (2016 and amendments), items soiled with blood or body fluids such as used cotton swabs, gauze, and dressings are categorized as soiled waste.

Soiled waste is disposed of in the yellow non-chlorinated bag, which is meant for incineration or deep burial.

| Examples of Waste | Category

| ----------------- | --------

| Cotton swabs contaminated with body fluids | Yellow

| Dressings and bandages | Yellow

| Human tissues or organs | Yellow

| Microbiology lab waste | Yellow

Red bags are reserved for contaminated recyclable plastics, and chlorinated bags are no longer recommended due to environmental concerns.
questions.learning: Yellow non-chlorinated Under Biomedical Waste Management Rules (2016 and amendments), items soiled with blood or body fluids such as used cotton swabs, gauze, and dressings are categorized as soiled waste.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child is brought to you with complaints of noisy breathing. On examination, you notice inspiratory stridor in the child and laryngeal examination is as below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Laryngomalacia

This child with inspiratory stridor and Omega-shaped epiglottis has laryngomalacia.

Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of stridor in newborns. It presents just after birth and subsides by 2 years of age. On examination, the omega-shaped epiglottis is seen.

Factors increasing Stridor in laryngomalacia:

* Supine Position

* Sleep

* Agitation

* URI (Upper Respiratory tract Infection)

Stridor is increased on crying but subsides on placing the child in a prone position; crying is normal.

Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. It may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both.

* Inspiratory stridor is often produced in obstructive lesions of supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

* Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g. laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

* Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of the thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis.

Treatment is mainly conservative. Tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction. In cases of severe laryngomalacia, supraglottoplasty is done.
questions.learning: Laryngomalacia — This child with inspiratory stridor and Omega-shaped epiglottis has laryngomalacia. Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of stridor in newborns.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient says that he feels that there is something wrong with him mentally and it is because of the summer season. How much would he score on the insight scale?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3

The patient would score 3, as he is aware of being sick but has attributed it to external factors.

Insight is rated on a 5 point scale:

1. Complete denial of illness.
2. Slight awareness of being sick and needing help but denying it at the same time.
3. Awareness of being sick, but is attributed to physical or external factors.
4. Intellectual insight - awareness of being ill, and that the symptoms are due to own particular irrational feelings and thoughts.
5. Emotional insight - the highest level of insight. Intellectual insight with making significant changes in future behavior.

Loss of insight is seen in schizophrenia, mania, delusional disorders, etc.
questions.learning: 3 The patient would score 3, as he is aware of being sick but has attributed it to external factors. Insight is rated on a 5 point scale: 1.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old female presented to the urologist with complaints of abdominal pain and recurrent urinary tract infections. Upon examination, the physician noted tenderness in the lower abdomen and a palpable mass in the right flank area. Further evaluation revealed the following. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelviureteric junction obstruction

The most likely diagnosis is A) Pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction.

• Abdominal pain
• Recurrent urinary tract infections
• Palpable flank mass

These symptoms commonly occur with chronic hydronephrosis due to PUJ obstruction, where urine cannot drain properly from the renal pelvis into the ureter.

CT image findings

From the CT scan:

• Marked hydronephrosis (very dilated renal pelvis)
• Ballooned renal pelvis
• Calyceal dilatation
• Abrupt narrowing at the PUJ
• Ureter distal to the PUJ is not dilated

This pattern is classic for PUJ obstruction.

Why are the other options wrong

B) Putty kidney

• Seen in renal tuberculosis, the kidney becomes calcified and shrunken
• CT would show dense calcification, not hydronephrosis.

C) Staghorn calculus

• Large branching stone filling renal pelvis and calyces.
• CT would show hyperdense calculus, not a huge fluid-filled pelvis.

D) Cystic kidney (e.g., polycystic kidney disease)

• Shows multiple cysts in both kidneys, not a single massively dilated pelvis.
questions.learning: Pelviureteric junction obstruction — The most likely diagnosis is A) Pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction. • Abdominal pain • Recurrent urinary tract infections • Palpable flank mass These symptoms commonly occur with chronic hydronephrosis due to PUJ…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which is the most common lacrimal gland tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pleomorphic adenoma

Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common lacrimal gland tumor. It is also the most common epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland.

Pleomorphic adenoma, or benign mixed tumor, presents commonly in middle age as a slowly progressive painless swelling in the upper outer quadrant of the eyelid. The bone is usually not invaded in these tumors. They are treated by surgical removal along with their intact pseudo-capsule.

Malignant tumors of the lacrimal gland such as adenoid cystic carcinoma (option A), mucoepidermoid carcinoma (option C) and malignant mixed tumor (option D) generally occur in the elderly with a short history of appearance, rapid progression and pain. These tumors also present in the upper eyelid and are known to invade the adjacent bones. Radical surgical procedures and high dose radiotherapy are necessary for the removal of the tumor. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is the most common malignant epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland.

Both malignant and benign tumors are known to push the eyeball downwards and inwards while restricting the upwards and outwards movement of the eyeball.

The most common epithelial tumors, in order of frequency, are as follows:

1. Benign mixed tumor (BMT), also known as a pleomorphic adenoma (PA)
2. Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC)
3. Pleomorphic adenocarcinoma (ACA)
4. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
questions.learning: Pleomorphic adenoma Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common lacrimal gland tumor. It is also the most common epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The mask given below works on which of the following principles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bernoulli principle

The given image shows a Venturi mask and it works using the Bernoulli principle in delivering a predetermined and fixed concentration of oxygen to the patient.

In the Venturi mask ,the size of the constriction present in the device determines the final concentration of oxygen for a given gas flow. This is achieved in spite of the patient's respiratory pattern by providing a higher gas flow than the peak inspiratory flow rate.

Patients with COPD require greater FiO2 than those provided by low-flow devices and are ideal candidates for the use of a Venturi mask.

In the Venturi mask system, oxygen inflow is connected to a specific color-coded entrainment device at the base of the mask that provides a set Fio2 at a set oxygen inflow rate. Various entrainment devices can provide a Fio2 of 0.24 to 0.5, with an oxygen inflow of 4 to 15 l/min and a delivered total flow of 35 to 45 l/min.
questions.learning: Bernoulli principle — The given image shows a Venturi mask and it works using the Bernoulli principle in delivering a predetermined and fixed concentration of oxygen to the patient.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common feature of third nerve palsy, in a case of long-standing, uncontrolled diabetes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ptosis

The most common feature seen in diabetic oculomotor palsy among the given options is ptosis.

In the anatomical arrangement of the nerve fibers of the 3rd cranial nerve, the fibers controlling the pupillary reflex are present superficially and are thus spared from diabetic ischemia-induced injury which starts from the central nerve fibres. Thus, pupil sparing is commonly seen in diabetic patients.

The etiology of diabetic neuropathy is hyperglycemia-induced damage to nerve cells and neuronal ischemic change due to microvascular angiopathy.

Involvement of the third cranial nerve is most common and it often presents with early features of ptosis and diplopia with pupil sparing.

The involvement of levator palpebrae superioris muscle of the eyelid manifests as ptosis and the involvement of extraocular muscles such as medial rectus,inferior rectus and inferior oblique presents as opthalmoplegia with diplopia. All the muscles mentioned above are supplied by the Occulomotor nerve.

Note: Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery is an important cause of isolated third nerve palsy with involvement of the pupil. This is because the aneurysm impinges on the superficial pupil nerve fibres of the 3rd cranial nerve.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is correct about the management of HIV patient with multiple dog bites?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rabies vaccine + immunoglobuin+ wound management

In the given scenario, an HIV patient with multiple dog bites falls under Category 3 for rabies vaccination and should receive rabies vaccine, immunoglobulin, and proper wound care.

Rabies is a fatal viral disease transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal, primarily dogs. Rabies vaccination is the most effective way to prevent the disease after exposure.

The post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimen includes thorough wound cleaning, administration of the rabies vaccine, and in severe cases (Category 3 exposure), rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) for immediate virus neutralization. The rabies vaccine is administered in a series of intramuscular or intradermal doses, following schedules like the Essen regimen (0, 3, 7, 14, and 28 days) or the Zagreb regimen (0, 7, and 21 days). Immediate treatment is crucial, as rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptoms appear.

In addition to post-exposure vaccination, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is recommended for individuals at high risk, such as veterinarians, animal handlers, and travellers to rabies-endemic regions. The PrEP schedule consists of two doses on days 0 and 7, with an optional booster if needed. Mass vaccination of dogs and public awareness programs are essential for rabies prevention and control. Since human rabies cases are still reported in many countries, widespread vaccination efforts play a critical role in achieving the WHO goal of eliminating human rabies deaths by 2030.

Pearl PF1934: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules

According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India:

WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.

One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size.

Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted).

Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG):

* Passive immunization

* Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine

* Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight

* Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG.

* Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus.

Administration of RIG:

* RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites.

* The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration.

* RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated.

Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order):

* Multiple bites

* Deep wounds

* Bites to head, neck, and hands

* Patients with severe immunodeficiency

* Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal

* Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

PrEP is considered in the following conditions:

* High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions.

* Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult

* Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year

* Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present.

Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of two intramuscular (IM) or two intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0 and 3.

* Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm

* Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended.

* Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers.

For exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP the following guidelines would be applicable:

* Proper wound management should be done.

* There is no need for the administration of RIG.

* One site ID or IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3.

Only adequate wound washing would be required in case of re-exposure where the animal bite victim has documented proof of complete PEP within the last three months.

The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP:

* Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency

* Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment
questions.learning: Rabies vaccine + immunoglobuin+ wound management — In the given scenario, an HIV patient with multiple dog bites falls under Category 3 for rabies vaccination and should receive rabies vaccine, immunoglobulin, and proper wound care.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An intern is assisting with laparoscopic surgery, and the resident is orienting the intern to the instruments and the operating ports. Your surgeon asks you what the angle between the camera port and the working port is.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Azimuth's angle

The angle between the camera port and the working port is known as Azimuth's angle. The angle must be a minimum of 30° to avoid any clashing between these instruments.

Other options

Option B: Manipulation angle is the angle between two working ports. The minimum angle should be 60°.

Option C: Crossing angle refers to the intersection of instruments inside the abdominal cavity.

Option D: The elevation angle is the angle between the working port and the horizontal line. The minimum angle must be 60° to avoid colliding the instrument with the abdominal wall.
questions.learning: Azimuth's angle — The angle between the camera port and the working port is known as Azimuth's angle. The angle must be a minimum of 30° to avoid any clashing between these instruments.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old multiparous woman presents with a vaginal bulge that protrudes beyond the introitus, urinary leakage while coughing, and is able to void urine normally. She undergoes anterior colporrhaphy with mesh repair (colpopexy). Which condition is this surgery primarily performed to correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cystocele

A cystocele is the herniation of the urinary bladder through the weakened anterior vaginal wall due to defects in the pubocervical fascia. It commonly occurs in multiparous women as a result of pelvic floor weakness and presents with:

• Vaginal bulge or mass
• Stress urinary incontinence
• Pelvic pressure or heaviness
• Urinary frequency or incomplete bladder emptying

Anterior colporrhaphy is the standard surgical repair for cystocele. Mesh augmentation (colpopexy) may be used in selected patients with recurrent or severe pelvic organ prolapse to reinforce the anterior vaginal wall.

Why not the other options?

• A. Rectocele: Herniation of the rectum through the posterior vaginal wall, presenting with constipation, difficult defecation, or the need for digital pressure during defecation; treated with posterior colporrhaphy.
• C. Enterocele: Herniation of the pouch of Douglas containing small bowel through the vaginal apex, usually following hysterectomy.
• D. Vesicovaginal fistula: Presents with continuous leakage of urine through the vagina, not a vaginal bulge, and requires fistula repair.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding neonatal cholestasis?
options: Kasai procedure should be done within 90 days
HIDA scan is an investigation of choice
Biliary atresia is the most common cause
Liver biopsy rules out other causes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kasai procedure should be done within 90 days

Kasai procedure should be done within 60 days of age, and not 90 days.  Delay beyond 60 days significantly reduces success rates and increases the risk of requiring liver transplantation.

Neonatal cholestasis refers to prolonged jaundice in newborns caused by impaired bile flow.

Option B: HIDA scan is the investigation of choice. The hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan is used to evaluate bile flow from the liver into the intestine and can help differentiate biliary atresia from other causes of neonatal cholestasis.

Option C: Biliary atresia is the most common cause of neonatal cholestasis, this condition requires surgical intervention.

Option D: Liver biopsy is a key diagnostic tool in neonatal cholestasis as it can confirm biliary atresia and rule out other causes like metabolic diseases or neonatal hepatitis.
questions.learning: Kasai procedure should be done within 90 days Kasai procedure should be done within 60 days of age, and not 90 days. Delay beyond 60 days significantly reduces success rates and increases the risk of requiring liver transplantation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the shown image, which one of the following is a source of vitamin B1?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A

Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) is primarily obtained from whole grains, cereals, and pulses (unpolished rice, legumes)—represented by option A in the image.

Thiamine (as thiamine pyrophosphate, TPP) acts as a cofactor for:

• Pyruvate dehydrogenase
• α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
• Transketolase (HMP shunt)

Deficiency leads to:

• Beriberi (dry: neuropathy, wet: cardiac failure)
• Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome (in alcoholics)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Hormone replacement therapy is not indicated for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CAD Prophylaxis

Hormone replacement therapy is not indicated in coronary artery disease prophylaxis. There is currently insufficient evidence to recommend the initiation or continuation of either estrogen therapy (ET) or estrogen-progestin therapy (EPT) for the prevention of primary or secondary coronary heart disease (CHD).

In an 18-year reevaluation of WHI (women health initiative) participants, it was found that cardiovascular, cancer, and all-cause mortality rates were essentially the same in both the hormone therapy (HT) and placebo groups.

Currently, hormone therapy (HT) is only indicated for the treatment of bothersome vasomotor symptoms (VMS) and genitourinary symptoms, prevention of osteoporosis, and treatment of hypoestrogenism caused by hypogonadism, surgical menopause, or premature ovarian insufficiency.

Estrogen should not be used in women with the following conditions:

• undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding
• known, suspected, or history of breast cancer
• known or suspected estrogen-dependent neoplasia
• active or prior venous thromboembolism
• active or prior stroke, myocardial infarction, or transient ischemic attack (TIA)
• known thrombophilia, liver dysfunction, or disease
• untreated hypertension
• known hypersensitivity to the ingredients of the estrogen preparation
• known or suspected pregnancy

Risks of HRT:

• Endometrial cancer
• Breast cancer
• Ovarian cancer
• Thromboembolism
• Lipid profile dysfunction
• Gall stones, liver dysfunction

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with lung injury and rupture of the tympanic membrane following exposure to a blast. These findings are characteristic of which category of blast wave effect?
questions.explanation: Blast injuries are categorized by the physical mechanism of trauma. Primary (Level I) blast injuries result directly from the overpressure shock wave impacting the body. This wave most severely affects air-filled organs due to their unique density compared to surrounding tissues. Therefore, tympanic membrane rupture and blast lung injury (alveolar-capillary disruption) are pathognomonic Level I injuries. Level II injuries are caused by flying debris hitting the body. Level III injuries occur when the individual is physically thrown by the wind of the blast. Level IV injuries encompass all other effects, such as burns, toxic gas inhalation, or building collapse. Because the pressure wave itself is responsible for rupturing the eardrum and damaging the lung parenchyma, these findings specifically categorize the effect as a primary or Level I blast injury
questions.learning: Blast injuries are categorized by the physical mechanism of trauma. Primary (Level I) blast injuries result directly from the overpressure shock wave impacting the body.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are true about nephroblastoma except:
options: Treatment is chemotherapy followed by surgery
Most common intraabdominal malignancy in children
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Most common intraabdominal malignancy in children

Neuroblastoma, not nephroblastoma, is the most common intra-abdominal malignancy in children.

Wilms tumor/nephroblastoma is an embryonal renal neoplasm caused by faulty renal development that results in the metanephric blastema multiplying excessively. It is usually diagnosed before the age of five.

Children may present with a mass abdomen, fever, and hematuria, which is indicative of the extension of the tumor into the renal pelvis. Hypertension is also observed in a considerable percentage of patients.

Prognostic factors for Wilms tumor:

* Histology

* Stage

* Age

* Tumor weight

* Response to therapy

* Loss of heterozygosity at 1p and 16q

The two most important factors are the histology and the stage of the tumor.

Most of the tumors have favorable histology and are characterized as the “classic” type that consists of three components—blastemal, stromal, and epithelial (tubules) tissues.

Unfavorable tumors are those with focal or diffuse anaplasia. Two principal staging systems are used:

* The COG system is based on findings prior to the initiation of treatment. There exists a local stage and a disease stage. The local stage defines the extent of abdominal disease while the disease stage considers both local disease and metastasis. Metastasis commonly occurs in the lungs.

* The SIOP classification is based on the histologic appearance of the tumors at resection and the outcomes. They are classified as completely necrotic (low risk), blastemal (high risk) and other histological types.

Imaging with USG abdomen and pelvis, CT scan, MRI, etc., shows a solid space-occupying lesion in the kidney.

Management is mainly by chemotherapy and nephrectomy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with recurrent Raynaud’s phenomenon. She also complained of thickening of skin in the hands and difficulty in swallowing. What is the diagnosis and immunofluorescence pattern shown?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anti-centromere pattern; Systemic sclerosis

| Feature | Interpretation

| ------- | --------------

| Recurrent Raynaud’s | Early vascular dysfunction

| Skin thickening (hands) | Sclerodactyly

| Dysphagia | Esophageal smooth muscle fibrosis

Recurrent Raynaud’s phenomenon with skin thickening of hands and dysphagia is classic for systemic sclerosis, especially the limited cutaneous form.

The characteristic ANA immunofluorescence pattern in this subset is anti-centromere, showing discrete nuclear dots.

Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with CREST features and relatively less renal involvement.

| Antibody | Type of SSc | Key Features

| -------- | ----------- | ------------

| Anti-centromere | Limited (CREST) | Better prognosis

| Anti-Scl-70 (Topoisomerase I) | Diffuse | Lung fibrosis

| Anti-RNA polymerase III | Diffuse | Renal crisis

Staining patterns of antinuclear antibodies.

(A) Homogeneous or diffuse staining of nuclei is typical of antibodies reactive with dsDNA, nucleosomes, and histones and is common in SLE.

(B) A speckled pattern is seen with antibodies against various nuclear antigens, including Sm and RNPs.

(C) The pattern of staining of anticentromere antibodies is seen in some cases of systemic sclerosis, Sjögren syndrome, and other diseases.

(D) A nucleolar pattern is typical of antibodies against nucleolar proteins.
