questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents to the dermatology clinic with recurrent skin lesions similar to those shown in the image. He reports that these lesions consistently appear within a few hours of taking NSAIDs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The description of a well-demarcated erythematous patch that recurs at the same site within hours of drug exposure is diagnostic of a Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE). Common triggers include NSAIDs, sulfa drugs, and certain antibiotics. FDEs typically heal leaving behind characteristic post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Erythema multiforme (Option B) presents with "target" or "iris" lesions and usually does not recur consistently on the exact same site upon re-exposure. Drug-induced pigmentation (Option C) involves persistent color changes like blue-grey or brown rather than acute inflammatory red plaques. Herpes (Option D) produces painful, grouped blistering lesions unrelated to specific drug intake. Given the history of recurrence at a specific site immediately following NSAID ingestion, FDE is the only viable clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The description of a well-demarcated erythematous patch that recurs at the same site within hours of drug exposure is diagnostic of a Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with hematuria and a mass in the right kidney on a CT scan, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal angiomyolipoma

The CT image showing renal lesions that has hypo-attenuating components consistent with macroscopic fat is highly suggestive of renal angiomyolipoma.

Angiomyolipomas are benign tumors that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. The mean age of presentation is 43 years and there is a female predilection. It can present as spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, especially with larger tumors. The patient can present with flank pain, palpable mass, hematuria, urinary tract infections, hypertension, or renal failure.

Imaging in renal angiomyolipoma: Demonstration of macroscopic fat is the main part of making a diagnosis. USG may show hyperechoic lesions in the cortex with posterior acoustic shadowing. In patients with tuberous sclerosis, the entire kidney is affected and produces an echogenic appearance with loss of normal corticomedullary junction.

CT findings:

• Cortical lesions that demonstrate macroscopic fat (less than -20 HU)
• Absence of ossification or calcification
• The presence of macroscopic fat is strongly suggestive of this condition, but not pathognomonic as RCC may rarely demonstrate macroscopic fat.
• Approximately 5% may be fat-poor.

MRI: It is an excellent tool to demonstrate intramural fat components. Two sequences are used:

• Fat-saturated techniques
• Phase-in and phase-out imaging that shows India ink artifacts at the junction between fat and non-fat components.

Digital subtraction angiography: They are hypervascular lesions showing a 'sunburst appearance' in the arterial phase and an 'onion peel appearance' in the venous phase.

They usually do not require any intervention. mTOR inhibitors like everolimus can be used to decrease the size of the lesion.

Other options:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC): It is the most common malignant tumor of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

Renal oncocytoma: They are relatively benign in nature and usually present in the 6th to 7th decade. An important point regarding this tumor is its similarity with RCC and hence it is very difficult to differentiate between them preoperatively. A sharp central stellate scar may be seen in one-third of the cases. But RCC may also show this stellate scar appearance in some cases.

Renal cyst: It is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions needs evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification of renal cysts is given above.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A girl is diagnosed with lead poisoning. Which of the following enzyme defects is the likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. ALA dehydratase

The enzyme defective in lead intoxication is ALA dehydratase.

The most common cause of lead poisoning in children is seen due to lead paint which was used in the older times.

It is toxic because it can substitute for calcium in many fundamental cellular processes. It crosses red blood cell membranes as well as the blood-brain barrier and enters the neuroglia cells which support brain function.

The fatal dose of lead acetate is 20 g. The fatal period is 1-2 days.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All are correct statements about muscle tension curves, except:
options: Passive tension increases with muscle stretch
Active tension is highest at optimal length
Total tension equals sum of passive and active tension
Passive tension is highest at resting muscle length
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Passive tension is highest at resting muscle length

The muscle length–tension relationship describes how muscle force varies with sarcomere length.

• Active tension: Produced by actin–myosin cross-bridge formation.
• Maximum at optimal sarcomere length (ideal overlap of actin and myosin).
• Passive tension: Produced by elastic elements of muscle (titin, connective tissue).
• Increases progressively as the muscle is stretched beyond resting length.
• Total tension:
• Total tension = active tension + passive tension

Passive tension is not highest at resting length; it is minimal at resting length and increases with stretch.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents to the outpatient department with poor appetite and failure to thrive. On examination, signs of dehydration such as decreased skin turgor and dry mucous membranes are noted. What is the glucose concentration of the oral rehydration solution used to manage this condition?
questions.explanation: The child presents with "poor appetite and failure to thrive" along with signs of dehydration, which in a 10-year-old in a clinical setting often implies severe acute malnutrition (SAM). For the rehydration of children with SAM, a specific solution called ReSoMal (Rehydration Solution for Malnutrition) is used. ReSoMal differs from standard ORS; it contains more glucose (125 mmol/L) and less sodium to account for the unique physiological needs and electrolyte imbalances of malnourished children. Standard low-osmolarity ORS contains of glucose. Options A, C, and D do not represent the standard glucose concentrations for these rehydration protocols. Management of dehydration in SAM must be very cautious and slow to prevent heart failure. ReSoMal is administered orally or via a nasogastric tube over a longer period compared to children without SAM. This specific biochemical composition is a critical detail in pediatric nutritional rehabilitation
questions.learning: The child presents with "poor appetite and failure to thrive" along with signs of dehydration, which in a 10-year-old in a clinical setting often implies severe acute malnutrition (SAM).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following inhibits the synthesis of glucocorticoid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metyrapone

Metyrapone inhibits the synthesis of glucocorticoids by inhibiting steroid 11β-hydroxylase reversibly.

It is used to test the hypothalamic-pituitary feedback pathway in the diagnosis of Cushing syndrome.
questions.learning: Metyrapone Metyrapone inhibits the synthesis of glucocorticoids by inhibiting steroid 11β-hydroxylase reversibly. It is used to test the hypothalamic-pituitary feedback pathway in the diagnosis of Cushing syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Type 2 lepra reaction is which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.explanation: Type 2 lepra reaction, clinically known as Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL), occurs primarily in multibacillary leprosy (lepromatous and borderline lepromatous types). It is a classic example of a Type 3 hypersensitivity reaction, characterized by the formation of immune complexes. These complexes result from the interaction between high levels of circulating mycobacterial antigens and antibodies, leading to systemic vasculitis and tissue damage. Patients typically present with painful, tender erythematous nodules, high-grade fever, malaise, and often multi-organ involvement like arthritis or glomerulonephritis. In contrast, Type 1 lepra reactions are Type 4 delayed hypersensitivity reactions involving changes in cell-mediated immunity. Hypersensitivity 1 (Option A) involves IgE-mediated allergies, while Hypersensitivity 2 (Option B) involves cytotoxic antibodies targeting cell surfaces. Recognizing the Type 3 immune-complex nature is vital for management, which often requires anti-inflammatory drugs like corticosteroids, thalidomide, or clofazimine to suppress the massive immune response and prevent chronic neurological complications or permanent organ failure
questions.learning: Type 2 lepra reaction, clinically known as Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL), occurs primarily in multibacillary leprosy (lepromatous and borderline lepromatous types).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 33-year-old woman presents with excessive daytime sleepiness and short-term memory difficulties. Her BMI is 43, blood pressure is 170/98 mmHg, and arterial blood gas shows PO₂ 70 mmHg, PCO₂ 53 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 33 mmol/L. Which condition is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: This patient has a Body Mass Index (BMI) of 43 kg/m², marked daytime sleepiness, and arterial blood gas (ABG) evidence of chronic hypercapnia (PaCO2 ≈ 53 mmHg) while awake, which together are diagnostic of Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS), also known as Pickwickian syndrome. Although Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) commonly coexists and contributes to daytime somnolence, the presence of awake hypoventilation with elevated PaCO2 is the defining feature of OHS. Central sleep apnea is characterized by absent respiratory effort during sleep and is not associated with severe obesity or persistent daytime hypercapnia. Narcolepsy causes excessive daytime sleepiness with features such as cataplexy but does not explain chronic respiratory acidosis, hypercapnia, or hypertension. The elevated serum bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) reflects metabolic compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis. Management includes weight reduction and positive airway pressure (PAP) therapy. If untreated, OHS can progress to pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, and increased mortality

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the diagnosis based on the x-ray given below?
questions.explanation: The provided pelvic X-ray (Option R) displays a large, radiopaque, oval-shaped mass located in the midline of the lower pelvis, immediately superior to the pubic symphysis. This anatomical position is diagnostic of a bladder stone (Option B). Renal calculi (Option A) would be located much higher in the flank or loin region. Ureteric calculi (Option D) would appear as smaller opacities along the path of the ureters, lateral to the vertebral column. Schistosomiasis (Option C) of the bladder classically appears as "egg-shell" or curvilinear calcification of the bladder wall itself rather than a discrete internal stone. Large bladder stones often result from chronic urinary stasis, such as in benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) or neurogenic bladder. They can cause symptoms of suprapubic pain, hematuria, and interrupted urine flow. Management usually involves cystolitholapaxy or open cystolithotomy
questions.learning: The provided pelvic X-ray (Option R) displays a large, radiopaque, oval-shaped mass located in the midline of the lower pelvis, immediately superior to the pubic symphysis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which is the nodal ministry of disaster management?
options: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Ministry of Human Resource and Development
questions.explanation: In India, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is the nodal ministry for the overall coordination of disaster management. It operates through the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), which was established by the Disaster Management Act of 2005. The MHA is responsible for formulating national policies, preparing disaster management plans, and coordinating responses across the country. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (Option A) plays a critical role in managing medical emergencies and disease outbreaks but is not the overall nodal agency. The Ministry of Human Resource and Development (now Education) (Options C and D) focuses on skill development and educational policy rather than disaster response. While state governments have the direct responsibility for executing field-level relief efforts, the Union MHA provides high-level coordination and security support
questions.learning: In India, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is the nodal ministry for the overall coordination of disaster management. It operates through the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), which was established by the Disaster Management Act of 2005.

questions.text: The Van Nuys grading system for ductal carcinoma in situ does not include:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hormone receptor staining

Staining for estrogen and progesterone receptors is not part of the Van Nuys system used for grading DCIS.

The components of the Van Nuys prognostic index (VNPI) are as follows:

• Size of the tumor
• Extent of resection margin
• Histological variant of DCIS - based on nuclear grade, presence of necrosis, presence of microcalcification
• Age of the patient

Patients with a high score in this grading system benefit from radiotherapy after excision, whereas those with low-grade and completely excised tumors, need no further treatment.

A score ranging from 1 (lesions with the best prognosis) to 3 (lesions with the worst prognosis) is given for each of the four prognostic predictors. Total scores range from 4 (least likely to recur) to 12 (most likely to recur).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents for evaluation of infertility, having unsuccessfully attempted conception for more than one year. Which single test is considered the most reliable for assessing her ovarian reserve?
questions.explanation: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) is considered the single best and most reliable blood test for assessing ovarian reserve. It is produced directly by the antral and pre-antral follicles; its levels correlate closely with the remaining quantity of eggs. Unlike FSH (Option A) and Estradiol (Option B), which must be checked on Day 3 of the menstrual cycle and can fluctuate, AMH levels are stable throughout the cycle. Serum Inhibin B (Option D) also reflects the follicle pool but is more variable and less consistent than AMH. AMH provides a highly predictive functional assessment of how a patient might respond to controlled ovarian stimulation. Therefore, while FSH and Antral Follicle Count (AFC) are also used, AMH remains the gold standard for a single, cycle-independent measurement of reproductive potential
questions.learning: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) is considered the single best and most reliable blood test for assessing ovarian reserve. It is produced directly by the antral and pre-antral follicles; its levels correlate closely with the remaining quantity of eggs.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following immunodeficiency disorders is least likely to cause rejection of a mismatched transplant due to absent or severely impaired immune function?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bare lymphocyte syndrome

Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome (BLS)

• There is defective expression of MHC molecules:

• Type I BLS → ↓ MHC I → affects CD8⁺ T cells
• Type II BLS → ↓ MHC II → affects CD4⁺ T cells  (more severe)

Without MHC:

• Antigens cannot be presented
• T cells cannot be activated
• Adaptive immune response collapses

Bare lymphocyte syndrome is characterized by absent MHC class II expression due to defective antigen presentation. This results in failure of CD4⁺ T-cell activation and severe impairment of cell-mediated immunity.

Transplant rejection is T-cell mediated and therefore markedly reduced in this condition.

Wiskott-Aldrich and Job syndromes retain functional T cells, while Chediak-Higashi has defective phagolysosome fusion but intact adaptive immunity.

A. Chediak–Higashi syndrome

• Defect: Lysosomal trafficking (LYST gene)
• Affects:

• Neutrophils (↓ killing)
• NK cells

• Features:

• Recurrent infections
• Albinism
• Giant granules

T-cell function relatively preserved

→ Can still mount rejection

B. Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome

• Defect: WAS protein → cytoskeletal dysfunction
• Triad:

• Thrombocytopenia
• Eczema
• Recurrent infections

Combined immunodeficiency (T + B affected)

BUT:

• Not completely absent immunity

→ Still capable of some rejection

D. Job syndrome (Hyper-IgE syndrome)

• Defect: STAT3 mutation → ↓ Th17 cells
• Features:

• High IgE
• Recurrent “cold” abscesses
• Coarse facies

Problem is neutrophil recruitment, not T-cell recognition

→ Transplant rejection still possible

| Disorder | Main Defect | T-cell Function | Graft Rejection

| -------- | ----------- | --------------- | ---------------

| Chediak-Higashi | Lysosomal trafficking | Near normal | Possible

| Wiskott-Aldrich | Cytoskeleton (WAS) | Impaired | Reduced but present

| Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome | No MHC | Severely impaired | Minimal

| Job Syndrome | Th17 deficiency | Mostly intact | Possible

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with a swelling in the subhyoid region of the neck that moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion. This congenital, midline neck mass shows characteristic mobility with these maneuvers. What is the recommended treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: A midline neck mass in the subhyoid region that moves with both swallowing and tongue protrusion is the pathognomonic clinical presentation of a thyroglossal duct cyst. This congenital anomaly occurs along the embryonic track of the thyroid gland descent. The recommended definitive treatment is Sistrunk's operation. This specialized surgical procedure involves the complete excision of the cyst, the entire remaining thyroglossal tract, and the central portion of the hyoid bone to ensure the removal of all potential epithelial remnants. Total thyroidectomy (Option A) and hemi-thyroidectomy (Option C) are procedures used for thyroid gland pathologies rather than midline cysts. Ramstedt's operation (Option B) is used to correct hypertrophic pyloric stenosis in infants. Sistrunk's technique is essential because simple excision of the cyst alone without the duct and hyoid bone leads to a high rate of recurrence

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the mode of insertion of this contraceptive?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hysteroscopic

The image shows an Essure coil which is inserted hysteroscopically to occlude both the fallopian tubes.

Essure(not yet licensed in India):

* It is a spring-like device introduced using a hysteroscope inserted through the vagina into the uterus and then into each fallopian tube.

* In 3 months' time, scar tissue grows into the device and plugs the fallopian tube; hence, sperms cannot pass through to fertilize an egg.

* Made of nickel and titanium alloy and is considered irreversible.

* Contraindicated in patients who are uncertain about ending fertility, can have only one insert placed (including contralateral proximal tubal occlusion or suspected unicornuate uterus), an abnormal uterine cavity that makes visualization of the tubal ostia impossible, and/or abnormal tubal anatomy or previous tubal ligation (including failed ligation), pregnant or suspect pregnancy, delivered or terminated a pregnancy less than 6 weeks, an active upper or lower genital tract infection, unexplained vaginal bleeding, a gynecological malignancy, known allergy to contrast media.

* Side effects-cramping, nausea/vomiting, back pain, abdominal pain, and dyspareunia.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Edematous villi with chromosome XY was found. What will be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A complete hydatidiform mole is characterized by a diploid karyotype, most commonly 46,XX but also 46,XY (Option A). It results from the fertilization of an "empty" ovum by one or two sperm, meaning the genetic material is entirely paternal. Histopathology classically shows diffuse hydropic swelling (edematous villi) and a complete absence of fetal tissue. In contrast, a partial mole (Option B) is usually triploid (e.g., 69,XXY) and contains identifiable fetal parts alongside both normal and edematous villi. A simple cyst (Option C) would not show placental villous architecture or specific chromosomal anomalies. An ectopic pregnancy (Option D) involves a normal embryo implanted outside the uterus and does not exhibit the diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia seen in molar pregnancies. Thus, the specific findings of edematous villi and an XY diploid karyotype confirm a complete molar pregnancy
questions.learning: A complete hydatidiform mole is characterized by a diploid karyotype, most commonly 46,XX but also 46,XY (Option A). It results from the fertilization of an "empty" ovum by one or two sperm, meaning the genetic material is entirely paternal.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs increases the uveoscleral outflow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Latanoprost

Latanoprost is a prostaglandin drug, which acts by increasing the uveoscleral outflow and thereby lowers the intraocular pressure.

Mechanism of action: Latanoprost is a prodrug and gets activated during its passage through the cornea. It acts by stimulating the prostanoid receptors on the ciliary muscles. This leads to the release of matrix metalloproteinases, which increases the uveoscleral outflow.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Following a blast, a man was brought from the scene to the emergency with multiple small puncture wounds to the right side of the chest, below the nipple, and multiple small abrasions and bruising over the left lower abdomen. Which of the following mechanisms is responsible for these injuries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flying missiles

The given history of multiple small puncture wounds to the right side of the chest, below the nipple, and multiple small abrasions and bruising over the left lower abdomen are highly suggestive of blast injuries sustained due to flying missiles.

Blast injury is a complex type of physical trauma resulting from direct or indirect exposure to an explosion causing a sudden increase or decrease in atmospheric pressure.

T.K.Marshall’s (Marshall's triad) described the characteristic injuries associated with bomb explosions. It includes:

• Abrasions
• Bruises/contusions
• Puncture lacerations

Blast injuries are classified as:

• Primary injuries: Effect of transmitted blast waves on gas-containing structures. The external injuries are absent and are characterized by internal injuries. The middle, ear, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract are the most susceptible to this.
• Secondary injuries: Injuries caused by shrapnel and other airborne debris propelled by the explosion. These injuries may affect any part of the body and sometimes result in penetrating trauma. Most casualties are caused by secondary injuries.
• Tertiary injuries: These are caused by blast wind that can throw victims against solid objects.
• Quaternary injuries: All other injuries caused by explosions are not included in the above three categories. eg, flash burns, crush injuries, respiratory effects due to toxic dust, gas, etc.

Option B: Blast of air or blast wave cause primary injuries which involve internal organs without external injury.

Option C: Explosion burns: When the bomb explodes, the temperature of the explosive gases can exceed 2000°C, and the heat radiated momentarily can cause flash burns. It is a quaternary type of blast injury.

Option D: Building collapse can cause crush injuries which is a quaternary blast injury.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The X-ray image of a child with muscle weakness and failure to thrive is attached below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rickets

The clinical vignette with the above X-ray image shows fraying and cupping of the metaphysis, suggestive of rickets.

Radiological features in rickets:

* Fraying (Widening and irregularity of the growth plate)

* Cupping (Concavity of the metaphysis)

* Splaying at metaphysis (widening of metaphyseal ends)

* Generalized rarefaction

Pearl PF0381: Radiological features of rickets

Radiological features of rickets:

* Delayed appearance of the epiphysis.

* Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.

* Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.

* Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis

* Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices.

* Loss of provisional zone of calcification (becomes denser in healing rickets, known as the white line of Frenkel).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Purkinje cells of cerebellum relay into _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dentate nucleus

Purkinje cells of the cerebellum relay into the dentate nucleus which is one of the deep cerebellar nuclei.

The input to the Purkinje cells come from the climbing fibres. The output of Purkinje cells is inhibitory to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

Options A and B: Caudate and lentiform nuclei are part of the basal ganglia.

Option D: Red nucleus receives afferents from the cerebellum and plays a role in modulating signals to the upper motor neurons of the cerebral cortex.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Reiter syndrome is associated with?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HLA-B27

Reiter syndrome is associated with HLA- B27.

Reiter's syndrome has a triad of urethritis, arthritis, and conjunctivitis, with or without iridocyclitis. The exact cause of the syndrome is not fully understood, but it typically affects young males who test positive for the HLA-B27 gene.

It has three forms: postvenereal, postdysenteric, and articular. Ocular symptoms may include acute mucopurulent conjunctivitis and non-granulomatous iridocyclitis in a subset of cases.

Treatrment -Iridocyclitis responds well to usual treatment and in cases suspected of being caused by Chlamydia infection, a course of systemic tetracycline (250 mg QID for 10 days) may be beneficial in postvenereal form.

HLA association and diseases

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following can be used to calculate the cardiac output?

A. ECHO.
B. Ventilation-perfusion scan.
C. Thermodilution.
D. Fick's principle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A, C, D

Fick principle, thermodilution, and ECHO can be used to measure cardiac output.

Cardiac output is the amount of blood pumped by the heart into the aorta every minute. The average cardiac output is 5L/min and can be measured by various indirect methods.

Fick's principle uses the total amount of oxygen absorbed from the air by the lungs and the arteriovenous oxygen difference of blood to calculate the cardiac output using the following formula:

Cardiac output (L/min) = (O2 absorbed per minute by the lungs (mL/min))  /  (Arterio-venous O2 difference(mL/L of blood))

Thermodilution method employs cold saline which is infused into the right atrium through a double-lumen Swan–Ganz thermodilution catheter and the temperature change is measured at the pulmonary artery using a thermistor at the end of the catheter. The mean decrease in the temperature of blood is inversely proportional to the cardiac output.

An ECHO uses ultrasound waves from a transducer placed on the chest wall to measure the velocity of blood flowing from the left ventricle into the aorta. Stroke volume can be calculated from this. Cardiac Output = Heart Rate X Stroke Volume.

The other methods that can be used to measure cardiac output include impedance cardiography a.k.a. thoracic electrical bioimpedance, electromagnetic or ultrasonic flowmeter,and  indicator dilution method.

Ventilation-perfusion scan is not a method of cardiac output measurement. It is used to assess pulmonary circulation.
questions.learning: A, C, D Fick principle, thermodilution, and ECHO can be used to measure cardiac output. Cardiac output is the amount of blood pumped by the heart into the aorta every minute.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following ovarian structures is responsible for the following finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Corpus luteum

The ovarian structure responsible for the following finding is the corpus luteum.

The histological image shows a corkscrew appearance of the glands, and this is characteristic of the secretory phase of the endometrium in the menstrual cycle. This phase is stimulated by progesterone, which is secreted by the corpus luteum.

Endometrial Biopsy of the various stages of the ovarian cycle:

1. Proliferative phase: The glands are simple, straight, and tubular glands. The lining of the glands shows pseudostratified columnar epithelium with mitotic figures, indicating active cell proliferation. The stroma is dense and compact, with numerous cells undergoing mitosis.

2. Early secretory phase: The initially straight glands begin to coil as the endometrium transitions into the secretory phase. Subnuclear Vacuolation is seen in the epithelial cells of the endometrial glands, caused by the accumulation of glycogen at the base of the cells.
3. Late secretory phase: The glands become maximally tortuous and assume a distinctive "saw-tooth" appearance due to extreme coiling. They are filled with secretions rich in glycogen and glycoproteins, essential for supporting a potential embryo. The stroma is edematous.

Other Options:

Option A: Secondary follicle

The secondary follicle is a more advanced stage of follicular development following the primary follicle. It contains a  fluid-filled cavity (antrum) surrounded by two layers: theca interna and theca externa.

Option B and C: Theca interna and Granulosa cell

The theca interna is a layer of stromal cells just outside the basal lamina of the granulosa cells. They are composed of cuboidal endocrine cells with lipid droplets and abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum, reflecting its role in steroidogenesis.

Granulosa cells line the interior of the follicle. Cells are organized in layers, initially single-layered in primary follicles and multilayered in secondary follicles.
questions.learning: Corpus luteum — The ovarian structure responsible for the following finding is the corpus luteum. The histological image shows a corkscrew appearance of the glands, and this is characteristic of the secretory phase of the endometrium in the menstrual cycle.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy falls on an outstretched hand and now has pain and swelling at the base of the thumb. Which bone is most likely fractured?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. The classic mechanism of injury is a fall on an outstretched hand with the wrist in extension. Clinical signs include pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, swelling at the base of the thumb, and pain with axial loading of the thumb. Lunate fractures (Option A) are less common and often associated with dislocations or Kienbock's disease. Pisiform (Option C) and trapezoid (Option D) fractures are rare carpal injuries that typically result from direct trauma rather than an indirect fall. Scaphoid fractures are notorious for their poor blood supply, specifically the retrograde flow to the proximal pole, which increases the risk of avascular necrosis and non-union if not properly managed. Initial X-rays may be negative, so a high index of clinical suspicion and follow-up imaging (MRI or repeat X-rays in 10–14 days) are often required
questions.learning: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. The classic mechanism of injury is a fall on an outstretched hand with the wrist in extension.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which demographic indicator is used to compare life expectancy between two different countries?
questions.explanation: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite statistical tool used to rank countries by level of human development, serving as a key indicator for comparing life expectancy across different nations. It encompasses three major dimensions: a long and healthy life (measured by life expectancy at birth), knowledge (mean and expected years of schooling), and a decent standard of living (GNI per capita). In contrast, Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALY) (Option A) measures the value of health outcomes by combining quantity and quality of life. Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALY) (Option B) quantifies the overall burden of disease, representing years lost due to ill-health or early death. The Human Poverty Index (HPI) (Option D) focuses specifically on deprivations rather than general development or expectancy. Therefore, HDI is the standard demographic measure used internationally to benchmark and compare the longevity and life expectancy of populations between distinct countries
questions.learning: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite statistical tool used to rank countries by level of human development, serving as a key indicator for comparing life expectancy across different nations.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Revised The vertical plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts is known as __________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coronal plane

The coronal plane is a vertical that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts.

Four imaginary planes are used in anatomical descriptions:

* Median (mid-sagittal) plane: Vertical plane that divides the body into equal right and left halves

* Sagittal plane: Vertical plane that divides the body into unequal right and left parts; parallel to the median plane

* Coronal (frontal) plane: Vertical plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts; perpendicular to the median plane

* Transverse (horizontal) plane: Horizontal plane that divides the body into upper and lower parts; perpendicular to both the sagittal and coronal planes

Note: Axial (or trans-axial) plane is a term used in radiology for the horizontal plane.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 62-year-old man develops sudden massive blood loss following trauma. His mean arterial pressure falls to 35 mmHg. Within seconds, he develops marked sympathetic activation with intense peripheral vasoconstriction and a sharp rise in heart rate. This powerful pressure response is mediated by which of the following mechanisms?
options: Direct ischemia of the vasomotor center
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Direct ischemia of the vasomotor center

When mean arterial pressure (MAP) falls to very low levels (<40 mmHg), the brainstem experiences ischemia, leading to activation of the central nervous system ischemic response.

Mechanism:

• Reduced cerebral perfusion causes CO₂ accumulation and decreased O₂ in the medullary vasomotor center.
• This strongly stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, producing:
• Intense peripheral vasoconstriction
• Marked increase in heart rate
• Rapid rise in blood pressure
• This response is one of the most powerful short-term mechanisms for restoring blood pressure during severe shock.
questions.learning: Direct ischemia of the vasomotor center When mean arterial pressure (MAP) falls to very low levels (<40 mmHg), the brainstem experiences ischemia, leading to activation of the central nervous system ischemic response.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the most dangerous lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. B/L Complete RLN lesion

Bilateral complete RLN (recurrent laryngeal nerve) lesion is the most dangerous lesion among the given options.

In bilateral RLN paralysis

• Both the cords lie in the median or paramedian position, the airway is inadequate causing dyspnea and stridor. This may lead to death if untreated.
• The voice is good.
• Dyspnea and stridor become worse on exertion or during an attack of acute laryngitis.

All laryngeal muscles are supplied by the ipsilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN), except cricothyroid which is supplied by the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN). Both SLN and RLN are branches of the vagus nerve.

The recurrent laryngeal nerves (RLN) on the right and the left side follow different courses-

• Right RLN takes origin in the root of the neck, winds around the first part of the subclavian artery, and then ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove.
• Left RLN takes origin in the thorax, winds around the arch of the aorta, and then ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove. Since it has a longer course, it is more likely to be injured.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A middle-aged male patient, who is on chronic antiarrhythmic drug therapy, presents with hypotension, photosensitivity, and cold intolerance. He also complains of difficulty in getting up from the squatting position. CXR is shown below. What is the most likely drug implicated in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Amiodarone

Amiodarone causes photosensitivity, thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism → cold intolerance), proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from squatting), and hypotension. Chronic use is also associated with pulmonary toxicity (interstitial pneumonitis/fibrosis), explaining the abnormal chest X-ray.

A. Adenosine – Very short-acting; causes transient AV block/flushing, not chronic toxicity.

B. Digoxin – Causes nausea, arrhythmias, visual halos; no photosensitivity or lung toxicity.

C. Quinidine – Causes cinchonism and hypotension, but not thyroid or pulmonary effects.
questions.learning: Amiodarone Amiodarone causes photosensitivity, thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism → cold intolerance), proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from squatting), and hypotension.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which blood component is not separated by centrifugation in the blood bank?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Albumin

Albumin is not separated by centrifugation in the blood bank.

In blood banks, centrifugation is used to separate the main components of blood into distinct layers for storage and transfusion purposes. These components include:

1. Red Blood Cells (RBCs): Separated by centrifugation and stored for patients with anemia or significant blood loss. (Option A)
2. Platelets: Isolated through centrifugation of plasma-rich blood for use in patients with bleeding disorders. (Option B)
3. Cryoprecipitate: Derived from plasma by controlled freezing and thawing, which allows the collection of clotting factors (e.g., Factor VIII, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor). (Option C)

Albumin is a plasma protein that is extracted through a process called fractionation, not simple centrifugation. This involves the use of chemical, temperature, and pH adjustments to isolate albumin from plasma.
questions.learning: Albumin Albumin is not separated by centrifugation in the blood bank. In blood banks, centrifugation is used to separate the main components of blood into distinct layers for storage and transfusion purposes.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The earliest stage at which erythropoietin is effective in red blood cell formation is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Burst forming units

BFU is the earliest stage of hematopoiesis where erythropoietin (EPO) acts

Under the influence of EPO, both BFU and CFU grow in semisolid culture media and give rise to colonies of well-hemoglobinized erythroblasts.

Erythroid burst-forming unit (BFU-E) is the most primitive single lineage committed erythroid progenitor. In addition to EPO, they form the sub-population of Erythroid Colony Forming Units (CFU-E).
CFU is derived from burst-forming units.

Note: While CFUs have the highest number of receptors for EPO, the earliest stage at which it acts is on the BFU.
questions.learning: Burst forming units BFU is the earliest stage of hematopoiesis where erythropoietin (EPO) acts Under the influence of EPO, both BFU and CFU grow in semisolid culture media and give rise to colonies of well-hemoglobinized erythroblasts.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In an industrial worker with suspected intraocular foreign body after an injury involving a hammer and iron chisel, which imaging modality is best for accurately localizing the foreign body, particularly if it is metallic?
questions.explanation: When a metallic foreign body is suspected in the eye (e.g., from an iron chisel), a Computed Tomography (CT) scan is the best and most appropriate imaging modality for localization. CT provides excellent spatial resolution and is highly sensitive for detecting radiopaque materials like iron or steel. MRI (Option A) is strictly contraindicated if a metallic foreign body is suspected; the powerful magnetic field can cause the metal to move or heat up, leading to catastrophic intraocular damage or blindness. A plain X-ray (Option C) can detect the presence of metal but is poor for precise anatomical localization. B-mode ultrasound (Option D) can be useful but is often difficult to perform in an acutely traumatized globe and is less definitive than CT. Therefore, for an industrial "hammer and chisel" injury, CT is the safest and most accurate tool for surgical planning
questions.learning: When a metallic foreign body is suspected in the eye (e.g., from an iron chisel), a Computed Tomography (CT) scan is the best and most appropriate imaging modality for localization.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What levels of prolactin are definitely suggestive of prolactinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. >200μg/L

The diagnosis of a prolactinoma is highly likely when prolactin levels are > 200 μg/L.

The normal range of serum prolactin (PRL) is 5-20 μg/L. Prolactin levels < 100 μg/L can be due to non-functioning pituitary adenomas or non-neoplastic causes of hyperprolactinemia. MRI brain must be done in all patients with hyperprolactinemia.

Prolactinoma are tumors arising from the lactotroph cells of the pituitary gland, they can be classified as microadenoma(<1cm in diameter, usually non invasive ) or macroadenoma(>1cm, locally invasive to adjacent structures). Clinical features include amenorrhea, infertility, and galactorrhea in women, impotence, loss of libido, infertility in men and if tumor extends beyond sella, there can be visual field defects and other mass effects.

Treatment - In asymptomatic patients and those where fertility is not desired, they do not require treatment and can be monitored using regular PRL measurements and MRI. In symptomatic microadenoma cases, oral dopamine agonists (cabergoline and bromocriptine) form the main treatment for hyperprolactinemia and reduction of tumor volume. For macroadenoma, before starting dopamine agonists visual field testing is to be done, and reassess it with MRI changes every 6-12 month intervals until maximum reduction is achieved, in unresponsive cases consider surgery.
questions.learning: >200μg/L The diagnosis of a prolactinoma is highly likely when prolactin levels are > 200 μg/L. The normal range of serum prolactin (PRL) is 5-20 μg/L.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the characteristic lesion of kaposi sarcoma in the oral cavity?
options: A white striated lesion that cannot be scraped off
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Purpulish red elevated lesions

Kaposi sarcoma(KS) is characterized by purplish-red elevated lesions. It is an AIDS defining illness due to multifocal endothelial proliferation with low-grade malignant potential, and the gammaherpesvirus HHV-8.

Classic KS typically affects older men of Eastern European and Mediterranean descent and progresses through three clinical stages: the patch stage, the plaque stage, and the nodular/tumour stage. Histopathological examination reveals a circumscribed tumour nodule within the dermis, characterized by a dense, whorled arrangement of spindle cells. Erythrocyte extravasation within slit-like spaces is often prominent, accompanied by readily observable mitoses and eosinophilic globules.

AIDS-associated KS is an AIDS-defining illness and is the most common malignancy associated with HIV infection. Involvement of the oral cavity is most common in AIDS-related KS, but it can be seen in other variants also. Oral KS (OKS) most often involves the hard and soft palate, gingiva, and dorsal tongue with plaques or tumors. The color of the lesions may range from non-pigmented to brownish-red or violaceous.

Other forms of KS include

* Classic Kaposi sarcoma: It has the following three clinical stages patches, plaques, and nodules.

* Endemic African KS

* Transplant-associated KS is more common after solid organ transplant patients receive immunosuppression as compared to the marrow or stem-cell transplant patients.

There is no definitive cure for KS, but it is highly radiosensitive, achieving complete responses in many cases. Treatment options include highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), which can lead to regression of lesions, as well as localized treatments such as excision, cryotherapy, and intra-lesional administration of agents like vinblastine and interferon-α2b.

The given images show coalescent red-purple macules and plaques of the skin and the violaceous growth on hard palate:

Other options:

Option A: A yellowish lesion containing pus describes an abscess or a pustular infection, bacterial in origin. Kaposi sarcoma is a neoplastic lesion with vascular proliferation not an abcess.

Option C: A white striated lesion that cannot be scraped off is more characteristic of Oral Lichen planus especially reticular form.

Option D: Small red erosions are more characteristic of herpetic stomatitis, traumatic ulcers, or aphthous ulcers, which are ulcerative.
questions.learning: Purpulish red elevated lesions Kaposi sarcoma(KS) is characterized by purplish-red elevated lesions. It is an AIDS defining illness due to multifocal endothelial proliferation with low-grade malignant potential, and the gammaherpesvirus HHV-8.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following infectious agents are associated with the development of lymphoid malignancies? 1. HIV 2. Hepatitis B 3. Hepatitis C Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

• 1. HIV: Correct

• Associated with HIV-related non-Hodgkin lymphomas, particularly aggressive B-cell lymphomas such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma.

• 2. Hepatitis B: Correct

• Chronic HBV infection is associated with an increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, although the association is less characteristic than with HCV.

• 3. Hepatitis C: Correct

• Chronic HCV infection is strongly associated with B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas, particularly marginal zone lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
• HCV-associated lymphoproliferation may occur through chronic antigenic stimulation.
questions.learning: HIV: Correct • Associated with HIV-related non-Hodgkin lymphomas, particularly aggressive B-cell lymphomas such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma. • 2.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis from the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pterygium

The likely diagnosis, based on the above image, is pterygium.

Pterygium is a subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a degenerative condition of the sub-conjunctival tissue and is never inflammatory. It occurs due to exposure to UV-B radiation and the most common site is the nasal.

It is made up of three parts, "cap" (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge), a head, and a body.

Clinical features:

• Astigmatism with the rule - most common finding
• Stocker's line - deposition of iron on the advancing edge
• Fuchs islets - small, discrete, whitish flecks consisting of clusters of pterygial epithelial cells, often present at the advancing edge.

The differential diagnosis is pseudo pterygium.

Pterygium
Pseudo-pterygium

Degenerative process
Inflammatory process

Occurs in elderly
Can occur at any age

Situated at the palpebral aperture
Can occur at any site

Either progressive, regressive, or stationary
Always stationary

A probe cannot be passed underneath
A probe can be passed under the neck

The treatment for pterygium is usually excision. To prevent a recurrence, mitomycin C or 5 fluorouracil is used. Other methods:

• Auto-grafting- Conjunctival limbal autograft (CLAG) from the superior limbal conjunctiva is the best method.
• Bare sclera technique- high recurrence rate of 30 to 80%.
• PERFECT surgery- zero rates of recurrence. (PERFECT stands for Pterygium Extended Removal Followed by Extended Conjunctival Transplant)
questions.learning: Pterygium — The likely diagnosis, based on the above image, is pterygium. Pterygium is a subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with loss of the right visual field in both eyes while central (macular) vision is preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A right-sided field defect in both eyes (right homonymous hemianopia) with central vision intact is characteristic of Homonymous Hemianopia with Macular Sparing. This condition typically results from a lesion in the contralateral (left) primary visual cortex, often following a stroke in the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) territory. Macular sparing occurs because the macular representation in the visual cortex has a dual blood supply from both the PCA and the middle cerebral artery (MCA). Heteronymous hemianopia (Option B) involves different sides of the visual field being lost (e.g., bitemporal), which is not the case here. An optic chiasm lesion (Option C) classically causes bitemporal hemianopia due to crossing nasal fibers. An optic tract lesion (Option D) causes a complete homonymous hemianopia but usually does not demonstrate macular sparing because it occurs before the cortical level of dual blood supply. This finding is key for cortical localization
questions.learning: A right-sided field defect in both eyes (right homonymous hemianopia) with central vision intact is characteristic of Homonymous Hemianopia with Macular Sparing.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the gold standard for measuring intraocular pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Goldmann applanation tonometer

Goldmann applanation tonometer is used to measure intraocular pressure (IOP).

The concept behind the procedure was introduced by Goldmann. It is based on Imbert-Fick law, which states that the pressure inside a sphere(P) is equal to the force (W) required to flatten its surface divided by the area of flattening (A).

P = W/A

The different types are Goldmann tonometer, Perkin’s tonometer, pneumatic tonometer, pulse air tonometer, tono-pen.

The image of a Goldmann applanation tonometer is given below:

Other options:

Gonioscope is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber (gonioscopy).

Hertel's exophthalmometer measures protrusion of the apex of the cornea from the outer orbital margin (with the eyes looking straight ahead).

Tonopen is a hand-held electronic contact tonometer which is used for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) in a scarred cornea.
questions.learning: Goldmann applanation tonometer Goldmann applanation tonometer is used to measure intraocular pressure (IOP). The concept behind the procedure was introduced by Goldmann.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In endometriotic lesion, histology represents its:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High estrogen

In endometriotic lesions, histology represents its high estrogen activity.

Endometriosis is defined by the presence of “ectopic” endometrial tissue at a site outside of the uterus.  Endometriosis is a proliferative hormone-dependent disease of the childbearing period. It is extremely rare before menarche and disappears after menopause.

The endometriotic implants show certain differences when compared to normal endometrium. There is increased production of estrogen by endometriotic stromal cells due to high levels of the enzyme aromatase. This is absent in normal endometrial stroma.

Management of endometriosis:

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 62-year-old man presents with increased urinary frequency, hesitancy, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. He has no history of urinary tract infection or kidney disease, and evaluation suggests benign prostatic hyperplasia. What is the most appropriate initial management for his urinary symptoms?
questions.explanation: For a patient presenting with bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) due to BPH without secondary complications, the initial management is usually medical. Tamsulosin, an alpha-1 blocker, is the most appropriate first-line choice because it rapidly relaxes the smooth muscle of the bladder neck and prostate, providing quick symptomatic relief (often within days). Finasteride (Option C), a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, is also used but typically takes 6–12 months to significantly shrink the prostate and is best suited for larger gland volumes. TURP (Option A) is the gold standard "surgical" treatment but is generally reserved for patients who fail medical therapy or develop complications like refractory urinary retention, bladder stones, or recurrent hematuria. Observation (Option D) is only suitable for patients with very mild, non-bothersome symptoms. Since this patient reports progressive symptoms, initiating tamsulosin is the most effective and commonly prescribed initial intervention to improve his quality of life
questions.learning: For a patient presenting with bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) due to BPH without secondary complications, the initial management is usually medical.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child has recurrent urinary tract infections, a weak urinary stream, and intermittent incontinence. The radiological image demonstrates the characteristic findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ureterocele

Ureteroceles appear as smooth, round "cobra head" filling defects at the ureterovesical junction, causing obstruction, recurrent UTIs, poor stream, and incontinence in children.

Key Radiological Sign:

• Round filling defect in bladder
• Surrounded by contrast → looks like cobra head

| Option | | Why

| ------ | --- | ---

| A. Ureterocele | ✅ | Cystic dilation + cobra head sign + obstruction symptoms

| B. Duplicated collecting system | ❌ | May coexist, but alone doesn’t give cobra head sign

| C. Posterior urethral valves (PUV) | ❌ | Seen in male infants, shows dilated posterior urethra

| D. Vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) | ❌ | Reflux of urine, not cystic lesion

| Condition | Key Feature | Imaging Finding

| --------- | ----------- | ---------------

| Ureterocele | Distal ureter dilation | Cobra head sign

| PUV | Male infant obstruction | Dilated posterior urethra

| VUR | Reflux of urine | Contrast going upward

| Duplicated system | Two ureters | Double collecting system
questions.learning: Ureterocele Ureteroceles appear as smooth, round "cobra head" filling defects at the ureterovesical junction, causing obstruction, recurrent UTIs, poor stream, and incontinence in children.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The finding seen in the image is?
questions.explanation: Herbert's pits are small, shallow, oval depressions located at the limbal conjunctiva. They are formed during the healing of limbal follicles and are considered pathognomonic evidence of a previous infection with Chlamydia trachomatis (trachoma). In the WHO grading system, they are typically seen during the scarring stage (TS). Horner-Trantas spots (Option A) are chalky white dots seen in vernal keratoconjunctivitis. Pannus (Option C) refers to superficial vascularization of the cornea. Arlt's line (Option D) is a linear scar on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, not the limbus. While both Arlt's line and Herbert's pits are associated with chronic trachoma, their anatomical locations differ significantly. The visual evidence of limbal pitting confirms the diagnosis of Herbert's pits
questions.learning: Herbert's pits are small, shallow, oval depressions located at the limbal conjunctiva. They are formed during the healing of limbal follicles and are considered pathognomonic evidence of a previous infection with Chlamydia trachomatis (trachoma).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: After three months, blood pressure readings are compared between two groups of hypertensive patients: one group of 100 patients received medical treatment, while the other group of 100 patients was advised lifestyle modifications. Which statistical test should be used to assess the significance of the difference in blood pressure between these two groups?
questions.explanation: In this scenario, researchers are comparing the mean values of a continuous variable (blood pressure) between two independent groups (medical advice group vs. lifestyle change group). The un-paired t-test (also known as the independent samples t-test) is the correct statistical method for this comparison. ANOVA (Option A) is used when comparing the means of three or more groups. The Chi-square test (Option C) is used for categorical data, such as comparing proportions of patients who reached a goal rather than the actual blood pressure values. McNemar's test (Option D) is used for paired categorical data, such as comparing results in the same group before and after an intervention. Because the study involves two distinct groups of 100 patients each and evaluates a quantitative variable, the un-paired t-test is the gold standard for determining if the observed difference between the interventions is statistically significant
questions.learning: In this scenario, researchers are comparing the mean values of a continuous variable (blood pressure) between two independent groups (medical advice group vs. lifestyle change group).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Anterior most air cells of anterior ethmoidal sinus are known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Agger nasi

Agger nasi is the anterior-most air cells of anterior ethmoid air cells. When enlarged it may cause mechanical obstruction to frontal sinus drainage.

Other options:

Option A: Bulla ethmoidalis is the largest air cell in the ethmoidal air sinus. It is situated behind the uncinate process and forms the posterior boundary of hiatus semilunaris through which the maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses drain.

The image below shows the ethmoidal bulla:

Option B: Onodi cell is formed from posterior ethmoidal air cell. The optic nerve lies in its lateral wall and can be injured while operating in the cells.

The image below shows Onodi air cell:

Option D: Haller cells are formed from either anterior or posterior ethmoid air cells. They present in relation to the floor of the orbit and roof of the maxillary sinus, enlargement may prevent drainage of the maxillary sinus.

The image below shows Haller cell:

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The procedure performed with the help of instrument given below is?
questions.explanation: The instrument shown is a specialized cannula or suction curette used for uterine aspiration, such as a Pipelle or Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) tool. This device is primarily used for endometrial sampling (Option D), allowing clinicians to obtain a tissue biopsy from the uterine lining in an office setting. This is essential for investigating postmenopausal bleeding or suspected hyperplasia. Hysterosalpingography (Option A) is a radiologic procedure using contrast media to visualize the fallopian tubes. Dilatation and curettage (D&C, Option B) is a more invasive surgical procedure involving mechanical dilation and metal curettes. Cervical sampling (Option C), like a Pap smear or colposcopic biopsy, targets the cervix using different tools like brushes or punch forceps. While MVA can be used for therapeutic evacuation, its diagnostic role is endometrial sampling. The minimally invasive nature of the pictured tool makes it the gold standard for initial endometrial evaluation
questions.learning: The instrument shown is a specialized cannula or suction curette used for uterine aspiration, such as a Pipelle or Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) tool.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A woman develops choking, hoarseness of voice, and a foreign body sensation in the throat while eating fish. Examination reveals a fish bone lodged in the pyriform fossa. Which nerve is primarily responsible for mediating this irritation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Internal branch of SLN

The correct answer is Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN).

The pyriform fossa mucosa is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve, which carries sensory fibres above the vocal cords.

Irritation here causes foreign body sensation, choking, and cough reflex.

Glossopharyngeal nerve supplies oropharynx, while RLN and external SLN are motor and do not mediate this sensory irritation.
questions.learning: Internal branch of SLN — The correct answer is Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN). The pyriform fossa mucosa is supplied by the internal laryngeal nerve, which carries sensory fibres above the vocal cords.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In the microbiology laboratory, a pathologist examines a sputum sample for suspected Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Which staining method should be used to confirm the presence of this bacterium?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is characterized by its waxy cell wall containing high levels of mycolic acids, which prevents traditional Gram staining. To visualize these organisms, an Acid-Fast stain is required. The Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain is the definitive microscopic technique used for this purpose. In this method, the bacteria appear as bright red, slightly curved rods against a blue background. Gomori Methenamine Silver (Option A) is used to detect fungal elements. Perl's Prussian Blue (Option B) is used to detect iron (hemosiderin). Masson-Fontana (Option D) is used to visualize melanin and argentaffin cells. Because the ZN stain specifically targets the "acid-fast" property of the Mycobacterium cell wall, it is the only correct microbiological tool listed for confirming TB in a sputum sample. This test remains the gold standard for rapid TB diagnosis in resource-limited settings
questions.learning: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is characterized by its waxy cell wall containing high levels of mycolic acids, which prevents traditional Gram staining. To visualize these organisms, an Acid-Fast stain is required.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are included in TRISS except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Limb ischemia

TRISS (Trauma and Injury Severity Score) is used to predict probability of survival in trauma patients by combining physiological and anatomical data.

• Components of TRISS:

• RTS (Revised Trauma Score) → physiological parameters (GCS, BP, RR)
• ISS (Injury Severity Score) → anatomical injury severity
• Age of the patient
• Mechanism of injury (blunt vs penetrating)

• Not included:

• Limb ischemia (a local clinical finding, not part of scoring)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the hormones represented by the following:
options: A - Somatostatin B - GH C - GHRH D - IGF1
A - Somatostatin B - GHRH C - GH D - IGF1
A - IGF1 B - GHRH C - GH D - Somatostatin
A - GHRH B - Somatostatin C - GH D - IGF1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A - Somatostatin B - GHRH C - GH D - IGF1

Correct answer is B because hypothalamus releases inhibitory somatostatin (A) and stimulatory GHRH (B) to regulate pituitary secretion.

The pituitary then releases growth hormone (C), which acts on the liver.

The liver produces IGF-1 (D), mediating peripheral growth effects and feedback control.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the clinical presentation of Frey's syndrome?
options: Acute painful swelling in the submandibular region, aggravated with food intake.
Loss of taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gustatory sweating

Frey's syndrome manifests as gustatory sweating and flushing while chewing food.

Frey’s syndrome (gustatory sweating/auriculotemporal syndrome) commonly develops after parotid surgery or other trauma that results in the opening of the parotid capsule. It results from damage to the autonomic innervation of the salivary gland. There is a regeneration of the parasympathetic nerve fibres that stimulate the sweat glands of the overlying skin in response to salivary stimulation or mastication. It is thought to reflect abnormal innervation of sweat glands on the face by regrowing parasympathetic secretomotor axons that would previously have innervated the parotid gland.

Clinical features: Sweating, warmth, and erythema over the region of surgical excision of the parotid gland. This is due to the autonomic stimulation of salivation by the smell/taste of food

Diagnosis: The starch iodine will aid in diagnosis. The affected area painted with iodine will turn blue on exposure to sweat.

Management:

* Prevention: Sternomastoid muscle flap, temporalis fascial flap, and insertion of an artificial membrane between the skin and the parotid bed will minimise the inappropriate regeneration of the autonomic nerve fibres

* Treatment:

*

* Antiperspirants with aluminium chloride

* Subcutaneous infiltration of purified botulinum toxin into the affected area

* Denervation by a tympanic neurectomy or auriculotemporal nerve avulsion has been advocated, but is often not curative

Other options:

Option A: Crocodile tear syndrome, or Bogard syndrome (gustatory lacrimation), is due to residual facial paralysis or faulty regeneration of the nervus intermedius of the facial nerve. It presents as unilateral lacrimation during eating and drinking.

Option B: In sialolithiasis, the patient usually presents with acute, painful swelling in the submandibular region, which is aggravated with food intake. Symptoms resolve 1-2 hours after the meal is completed. On examination, a tender and enlarged submandibular gland can be noted on bimanual examination.

Option D: Glossopharyngeal nerve is the 9th cranial nerve, and its injury causes loss of taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with a lesion involving the right lateral lemniscus presents with hearing difficulty. Which of the following is the most likely clinical finding?
options: Complete hearing loss in the right ear
Complete hearing loss in the left ear
Partial hearing loss in both ears
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Partial hearing loss in both ears

The central auditory pathway is bilaterally represented from the level of the cochlear nuclei onward:

• Cochlea → Cochlear nuclei → bilateral crossing (trapezoid body) → Superior olivary complex → Lateral lemniscus → Inferior colliculus → Medial geniculate body → Auditory cortex
• Because decussation occurs early (predominantly at the trapezoid body, with contributions continuing at multiple levels), each cochlear nucleus projects to both the ipsilateral and contralateral lateral lemniscus/superior olivary complex. This means each ear's signal is represented in both hemispheres beyond the brainstem entry point.

Clinical significance:

• Peripheral lesions (cochlea, auditory nerve, cochlear nucleus itself) → unilateral, often complete hearing loss, since these are pre-decussation and represent only one ear.
• Central lesions (lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate body, auditory cortex) → partial, bilateral hearing loss — true "cortical deafness" or complete central deafness is rare and requires bilateral lesions.

Why the other options are wrong?

• A. Complete hearing loss in the right ear, B. Complete hearing loss in the left ear: Complete unilateral deafness implies a peripheral (pre-crossing) lesion — cochlea, auditory nerve, or cochlear nucleus — not a lateral lemniscus lesion.
• D. No significant hearing deficit: A lesion at this level does produce a measurable deficit, just not complete or purely unilateral.
questions.learning: Partial hearing loss in both ears — The central auditory pathway is bilaterally represented from the level of the cochlear nuclei onward: • Cochlea → Cochlear nuclei → bilateral crossing (trapezoid body) → Superior olivary complex → Lateral lemniscus →…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with complaints of persistent cough and weight loss. He had a history of contact with multiple sexual partners. He was diagnosed as HIV positive 6 months back and is poorly adherent to his medications. The fungal culture of sputum was negative. On Gomori methamine silver staining, the cells showed darkly stained crescent-shaped cysts. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pneumocystis jerovecii

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii.

P. jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is an opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients. It usually occurs when the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/μL. Patients usually present with fever and nonproductive cough with progressive shortness of breath. It can also affect other organs like lymph nodes, spleen, and liver.

Laboratory and radiographic findings are also non-specific and show an increase in lactate dehydrogenase levels and symmetric, perihilar, and diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates, respectively. The classic radiographic appearance of symptomatic Pneumocystis pneumonia consists of diffuse bilateral symmetric interstitial infiltrates that are perihilar. CT will show diffuse ground-glass opacities. Giemsa stain, toluidine blue, methenamine silver, and calcofluor white stains demonstrate trophozoites. The cyst wall appears black with Gomori's methenamine silver stain.

Shown below is an image of the staining showing the black-stained crescent-shaped cysts resembling the crushed ping-pong balls of P. jirovecii. The stain used for staining the causative organism is Gomori’s methenamine silver stain.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole combination (commonly known as co-trimoxazole) is the treatment of choice for PCP, and it is administered for 21 days, followed by a course for secondary prophylaxis. Concomitantly, glucocorticoids should also be administered to reduce pulmonary inflammation.

Patients who are susceptible to PCP are also given co-trimoxazole as prophylaxis. For patients who are unable to tolerate co-trimoxazole, IV pentamidine is the drug of choice.

Prophylaxis is indicated for other opportunistic infections like Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection if CD4 counts fall below 50 cells/µL; Coccidioides, if CD count is <250/µL; and Cryptococcus, when the CD count is <100/µL.

Other options:

Option A: Paracoccidioides brasiliensis causes paracoccidioidomycosis, which usually presents with ulcerations in the oral and nasal mucosa, lymphadenopathy, and pulmonary lesions, but it does not form crescent-shaped cysts.

Option B: Histoplasma capsulatum causes histoplasmosis and may be associated with similar symptoms as Pneumocystis jirovecii, but it does not show crescent-shaped cysts on Gomori methenamine silver staining.

Option C: Coccidioides immitis causes coccidioidomycosis, which is characterized by respiratory symptoms, skin lesions, and joint pain. It also does not show crescent-shaped cysts on Gomori methenamine silver staining.
questions.learning: Pneumocystis jerovecii — The given clinical vignette is suggestive of pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii. P. jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is an opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the cause of death in smoke inhalation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anemic hypoxia

Victims of smoke inhalation are affected by carbon monoxide poisoning. In carbon monoxide poisoning, the cause of death is anemic hypoxia.

Carbon monoxide has a higher affinity to hemoglobin compared to oxygen and hence the amount of hemoglobin available for oxygen transport is markedly reduced. It displaces oxygen from its combination with hemoglobin and forms a relatively stable compound known as carboxyhemoglobin. It thus reduces the oxygen content of the blood, and hence, that of the tissues. It acts as a chemical asphyxiant and produces death due to anemic anoxia.

It is important to note that in the case of anemic hypoxia, O2 content is low but dissolved O2 is within normal limits so it does not stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors.

Note: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes both anemic (due to CO-Hb) and histotoxic (due to inhibition of cytochrome C oxidase) hypoxia. But the main cause of death is due to anemic hypoxia.

Option A - Histotoxic hypoxia- The most common example is cyanide poisoning. Cyanide inhibits important enzymes in the oxidative phosphorylation process, which is essential to the survival of our cells. Additional oxygen supplementation will not be able to overcome this inhibition, so it will have limited benefit. Hyperbaric oxygen may be helpful to some extent.

Option B - Stagnant hypoxia refers to ischemic hypoxia that results from inadequate circulation due to conditions such as heart failure and hypoxia in the setting of shock. In such conditions, administering intravenous fluids can improve the patient's condition because it is the circulation that is affected. If the shock is prolonged it can result in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which can be treated with positive pressure ventilation and not simply by increasing oxygen administration.
questions.learning: Anemic hypoxia Victims of smoke inhalation are affected by carbon monoxide poisoning. In carbon monoxide poisoning, the cause of death is anemic hypoxia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In a patient with liver cirrhosis who has esophageal varices, what is the most common cause of death?
questions.explanation: In patients with advanced liver cirrhosis and portal hypertension, esophageal varices (dilated submucosal veins) are prone to sudden and catastrophic rupture. The primary cause of mortality following such a rupture is acute, massive gastrointestinal hemorrhage leading to hypovolemic shock. The rapid loss of a large volume of blood results in inadequate tissue perfusion and multi-organ failure. Cardiogenic shock (Option B) results from heart failure, not blood loss. Obstructive shock (Option C) occurs due to physical blockage of blood flow (e.g., pulmonary embolism). Distributive shock (Option D) is seen in sepsis or anaphylaxis where there is widespread vasodilation. While cirrhotic patients may eventually develop other complications, the hyper-acute lethal event associated with variceal bleeding is definitively the volume depletion of hypovolemic shock. Immediate management involves airway protection, volume resuscitation, and urgent endoscopic intervention to ligate the bleeding vessels
questions.learning: In patients with advanced liver cirrhosis and portal hypertension, esophageal varices (dilated submucosal veins) are prone to sudden and catastrophic rupture.

This facilitates easy removal and allows the user to ensure that the IUD remains in the uterus.

It functions mainly by causing an inflammatory response within the uterus that impair the viability of the sperms and reduce its chances of fertilization. The same response also makes it difficult for blastocyst implantation.
