questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During post-mortem examination of a person who died due to starvation, which finding is most likely to be observed?
questions.explanation: Starvation leads to a generalized atrophy of almost all internal organs as the body consumes its own tissues for energy. However, a characteristic and somewhat paradoxical finding in chronic starvation is a distended gallbladder. This occurs because there is no ingestion of food (especially fats) to trigger the release of cholecystokinin, which normally causes the gallbladder to contract and empty. Consequently, bile accumulates and thickens within the organ. Enlarged liver (Option B) is incorrect; the liver actually shrinks significantly, although it may appear fatty. Expanded lungs (Option C) and a hypertrophied heart (Option D) are not features of starvation; the heart, like other muscles, undergoes brown atrophy and decreases in size. Starvation victims also show a complete loss of subcutaneous fat (Omentum appears like a "lacy veil") and a sunken abdomen (scaphoid). The distended gallbladder is a classic forensic indicator used to support a diagnosis of death by starvation
questions.learning: Starvation leads to a generalized atrophy of almost all internal organs as the body consumes its own tissues for energy. However, a characteristic and somewhat paradoxical finding in chronic starvation is a distended gallbladder.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct sequence of vaginal discharge during puerperium?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lochia rubra>Lochia serosa>Lochia alba

The correct sequence of vaginal discharge during puerperium- Lochia rubra>Lochia serosa>Lochia alba.

Lochia is the vaginal discharge for the first fortnight during puerperium that originates from the uterine body, cervix, and vagina.

Depending upon the variation of the color of the discharge, it is named:

(1) Lochia rubra- Seen in 1–4 days after delivery. The color of the discharge is red. It consists of blood, shreds of fetal membranes and decidua, vernix caseosa, lanugo, and meconium.

(2) Lochia serosa- Seen during 5-9 days. The color is yellowish or pink or pale brownish. It consists mainly of leukocytes, wound exudate, mucus from the cervix, and micro-organisms (anaerobic streptococci and staphylococci). The presence of bacteria is not pathognomonic unless associated with clinical signs of sepsis.

(3) Lochia alba- Seen during 10–15 days. The color of the discharge is pale white. Lochia alba contains plenty of decidual cells, leukocytes, mucus, cholesterin crystals, fatty and granular epithelial cells, and microorganisms.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following types of cataract would be present in a patient after a blunt trauma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rosette cataract

A rosette cataract typically follows closed globe injuries (blunt trauma).

In blunt trauma, there may be minute ruptures in the lens capsule resulting in an influx of aqueous humor, leading to hydration and subsequent opacification of the lens. Commonly there is posterior subcapsular opacification in a flower shape along the posterior sutures. Hence it is called rosette cataract.

Iridodialysis occurs due to dehiscence of the iris from the ciliary body at its root. The pupil becomes D-shaped.

The following image shows a rosette cataract.

Apart from this, blunt trauma can cause a ring-shaped anterior subcapsular opacity underneath the Vossius ring.

Other options:

(a) Sunflower cataract: Sunflower cataract is associated with Wilson's disease, a genetic disorder that leads to copper accumulation in the body. It is not related to blunt trauma.

(c) Christmas tree cataract: Christmas tree cataract is often seen in cases of myotonic dystrophy, a genetic neuromuscular disorder. It is not related to blunt trauma.

(d) Sparkle cataract: It does not correspond to a well-defined category of cataract associated with blunt trauma or any other specific condition.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A midwife is examining a pregnant woman in labour when she noticed that the cord is prolapsed. What should be the next immediate step of management?
options: Gently replace the cord inside the vagina
Inform the doctor and shift to OT
Do vaginal examination and find the fetal presentation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Put her in Trendelenberg position

In this scenario the midwife should put the pregnant women in a Trendelenburg position or in an exaggerated and elevated Sims’ position with a pillow or wedge under the hip or thigh.

Caesarean section is the recommended treatment of choice for cord prolapse. Prior to performing the procedure, several measures can be taken to alleviate cord compression. These measures involve:

• Manually elevating the fetal presenting part using two fingers or the entire hand through the vagina
• Positioning the patient in steep Trendelenburg, exaggerated Sim's position, or knee-chest position
• Filling the bladder with 500–700 cc or more of saline (known as the Vagos method)

After the diagnosis of cord prolapse is made, it is crucial not to attempt cord replacement. Such attempts are not only ineffective but also result in the inevitable rupture of the membranes, leading to cord prolapse.
questions.learning: Put her in Trendelenberg position — In this scenario the midwife should put the pregnant women in a Trendelenburg position or in an exaggerated and elevated Sims’ position with a pillow or wedge under the hip or thigh.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 56-year-old man with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is being managed in the ICU. The intensivist decides to implement Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) in his ventilatory support. Which of the following statements about PEEP is incorrect?
options: Useful in situations where PO2 is low
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreases intracranial tension (ICT)

PEEP is widely used in ARDS to improve oxygenation by preventing alveolar collapse and increasing functional residual capacity, hence it is useful when PaO₂ is low. By improving alveolar recruitment, PEEP can also enhance CO₂ elimination in some patients. However, PEEP increases intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and may impair renal perfusion and function. Importantly, raised intrathoracic pressure impedes cerebral venous drainage, leading to a rise in intracranial pressure, not a decrease.

Why others are correct:

• A. Useful in hypoxemia – True
• B. May help CO₂ clearance – True
• C. Can impair renal function – True
questions.learning: Decreases intracranial tension (ICT) PEEP is widely used in ARDS to improve oxygenation by preventing alveolar collapse and increasing functional residual capacity, hence it is useful when PaO₂ is low.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Type of mutation seen in sickle cell anemia:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Point mutation

Point mutation is seen in sickle cell anemia.

• Sickle cell anemia is caused by the mutation of a single base in the β-globin gene, where adenine is replaced with thymine in the sixth codon of the DNA sequence.
• This leads to change from GAG in the normal gene to GTG in the sickle cell gene, leading to a change in mRNA sequence from GAG to GUG.
• As a result, the mutant gene now codes for valine instead of glutamic acid.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy, identify the marked structure.
questions.explanation: In the laparoscopic image of the hepatobiliary "Calot's Triangle," the circled structure is the cystic duct. During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, achieving the "Critical View of Safety" is paramount, which involves identifying the cystic duct and the cystic artery as the only two structures entering the gallbladder. The cystic duct is the tubular structure that connects the gallbladder neck to the common hepatic duct. The cystic artery (Option A) is typically smaller and located superior and posterior to the duct within the triangle. The right hepatic artery (Option C) and the common hepatic duct (Option D) are vital structures that form the boundaries of Calot's Triangle but should not be ligated or clipped; damaging these can lead to severe bile duct injuries or liver ischemia. Correct identification of the cystic duct (Option B) ensures that the surgeon safely detaches the gallbladder while preserving the integrity of the main biliary tree and arterial supply to the liver

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Accurate assessment of renal perfusion requires an appropriate diagnostic investigation to evaluate blood flow to the kidneys. This is essential for detecting conditions such as renal artery stenosis or impaired renal function. Among the following options, which investigation is most appropriate for assessing renal perfusion?
questions.explanation: The DTPA (Diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid) scan is a nuclear medicine study and is considered the best investigation for assessing renal perfusion and glomerular filtration rate (GFR). DTPA is handled by the kidneys purely through glomerular filtration, allowing for the real-time visualization of blood flow to each kidney and the calculation of their individual functional contribution. RGU (Retrograde Urethrogram, Option B) is used to visualize the urethra. DMSA (Dimercaptosuccinic acid, Option C) is another nuclear scan, but it binds to the renal cortex and is the gold standard for identifying renal scarring and cortical defects rather than acute perfusion. CT Urogram (Option D) provides excellent anatomical detail of the entire urinary tract but is not a primary tool for quantifying physiological perfusion. DTPA scans are particularly valuable for diagnosing renal artery stenosis (often using a captopril-enhanced scan) and monitoring the function of transplanted kidneys. Accurate assessment of perfusion is essential for determining the viability of a diseased kidney
questions.learning: The DTPA (Diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid) scan is a nuclear medicine study and is considered the best investigation for assessing renal perfusion and glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the method used to assess the relative risk (RR)?
questions.explanation: Relative Risk (RR) is a measure of the strength of the association between an exposure and an outcome. It is defined as the ratio of the incidence of the disease in the exposed group to the incidence in the non-exposed group. Because a cohort study begins with exposed and non-exposed individuals and follows them forward in time to observe the development of disease, it allows for the direct calculation of incidence, and thus, the Relative Risk. A Case-control study (Option A) uses the Odds Ratio (OR) because it looks backward and cannot determine true incidence. A Randomized Controlled Trial (Option C) also allows for RR calculation but is an experimental rather than observational design. A Cross-sectional study (Option D) measures prevalence rather than incidence. Therefore, the cohort study is the classic observational method for determining RR
questions.learning: Relative Risk (RR) is a measure of the strength of the association between an exposure and an outcome. It is defined as the ratio of the incidence of the disease in the exposed group to the incidence in the non-exposed group.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the pathology in the child shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Umbilical hernia

The hernia appears which as a soft bulge at the umbilicus and covered by normal skin points towards umbilical hernia.

An umbilical defect is present at birth and normally closes as the umbilical cord stump heals within a week. If this process is delayed, herniation may develop during the neonatal period. Umbilical hernia occurs in up to 10% of infants and is more common in premature babies.

It usually appears within a few weeks after birth, often symptomless, but increases in size during crying and assumes a classic conical shape. Both sexes are equally affected, though the incidence is significantly higher in black infants compared to white. Obstruction and strangulation are extremely rare below the age of 3 years.

Treatment of Umbilical Hernia in Children

* Conservative management is preferred for children under 2 years of age when the hernia is symptomless, as about 95% resolve spontaneously. Parental reassurance is essential during this period.

* If the hernia persists beyond 2 years or is large and symptomatic, surgical repair is indicated.

* Surgery involves making a small curved incision below the umbilicus, defining and opening the neck of the sac, reducing the contents, excising the redundant sac, and closing the defect in the linea alba.

Other options:

Option A: In paraumbilical hernia, the hernia is beside the umbilicus & push it to one side taking a crescent shape and the defect in the median raphe is immediately adjacent to the true umbilicus.

Option B: Spigelian hernia is a type of interparietal hernia that occurs at the level of the arcuate line through the Spigelian point.

Option C: A femoral hernia passes through the femoral triangle. Femoral hernia is below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
questions.learning: Umbilical hernia — The hernia appears which as a soft bulge at the umbilicus and covered by normal skin points towards umbilical hernia. An umbilical defect is present at birth and normally closes as the umbilical cord stump heals within a week.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 76 year old elderly man presents with confusion. He is on antihypertensive medication, and on aspirin after a recent MI. He recalls a trivial fall from chair 3 weeks ago. Other neurological examination was normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subdural hemorrhage

The given clinical vignette along with the CT image showing a crescent-shaped hyperdense lesion that crosses the suture lines is indicative of chronic subdural hematoma/hemorrhage.

Subdural hemorrhage (SDH) is a collection of blood between the dura and the arachnoid layers of the meninges. Most commonly, it results from the rupture of cortical bridging veins. Non-contrast CT is the investigation of choice.

Radiographic features of subdural hemorrhages:

• Typically unilateral (85%)
• Crescent-like distribution (concavo-convex) around the periphery of the brain.
• They are not limited by sutures and can fill dural reflection
• Crescent-shaped hypodense lesion on axial CT: Chronic subdural hemorrhage
• Hyperdense collections on CT: Acute subdural hemorrhage.

CT image showing acute subdural hemorrhage

CT image showing acute on chronic subdural hemorrhage.

Other Options:

Option A: Epidural haemorrhage will be usually lens-shaped and is limited by sutures.

Option B: Subarachnoid haemorrhage will show Hyperdensity in the subarachnoid space.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which amongst the following molecules helps in the adhesion of the leucocyte to the endothelium during inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Selectins

Of the above options, selectins help in the adhesion of the leucocyte to the endothelium during inflammation.

The two major families of molecules involved in leukocyte adhesion and migration are the selectins and integrins. The initial rolling interactions are mediated by a family of proteins called selectins. These are low-affinity interactions with a fast off-rate, and they are easily disrupted by the flowing blood.

There are three types of selectins:

* L-selectin on leukocytes - CD62L

* E-selectin on endothelium - CD62E

* P-selectin in platelets - CD62P

The expression of selectins and their ligands is regulated by cytokines produced in response to infection and injury.

The recruitment of leukocytes to the site of inflammation is a multi-step process, that is mediated by adhesion molecules and cytokines called chemokines. This process can be divided into sequential phases:

* In the lumen: margination, rolling and adhesion to the endothelium occurs.

* Migration of the leukocytes across the endothelium and vessel wall

* Migration in the tissues towards a chemotactic stimulus.

The process of leukocyte recruitment is as follows:

* Margination: Because of dilation of the inflamed postcapillary venues, there is stasis of blood flow and hence more leukocytes assume a peripheral position along the endothelial surface; this process of leukocyte redistribution is called margination.

* Rolling: the slowed leukocytes then sense the signals from the endothelium and start rolling on the vessel wall.

* Cytokine-mediated integrin activation: the attachment of leukocytes to the endothelial cells requires adhesion molecules that are activated by cytokines. The major families of proteins involved in adhesion and migration are selectins and integrins and their ligands.

* Adhesions: the weak rolling interactions slow down the leukocytes and allow them to bind more firmly to the endothelium. Chemokines that were produced at the site of injury bind to the endothelial cell proteoglycans. These chemokines then bind to the rolling leukocytes and activate them. This is turn converts the ligands for β1 and β2 integrins, VLA-4 and LFA-1 present on the leukocytes to a high-affinity state.

* This combination of cytokine-induced expression of integrin ligands on the endothelium and increased integrin affinity on the leukocytes leads to firm adhesion of leukocytes to the endothelium at the site of inflammation.

* Leukocyte migration: this is the movement of leukocytes through intact endothelium, called transmigration or diapedesis. This occurs in postcapillary venules. This migration occurs through the inter endothelial gap towards the chemical concentration gradient created by the chemokines at the site of injury. This occurs with the help of adhesion molecules present in the intercellular junctions such as Platelet Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecule (PECAM-1) or CD31.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Tall and tented T waves, wide QRS, and absent P wave are features of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyperkalemia

Hyperkalemia produces a sequence of changes usually beginning with narrowing and peaking (tenting) of the T waves. Further elevation of extracellular K+ leads to:

* AV conduction disturbances.

* Diminution in P-wave amplitude.

* Widening of the QRS interval.

The ECG changes that can be seen in hyperkalemia depend on the extent of hyperkalemia.

4

Severe hyperkalemia eventually causes cardiac arrest with a slow sinusoidal type of mechanism("sine-wave" pattern) followed by asystole.

The most common cause of hyperkalemia is kidney failure. Drugs that cause hyperkalemia include angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics.

Treatment of hyperkalemia involves the following

* Administer intravenous calcium gluconate which raises the threshold and reduces excitability. It is cardioprotective

* Administer regular insulin with dextrose. The insulin will reduce the serum potassium concentration by causing an intracellular shift. The dextrose will counteract the hypoglycemic effects of insulin.

* Remove potassium with calcium-based resins, diuretics, or hemodialysis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An elderly woman reports difficulty in buttoning her shirt and increased clumsiness in performing daily activities. On examination, the clinician asked her to make an 'O' using her thumb and index finger, which she was unable to do. Which of the following muscles is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flexor pollicis longus

Inability to make an “O” sign indicates weakness of flexion at the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, which is the primary action of flexor pollicis longus.

This muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve (median nerve branch), and its paralysis produces the classic positive pinch sign.

Opponens pollicis and abductor pollicis brevis mediate opposition and abduction, while palmar interossei act on digits, not the thumb IP joint.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A gentleman of 60 years presented with a brawny swelling of the submandibular region with inflammatory oedema of mouth and putrid halitosis. Most likely he is suffering from:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ludwig’s angina

Ludwig’s angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis involving the bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, most commonly arising from an infected mandibular second or third molar tooth. It is a surgical emergency because of the risk of airway obstruction.

Why not other options?

• A. Tubercular adenitis: Presents as chronic, painless cervical lymph node enlargement, often with matted nodes and cold abscesses, not acute brawny swelling.
• B. Chronic lymphadenitis: Causes chronic lymph node enlargement without diffuse floor-of-mouth cellulitis or putrid halitosis.
• C. Acute lymphadenitis: Produces tender enlarged lymph nodes but does not cause the characteristic brawny submandibular swelling with floor-of-mouth edema.
questions.learning: Ludwig’s angina Ludwig’s angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis involving the bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, most commonly arising from an infected mandibular second or third molar tooth.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which of the following diagnostic markers is/are incorrectly paired?

1. Beta glucocerebrosidase
Von Gierke disease

2. Lipase
Acute pancreatitis

3. Ceruloplasmin
Hepatolenticular degeneration

4. High LDH1:LDH2 ratio
Myocardial infarction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 only

Beta glucocerebrosidase deficiency is seen in Gaucher's disease. It is an inborn error of metabolism due to the deficiency of the enzyme β-glucocerebrosidase (β-glucosidase) that leads to the accumulation of glucocerebroside in the lysosomes of cells.

• It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder. It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.
• The clinical features result from the accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, bone marrow, bone, and other tissues.
• There are 3 clinical subtypes, delineated by the difference of neurologic manifestations: type 1, or the adult, non-neuronopathic form; type 2, the infantile or acute neuronopathic form; and type 3, the juvenile or subacute neuronopathic form
• Typical clinical features include delayed puberty, painless hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, liver cirrhosis, hypersplenism and pancytopenia, bleeding tendencies, bone pain due to avascular necrosis, osteoporosis, and pathological fractures.
• Neurological symptoms such as developmental delay, hypertonia, strabismus, and supranuclear gaze palsy (seen in type 3).
• Bone marrow examination usually reveals the presence of Gaucher cells having a characteristic wrinkled-paper appearance.
• Enzyme replacement therapy for Gaucher's disease includes imiglucerase, velaglucerase alfa, taliglucerase alfa, and eliglustat.

Von Gierke disease occurs due to deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme in the liver, kidney, and intestinal mucosa. Patients present commonly by 3-4 months of age with hypoglycemia (leading to seizures), lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly. Affected children often have a doll-like face with fat cheeks, relatively thin extremities, short stature, and a protuberant abdomen due to massive hepatomegaly. The kidneys are also enlarged, whereas spleen and heart are not involved. Laboratory findings include hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.

Elevated serum lipase and serum amylase levels are associated with acute pancreatitis. Serum amylase levels do not correlate with the severity of pancreatitis and lack specificity whereas serum lipase is a more specific marker.

Low serum ceruloplasmin level is suggestive of hepatolenticular degeneration seen in Wilson's disease. However, it should not be used for definitive diagnosis as levels are normal in 10% of the affected patients and reduced in 20% of carriers. The diagnosis of Wilson's disease is based on the following:

• Increased 24-hour urinary excretion of copper (screening test)
• Decrease in serum ceruloplasmin
• Kayser–Fleischer rings under slit lamp
• Genetic testing for mutations in ATP7B gene
• Liver biopsy with quantitative copper assay (>200 μg/g dry weight of liver) is the gold standard investigation.

A higher level of LDH1 than LDH 2 in the blood is suggestive of myocardial infarction. Under normal conditions, LDH 2 is predominantly present in the blood and LDH 1 is predominantly present in the heart. When cardiac tissue is damaged LDH 1 is released into the bloodstream resulting in a high LDH1:LDH2 ratio known as the flipped LDH ratio (LDH1 > LDH2). LDH is a tetrameric enzyme with 4 subunits. It has four subunits with two isoforms: H isoform (Heart) and M isoform (Muscle)

• LDH-1: Heart
• LDH-2: Blood
• LDH-3: Brain, kidney, lungs, spleen, pancreas
• LDH-4: Liver and skeletal muscle
• LDH-5: Liver and skeletal muscle

questions.text: To be effective, the size of the openings in the mosquito net should not exceed:

Correct answer: A. 0.0475 inch in diameter

For a mosquito net to effectively prevent mosquito entry, the mesh openings should not exceed approximately 0.0475 inch (≈1.2 mm) in diameter.

• (c) 0.0475 cm — Incorrect: This equals 0.475 mm, which is smaller than the standard value.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman develops progressive swelling and pain of her thigh after a trivial bump against a table. Examination reveals a large expanding hematoma and multiple ecchymoses over the trunk and extremities. Laboratory studies show: • Hemoglobin: 12.5 g/dL • Platelet count: 240,000/mm³ • PT: Normal • aPTT: Prolonged She has no personal or family history of bleeding disorders. Which of the following best explains this patient's bleeding tendency?
options: Development of an acquired coagulation factor inhibitor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Development of an acquired coagulation factor inhibitor

This patient has acquired hemophilia A, caused by autoantibodies against factor VIII.

Typical findings include:

• Large spontaneous hematomas
• Normal platelet count
• Normal PT with isolated prolonged aPTT
• No family history of bleeding
• Adult onset

These antibodies neutralize factor VIII, producing an intrinsic pathway defect.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Reduced clotting factor synthesis: Liver disease or vitamin K deficiency usually prolongs PT.
• C. Endothelial dysfunction: Causes thrombosis rather than isolated prolonged aPTT.
• D. DIC: Causes thrombocytopenia with prolonged PT and aPTT.

High-yield pearl:

• Adult-onset bleeding with isolated prolonged aPTT and no family history strongly suggests an acquired factor VIII inhibitor.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During the court proceedings, the defense lawyer asks a leading question, which the prosecutor appeals against. The judge grants the appeal. Leading questions are not allowed in all of the following except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cross examination

Leading questions are not allowed in all of the given options except cross-examination, i.e leading questions are allowed during cross-examination.

As per section 141 of the Indian Evidence Act, a leading question is one which is suggestive of the answer that is desired or one which includes a fact and leads to the admitting of a conclusive answer, such as yes or no.

Cross-examination is one wherein the witness is questioned by the opposite party's lawyer, i.e the lawyer for the accused or the defense lawyer. It is undertaken with the objective to demonstrate favorable facts to their case, to test the accuracy of the witness statements, to unearth new or old facts, and to discredit the witness.

The sequence of examination while recording evidence is as follows:

1. Examination-in-Chief/direct examination by the party that summoned the witness to elicit all the facts from the witness. Leading questions are not allowed (option C). The only exception is if the judge is satisfied that the witness is hostile.
2. Cross-examination is done by the defence lawyer.
3. Re-examination is done by the party that summoned the witness to correct or clarify or detail the statements made by the witness during cross-examination. Leading questions are not allowed (option A).

Other options:

Option D: A dying declaration is an oral or written statement made by a person who is dying. The doctor should certify that the person is conscious and with normal mental faculties before the declaration is recorded. It is recorded by the executive magistrate, or a doctor in the presence of two witnesses, if there is no time for the magistrate to come. Leading questions should not be asked.
questions.learning: Cross examination Leading questions are not allowed in all of the given options except cross-examination, i.e leading questions are allowed during cross-examination.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Distributive shock is described by which of the following patterns of cardiovascular responses? 1. Vasodilatation 2. Reduced peripheral vascular resistance 3. Inadequate ‘afterload’ 4. Low cardiac output Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Why is D correct?

• 1. Vasodilatation ✓

• The hallmark of distributive shock is generalized peripheral vasodilatation due to inflammatory mediators or loss of sympathetic tone.

• 2. Reduced peripheral vascular resistance ✓

• Vasodilatation causes a marked decrease in systemic vascular resistance (SVR), leading to hypotension.

• 3. Inadequate ‘afterload’ ✓

• Because SVR is reduced, the afterload decreases, making it difficult to maintain adequate arterial pressure despite preserved cardiac function.

• 4. Low cardiac output ✗

• Early distributive shock usually has a normal or increased cardiac output due to compensatory tachycardia and reduced afterload. Cardiac output may decrease only in the late stages.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 32-year-old male presents to OPD with eruptive xanthomas and a deranged lipid profile showing high TAG and VLDL; however, the cholesterol level was normal. The plasma sample was lipemic secondary to raised chylomicron levels. Which of the following points towards the metabolic defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency

In the given clinical vignette, the most probable diagnosis is type I hyperlipoproteinemia, which is caused by lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

Type I Hyperlipoproteinemia: Deficiency in lipoprotein lipase (LPL) leads to hyperchylomicronemia (Type I Hyperlipoproteinemia). This condition results from defects in LPL or apo C-II, causing elevated levels of chylomicrons and VLDL, with decreased levels of LDL and HDL. Patients often develop eruptive xanthomas but are not at risk for coronary artery disease. However, they are at an increased risk of acute pancreatitis due to extremely high triglyceride levels, which can also cause a milky appearance in the plasma.

Type IIa Hyperlipoproteinemia: Defective LDL receptor points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolaemia (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia). This defect causes a decrease in the uptake of LDL and cholesterol. As a result, the blood levels of both LDL and cholesterol are elevated. Such patients are at increased risk of developing atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.

Type III Hyperlipoproteinemia: It is also known as broad β-disease, remnant removal disease, or familial dysbetalipoproteinemia. Type III hyperlipoproteinemia is caused by a defective ApoE that mediates the removal of lipoprotein remnants. Clinical features include hypercholesterolaemia, xanthomas, and atherosclerosis. There is an increase in remnant chylomicrons, remnant VLDL (i.e., intermediate-density lipoprotein), cholesterol, and triglyceride levels. Fibrates are effective in treating patients with type III hyperlipoproteinaemia.

Type IV Hyperlipoproteinemia: It is also known as familial hypertriacylglycerolemia. It is caused by overproduction of VLDL. Cholesterol levels rise with the VLDL concentration  , and it is commonly associated with coronary heart disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, alcoholism, and administration of progestational hormones.
